days.title: Spring Flowers, part 1: daffodils and wind-flowers
days.challenge: Compare two flowers part by part.
days.focus: Description by contrast: leaves, flower shape, and how each plant responds to weather.
days.context: In England, wild daffodils and wood-anemones bloom in early spring. “Lent lilies” is a local name for daffodils. A bulb is an underground food store, like an onion.

excerpt.locator: Book I, Spring Flowers, printed pages 14–15, paragraphs 1–4; begins “We are always glad when April comes. Then we can …” and ends “… shuts up in a tight bud, till sunshine comes again.”.

blocks.text: We are always glad when April comes. Then we can find many flowers on our way to school. Even in February there are snowdrops in the orchard, and Peter knows where he can sometimes find a primrose or violet in flower.
But we cannot get a good bunch till April. Before that the plants are busy growing their leaves.

The first bright flowers we find are the daffodils in the fields, and the anemones in the woods. We call the daffodils "Lent lilies" and we put them in the church at Easter. They have very long, narrow leaves which come straight out of the ground. Each flower hangs on its own tall stalk. It has a deep yellow tube in the middle, with a crown of pale yellow leaves round it. If you dig up a daffodil plant you will find that it has a bulb like an onion. Paul says this is why it blooms so early. It stores up food in the bulb in the autumn. Then it uses this food in January to make its leaves and flowers.

The wood-anemone is Peggy's favourite flower. It is called the "wind-flower" because it nods so prettily in the wind. Its soft pink and white flower stands high up on a long stalk, which has three feathery green leaves half-way down. When the sun shines, it is a little pink and white cup, but when the clouds gather and the rain falls, it shuts up in a tight bud, till sunshine comes again.

questions.prompt: Why are the children glad when April comes?
facilitatorNotes: Many more flowers appear on their way to school; before April there are only a few. Accept either part of the contrast.
evidence: We are always glad when April comes.

questions.prompt: What does the wood-anemone do when the clouds gather and rain falls?
facilitatorNotes: It shuts into a tight bud until the sun comes back. Contrast it with the open pink and white cup in sunshine.
evidence: it shuts up in a tight bud, till sunshine comes again.

questions.prompt: Paul says the daffodil blooms early because of its bulb. How does he explain it?
facilitatorNotes: It stores food in the bulb in autumn and uses it in January to make leaves and flowers. This is Paul’s explanation; let the child retell it.
evidence: It stores up food in the bulb in the autumn.

days.title: Spring Flowers, part 2: where the honey hides
days.challenge: Follow a description that explains how a plant works.
days.focus: Close looking explains how leaves carry water and where bees find honey.
days.context: Primroses and violets are small wild spring flowers. The flower’s “honey” is nectar, which bees gather. Children at that time tasted leaves and flowers; many wild plants, including the anemone in this lesson, are poisonous.
days.contentNote: Peggy bites a poisonous leaf, and the children suck flower parts to taste the nectar.

excerpt.locator: Book I, Spring Flowers, printed pages 15–17, paragraphs 5–10 (end of lesson); begins “Peggy once bit one of the leaves of the anemone. …” and ends “… can now find plenty of honey to fill their hives.”.

blocks.text: Peggy once bit one of the leaves of the anemone. It burnt her tongue and tasted very bitter. Then Paul told us that the plant is poisonous. This is one reason why there are so many anemones in the wood. Animals will not eat the leaves, but leave them alone to grow.
The anemone has not got a bulb. It has a thick brown stem under the ground in which it stores its food.

Before the daffodils and anemones are over, the primroses and violets cover the banks. It is pretty to watch the primrose plant on a wet morning. The leaves are not smooth. They have hills and valleys all along them. The water runs so cleverly down the valleys of the leaf. These guide it down to the roots, so that the plant can drink.

How busy, too, the bees and flies are. They settle first on one primrose, then on another. We know what they find there. If you pull off the yellow crown of the primrose, and suck the end of the tube, you will taste something sweet. This is the honey that the bees come to find. And besides the honey they carry off some yellow dust from flower to flower. Paul says that this is good for the flowers, as we shall learn some day.

The honey in the violets is not so easy to find. But we have found it. When a violet looks straight at you, it shows five purple leaves and a little yellow beak in the middle. But if you look behind, you will find a small long bag, like the finger of a glove. We have often pulled this off and sucked it. It is full of honey. When the bee sits on the flower, and thrusts her head into the yellow beak in the middle, she sips out the honey with her tongue from the bag or spur behind the flower.
With primroses and violets and blue-bells the bees can now find plenty of honey to fill their hives.

questions.prompt: What happened when Peggy bit an anemone leaf, and what did Paul tell her?
facilitatorNotes: It burned her tongue and tasted bitter; Paul said the plant is poisonous, which is why animals leave it alone.
evidence: It burnt her tongue and tasted very bitter.

questions.prompt: How do the bumpy primrose leaves help the plant drink?
facilitatorNotes: Their hills and valleys guide rainwater down to the roots. A hand cupped into a channel can show the idea.
evidence: These guide it down to the roots

questions.prompt: Where is the violet’s honey, and how does a bee reach it?
facilitatorNotes: In a small bag or spur behind the flower; the bee pushes her head into the yellow beak and sips with her tongue.
evidence: she sips out the honey with her tongue from the bag or spur behind the flower.

days.title: A Cherry
days.challenge: Use the title and two physical clues to solve a playful riddle.
days.focus: A familiar fruit is hidden under a person-like description.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from The Real Mother Goose aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “A CHERRY”; opening “As I went through the garden gap,”; ending “If you'll tell me this riddle, I'll give you a groat.”.

blocks.text:
As I went through the garden gap,
Who should I meet but Dick Red-cap!
A stick in his hand, a stone in his throat,--
If you'll tell me this riddle, I'll give you a groat.

questions.prompt: Where does the speaker meet the mysterious Dick Red-cap?
facilitatorNotes: At or through the garden gap. The garden setting helps prepare a fruit answer.
evidence: As I went through the garden gap,

questions.prompt: If the answer is a cherry, what might its stick and stone really be?
facilitatorNotes: The stick can be its stalk and the stone its pit. Present this as solving the figurative clues, not a person swallowing a stone.
evidence: A stick in his hand, a stone in his throat,

questions.prompt: What reward does the speaker promise for solving the riddle?
facilitatorNotes: A groat, an old coin. The promise makes the rhyme sound like a little guessing game between speaker and listener.
evidence: I'll give you a groat.

days.title: The Field Daisy
days.challenge: Identify a flower through its imagined self-description.
days.focus: A daisy speaks about its shape and asks for gentle footsteps.
days.context: The title tells us the speaker is a daisy. “O’er” means over.

excerpt.locator: The Field Daisy; begins “I’m a pretty little thing,”; ends ““Surly Winter’s gone away.””.

blocks.text:
I’m a pretty little thing,
Always coming with the spring;
In the meadows green I’m found,
Peeping just above the ground.
And my stalk is cover’d flat,
With a white and yellow hat.

Little lady, when you pass
Lightly o’er the tender grass,
Skip about, but do not tread
On my meek and healthy head.
For I always seem to say,
“Surly Winter’s gone away.”

questions.prompt: What is the daisy’s white-and-yellow “hat”?
facilitatorNotes: Its flower head has white petals and a yellow center; a drawing can express this.
evidence: With a white and yellow hat.

questions.prompt: What does the daisy ask the passing child not to do?
facilitatorNotes: It asks not to be stepped on.
evidence: Skip about, but do not tread

questions.prompt: Why might seeing this daisy suggest that winter is over?
facilitatorNotes: It says it comes with spring; the closing words echo that beginning.
evidence: Always coming with the spring;

days.title: Chorus of Fairies
days.challenge: Follow several settings while hearing recurring words and sound patterns.
days.focus: Repeated summer-day lines give a landscape poem a singing chorus.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “CHORUS OF FAIRIES.”; opening “GOLDEN, golden,”; ending “All the livelong Summer day!”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 23.

blocks.text:
GOLDEN, golden,
Light unfolding,
Busily, merrily, work and play,
In flowery meadows,
And forest shadows,
All the length of a Summer day!
All the length of a Summer day!

Sprightly, lightly,
Sing we rightly,
Moments brightly hurry away;
Fruit-tree blossoms,
And roses' bosoms,--
Clear blue sky of a Summer day!
Dear blue sky of a Summer day!

Springlets, brooklets,
Greeny nooklets,
Hill and Valley, and salt sea-spray,
Comrade rovers,
Fairy lovers,--
All the length of a Summer day
All the livelong Summer day!

questions.prompt: Where do the fairies work and play? Name two places.
facilitatorNotes: Flowery meadows and forest shadows are stated; hill, valley and sea-spray appear later. Accept any two actual locations.
evidence:
In flowery meadows,
          And forest shadows,

questions.prompt: Which words make their movement sound light and lively?
facilitatorNotes: Sprightly and lightly, or busily and merrily, work. Echo a chosen pair and ask what sort of movement it suggests.
evidence: Sprightly, lightly,

questions.prompt: What stretch of time keeps returning at the ends of the verses?
facilitatorNotes: The length of a summer day. The repeated phrase holds the changing scenes together like a song refrain.
evidence: All the length of a Summer day!

days.title: Lawkamercyme: a puzzling recognition test
days.challenge: Follow how one mistaken test leads to an impossible conclusion.
days.focus: A refrain turns confusion about appearance into a comic identity puzzle.
days.context: This old rhyme uses Lawkamercyme as an exclamation, rather like goodness me. A pedlar sells goods while traveling; petticoats are skirts worn beneath other clothing.
days.contentNote: A stranger damages the sleeping woman’s clothing. Treat that as unkind conduct, while exploring the rhyme’s comic confusion.

excerpt.locator: Lawkamercyme, 1922 edition pp. 331–332, complete; begins “There was an old woman, as I've heard tell, / …” and ends “… began to cry-- / "Lawkamercyme! this is none of I!"”.

blocks.text:
There was an old woman, as I've heard tell,
She went to the market her eggs for to sell;
She went to the market, all on a market-day,
And she fell asleep on the king's highway.

There came by a pedlar, whose name it was Stout,
He cut all her petticoats all round about;
He cut her petticoats up to the knees,
Which made the old woman to shiver and freeze.

When this old woman first did awake,
She 'gan to shiver, she 'gan to shake;
She 'gan to wonder, she 'gan to cry--
"Lawkamercyme! this is none of I!"

"But if it be I, as I do hope it be,
I've a little dog at home, and sure he'll know me;
If it be I, he'll wag his little tail,
And if it be not I, then he'll bark and wail."

Home went the old woman, all in the dark;
Up got the little dog, and he began to bark,
He began to bark, and she began to cry--
"Lawkamercyme! this is none of I!"

questions.prompt: What does the woman plan to sell, and what interrupts her trip?
facilitatorNotes: She takes eggs to market but falls asleep on the road. Establish the setting before discussing the strange change.
evidence: her eggs for to sell

questions.prompt: What has changed when she wakes?
facilitatorNotes: Someone has cut her skirts shorter, and she is cold. Her clothes have changed; she remains the same person.
evidence: He cut her petticoats up to the knees

questions.prompt: Why is a barking dog a poor way to decide who she is?
facilitatorNotes: Dogs can bark for many reasons, especially at night. The rhyme gives her conclusion, but listeners can question the test that led to it.
evidence: If it be I, he'll wag his little tail

days.title: Little Green Hummer
days.challenge: Picture rapid movement using a chain of short phrases.
days.focus: Jewel colors and quick rhythms describe a hummingbird.
days.context: This is the hummingbird poem in “Garden Songs.” Some phrases are imaginative exaggeration: a real bird weighs more than one feather.

excerpt.locator:
Little Green Hummer; begins “LITTLE green Hummer
Was born in the summer;”; ends “This sweet little Hummer
That came with the summer.”.

blocks.text:
LITTLE green Hummer
Was born in the summer;
His coat was as bright
As the emerald's light.
Short was his song,
Though his bill it was long;
His weight altogether
Not more than a feather.
From dipping his head
In the sunset red,
And gilding his side
In its fiery tide,
He gleamed like a jewel,
And darted around,
'Twixt sunlight and starlight,
Ne'er touching the ground.
Now over a blossom,
Now under, now in it;
Here, there, and everywhere,
All in a minute.
Ah! never he cared
Who wondered and stared,--
His life was completeness
Of pleasure and sweetness;
He revelled in lightness,
In fleetness and brightness,
This sweet little Hummer
That came with the summer.

questions.prompt: What color is Hummer’s coat, and what shining thing does it resemble?
facilitatorNotes: Green and emerald are paired; jewel is another later comparison.
evidence: As the emerald's light.

questions.prompt: What words show Hummer moving around a blossom?
facilitatorNotes: Over, under, and in make a changing route the child can trace.
evidence:
Now over a blossom,
Now under, now in it;

questions.prompt: Does the poem make Hummer seem slow or quick?
facilitatorNotes: “All in a minute” and “darted” support quick; reread the short phrases at a lively but clear pace.
evidence:
Here, there, and everywhere,
All in a minute.

days.title: Amy Margaret
days.challenge: Move from literal age and hair to comparisons that describe character.
days.focus: Flower and jewel images express affection for a named child.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “AMY MARGARET.”; opening “AMY MARGARET'S five years old,”; ending “Be ever,--Amy Margaret!”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 26.

blocks.text:
AMY MARGARET'S five years old,
Amy Margaret's hair is gold,
Dearer twenty-thousand-fold
Than gold, is Amy Margaret.

"Amy" is friend, is "Margaret"
The pearl for crown or carkanet?
Or peeping daisy, Summer's pet?
Which are you, Amy Margaret?

A friend, a daisy, and a pearl;
A kindly, simple, precious girl,--
Such, howsoe'er the world may twirl,
Be ever,--Amy Margaret!

questions.prompt: How old is Amy Margaret, and what colour is her hair called?
facilitatorNotes: She is five and her hair is gold. Gold can describe a yellow hair colour here.
evidence:
AMY MARGARET'S five years old,
    Amy Margaret's hair is gold,

questions.prompt: Does the speaker say gold is more precious than Amy?
facilitatorNotes: No; Amy is described as far dearer than gold. The very large number expresses affection rather than a price.
evidence:
Dearer twenty-thousand-fold
          Than gold, is Amy Margaret.

questions.prompt: What three things is Amy compared with near the end?
facilitatorNotes: A friend, a daisy and a pearl. Let the child choose which comparison sounds kind, fresh or precious and explain; several readings fit.
evidence: A friend, a daisy, and a pearl;

days.title: My Bed Is a Boat
days.challenge: Connect details of an ordinary bed with an imagined voyage.
days.focus: An extended comparison turns falling asleep into travel.
days.context: A nurse here is a caregiver. “Embark” means begin a boat journey; “fast” at the end means secured.

blocks.text:
MY bed is a little boat;
Nurse helps me in when I embark
She girds me in my sailor's coat
And starts me in the dark.

At night, I go on board and say
Good night to all my friends on shore;
I shut my eyes and sail away
And see and hear no more.

And sometimes things to bed I take,
As prudent sailors have to do:
Perhaps a slice of wedding-cake,
Perhaps a toy or two.

All night across the dark we steer:
But when the day returns at last,
Safe in my room, beside the pier,
I find my vessel fast.

questions.prompt: What familiar object is the child imagining as a boat?
facilitatorNotes: The bed becomes the boat while the room supplies its setting.
evidence: MY bed is a little boat;

questions.prompt: What does the child take aboard for the night?
facilitatorNotes: Toys and perhaps a slice of wedding cake travel with the child.
evidence: Perhaps a toy or two.

questions.prompt: What tells you that the child is safe at the end of this voyage?
facilitatorNotes: Morning brings the child back to the room and the vessel is secured.
evidence: Safe in my room, beside the pier,

days.title: Jeremy Fisher, part 1: rain and a fishing plan
days.challenge: Infer why weather pleasant to a frog might seem unpleasant to a person.
days.focus: Human clothing and tools are imaginatively fitted to pond life.
days.context: Jeremy is a storybook frog preparing a meal for friends. A macintosh is a raincoat; goloshes are waterproof overshoes; minnows are small fish.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Mr. Jeremy Fisher, paragraphs 1–10; begins “Once upon a time there was a frog called Mr. …” and ends “… and he tied a little wriggling worm at the end.”.

blocks.text: Once upon a time there was a frog called Mr. Jeremy Fisher; he lived in a little damp house amongst the buttercups at the edge of a pond.
The water was all slippy-sloppy in the larder and in the back passage.
But Mr. Jeremy liked getting his feet wet; nobody ever scolded him, and he never caught a cold!
He was quite pleased when he looked out and saw large drops of rain, splashing in the pond--

"I will get some worms and go fishing and catch a dish of minnows for my dinner," said Mr. Jeremy Fisher. "If I catch more than five fish, I will invite my friends Mr. Alderman Ptolemy Tortoise and Sir Isaac Newton. The Alderman, however, eats salad."
Mr. Jeremy put on a macintosh, and a pair of shiny goloshes; he took his rod and basket, and set off with enormous hops to the place where he kept his boat.
The boat was round and green, and very like the other lily-leaves. It was tied to a water-plant in the middle of the pond.
Mr. Jeremy took a reed pole, and pushed the boat out into open water. "I know a good place for minnows," said Mr. Jeremy Fisher.
Mr. Jeremy stuck his pole into the mud and fastened the boat to it.

Then he settled himself cross-legged and arranged his fishing tackle. He had the dearest little red float. His rod was a tough stalk of grass, his line was a fine long white horse-hair, and he tied a little wriggling worm at the end.

questions.prompt: Why does Jeremy enjoy his wet home?
facilitatorNotes: He likes wet feet and is comfortable in dampness. This is a fictional frog’s viewpoint, not advice about staying in wet clothes.
evidence: Mr. Jeremy liked getting his feet wet

questions.prompt: What must happen before he will invite his friends?
facilitatorNotes: He plans to invite them if he catches more than five fish. Let the child explain his plan without turning discussion into a counting test.
evidence: If I catch more than five fish, I will invite my friends

questions.prompt: What familiar pond object does his boat resemble?
facilitatorNotes: A lily leaf. Notice how a small frog can use pond materials as people use boats and rods.
evidence: very like the other lily-leaves.

days.title: Jeremy Fisher, part 2: a troublesome catch
days.challenge: Follow the difference between what Jeremy hopes for and what he catches.
days.focus: Small surprises build from a tickled toe to a prickly fish.
days.context: Jeremy has anchored his leaf-like boat and waited for fish. A stickleback is a small fish with sharp spines; rushes are tall waterside plants.
days.contentNote: A fish’s spines prick Jeremy’s fingers; no graphic injury is described.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Mr. Jeremy Fisher, paragraphs 11–23; begins “The rain trickled down his back, and for nearly an …” and ends “… put their heads out, and laughed at Mr. Jeremy Fisher.”.

blocks.text: The rain trickled down his back, and for nearly an hour he stared at the float.
"This is getting tiresome, I think I should like some lunch," said Mr. Jeremy Fisher.
He punted back again amongst the water-plants, and took some lunch out of his basket.
"I will eat a butterfly sandwich, and wait till the shower is over," said Mr. Jeremy Fisher.
A great big water-beetle came up underneath the lily leaf and tweaked the toe of one of his goloshes.
Mr. Jeremy crossed his legs up shorter, out of reach, and went on eating his sandwich.
Once or twice something moved about with a rustle and a splash amongst the rushes at the side of the pond.
"I trust that is not a rat," said Mr. Jeremy Fisher; "I think I had better get away from here."
Mr. Jeremy shoved the boat out again a little way, and dropped in the bait. There was a bite almost directly; the float gave a tremendous bobbit!
"A minnow! a minnow! I have him by the nose!" cried Mr. Jeremy Fisher, jerking up his rod.
But what a horrible surprise! Instead of a smooth fat minnow, Mr. Jeremy landed little Jack Sharp the stickleback, covered with spines!
The stickleback floundered about the boat, pricking and snapping until he was quite out of breath. Then he jumped back into the water.
And a shoal of other little fishes put their heads out, and laughed at Mr. Jeremy Fisher.

questions.prompt: What makes Jeremy stop waiting and take a break?
facilitatorNotes: He has waited nearly an hour and wants lunch. Invite the child to use the time and his spoken complaint.
evidence: This is getting tiresome, I think I should like some lunch

questions.prompt: How does Jeremy protect his toes without stopping lunch?
facilitatorNotes: He draws his legs up out of reach. Trace the beetle’s action and Jeremy’s response.
evidence: Mr. Jeremy crossed his legs up shorter, out of reach

questions.prompt: Why is the fish he catches a surprise?
facilitatorNotes: He expects a smooth minnow but catches a spiny stickleback that pricks and escapes. Accept a contrast of the two descriptions.
evidence: Instead of a smooth fat minnow, Mr. Jeremy landed little Jack Sharp the stickleback, covered with spines!

days.title: Jeremy Fisher, part 3: a different dinner
days.challenge: Connect the raincoat introduced earlier to the escape.
days.focus: A frightening reversal ends in a comic change of menu.
days.context: Jeremy has had no success fishing and is sitting in his boat. Listen for how the raincoat helps him. The animal friends’ meal is fantasy, not a recipe.
days.contentNote: Brief fantasy peril: a trout catches Jeremy, then immediately spits him out. Jeremy reaches home safely.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Mr. Jeremy Fisher, paragraphs 24–33 (end); begins “And while Mr. Jeremy sat disconsolately on the edge of …” and ends “… beautiful treat; but _I_ think it must have been nasty!”.

blocks.text: And while Mr. Jeremy sat disconsolately on the edge of his boat--sucking his sore fingers and peering down into the water--a _much_ worse thing happened; a really _frightful_ thing it would have been, if Mr. Jeremy had not been wearing a macintosh!
A great big enormous trout came up--ker-pflop-p-p-p! with a splash--and it seized Mr. Jeremy with a snap, "Ow! Ow! Ow!"--and then it turned and dived down to the bottom of the pond!
But the trout was so displeased with the taste of the macintosh, that in less than half a minute it spat him out again; and the only thing it swallowed was Mr. Jeremy's goloshes.
Mr. Jeremy bounced up to the surface of the water, like a cork and the bubbles out of a soda water bottle; and he swam with all his might to the edge of the pond.
He scrambled out on the first bank he came to, and he hopped home across the meadow with his macintosh all in tatters.
"What a mercy that was not a pike!" said Mr. Jeremy Fisher. "I have lost my rod and basket; but it does not much matter, for I am sure I should never have dared to go fishing again!"
He put some sticking plaster on his fingers, and his friends both came to dinner. He could not offer them fish, but he had something else in his larder.
Sir Isaac Newton wore his black and gold waistcoat,
And Mr. Alderman Ptolemy Tortoise brought a salad with him in a string bag.
And instead of a nice dish of minnows--they had a roasted grasshopper with lady-bird sauce; which frogs consider a beautiful treat; but _I_ think it must have been nasty!

questions.prompt: Why does the trout spit Jeremy out?
facilitatorNotes: It dislikes the taste of his raincoat. The coat becomes unexpectedly useful in a new way.
evidence: the trout was so displeased with the taste of the macintosh

questions.prompt: What does Jeremy decide about fishing after he escapes?
facilitatorNotes: He does not expect to dare go fishing again. Accept fear or relief supported by his words.
evidence: I am sure I should never have dared to go fishing again!

questions.prompt: How can the friends still have dinner without the minnows?
facilitatorNotes: Jeremy has other food and the tortoise brings salad. Notice how the narrator dislikes the menu even though the frogs enjoy it.
evidence: Mr. Alderman Ptolemy Tortoise brought a salad with him in a string bag.

days.title: Dreaming
days.challenge: Track the imagined journey into sleep and the sudden return on waking.
days.focus: A dream becomes a travelling visitor that opens an impossible world.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “DREAMING.”; opening “A STRANGE little Dream”; ending “For its end could never be found.”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 30, 31.

blocks.text:
A STRANGE little Dream
On a long star-beam
Ran down from the midnight skies,
To curly-hair'd Fred
Asleep in his bed,
With the lids on his merry blue eyes.

Under each lid
The thin Dream slid,
And spread to a picture inside,
A new World there,
Most strange and rare,
Tho' just by our garden-side.

Rivers and Rocks,
And a Treasure-Box,
And Floating in Air without wings,
And the Speaking Beast,
And a Royal Feast,
My chair beside the King's;

A Land of Flowers,
And of lofty Towers
Carved over in marble white
With living Shapes
Of Panthers and Apes
That gambol in ceaseless flight;

And a Cellar small
With its Cave in the Wall
Stretching many a mile underground!
And the Rope from the Moon!--
Fred woke too soon,
For its end could never be found.

questions.prompt: How does the little Dream reach sleeping Fred?
facilitatorNotes: It comes down a long star-beam and slips under his eyelids. Treat this as a fantasy picture, not an explanation of sleep.
evidence: On a long star-beam

questions.prompt: Choose one sight that tells you this new world can do impossible things.
facilitatorNotes: Floating without wings, a speaking beast or a rope from the moon all work. Ask the child to name the particular sight.
evidence: And Floating in Air without wings,

questions.prompt: Why is the end of the moon-rope never found?
facilitatorNotes: Fred wakes too soon. The waking cuts off the dream’s unfinished discovery.
evidence:
Fred woke too soon,
    For its end could never be found.

days.title: A house of cards
days.challenge: Notice how the same action changes from a warning into an invitation.
days.focus: Building and falling are both parts of the speaker’s play.
days.context: Court cards are the picture cards in a pack. Read both references to shaking the table.

excerpt.locator:
A house of cards; begins “A house of cards
Is neat and small”; ends “Shake the table!
That’s the fun.”.

blocks.text:
A house of cards
Is neat and small
Shake the table,
It must fall.

Find the Court cards
One by one;
Raise it, roof it,—
Now it’s done:—
Shake the table!
That’s the fun.

questions.prompt: What happens to this house if the table shakes?
facilitatorNotes: The card house falls because its balance is disturbed.
evidence: It must fall.

questions.prompt: Which words tell the builder to add the top of the house?
facilitatorNotes: “Roof it” names adding the roof.
evidence: Raise it, roof it,—

questions.prompt: Does the ending sound upset about the falling house?
facilitatorNotes: No: the speaker calls it fun and gives the shaking command enthusiastically.
evidence: That’s the fun.

days.title: I Love You, Dear
days.challenge: Compare the butterfly wish, bird wish and final real gift.
days.focus: Imagined animal forms turn affection into actions of staying close.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “I LOVE YOU, DEAR.”; opening “I LOVE you, Dear, I love you, Dear,”; ending “And my love along with this, you Dear!”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 32.

blocks.text:
I LOVE you, Dear, I love you, Dear,
You can't think how I love you, Dear!
Supposing I
Were a Butterfly,
I'd waver around and above you, Dear.

A long way off I spied you, Dear,
No bonnet or hat could hide you, Dear,
If I were a Bird,
Believe my word,
I'd sing every day beside you, Dear,

When you're away I miss you, Dear,
And now you're here I'll kiss you, Dear,
And beg you will take
This flow'r for my sake,
And my love along with this, you Dear!

questions.prompt: If the speaker became a butterfly, what would it do near the loved person?
facilitatorNotes: Waver around and above them. Invite a hand movement that follows those position words.
evidence: I'd waver around and above you, Dear.

questions.prompt: How would being a bird offer a different way to show affection?
facilitatorNotes: The bird would sing beside the person every day. Compare flying nearby with providing song.
evidence: I'd sing every day beside you, Dear,

questions.prompt: At the end, what gift carries the speaker’s love without needing to become an animal?
facilitatorNotes: A flower is offered with love. The kiss is also mentioned, but the question’s gift is the flower.
evidence: This flow'r for my sake,

days.title: Rain
days.challenge: Hold a near place and a far place in one small picture.
days.focus: Four lines expand the rain’s reach beyond the speaker.
days.context: Read slowly twice; the listener may point nearby for umbrellas and far away for ships.

excerpt.locator:
Rain; begins “THE rain is raining all around,
It falls on field and tree,”; ends “It rains on the umbrellas here,
And on the ships at sea.”.

blocks.text:
THE rain is raining all around,
It falls on field and tree,
It rains on the umbrellas here,
And on the ships at sea.

questions.prompt: What two things receive rain in the second line?
facilitatorNotes: The field and tree are both named.
evidence: It falls on field and tree,

questions.prompt: Where does rain fall far from the umbrellas?
facilitatorNotes: It also falls on ships at sea, widening the scene.
evidence: And on the ships at sea.

questions.prompt: Which words do you hear again and again? What do they make the rain seem to do?
facilitatorNotes: Rain/raining/rains return through the short poem; they can suggest ongoing rain everywhere.
evidence: THE rain is raining all around,

days.title: Miss Moppet: a trick with a hole
days.challenge: Remember the hole before it changes the ending.
days.focus: A small object becomes the cause of a surprising escape.
days.context: Listen to a complete short animal story. A duster is a cleaning cloth; a bell-pull is a hanging cord that rings a bell.
days.contentNote: Comic animal chasing and rough handling: a kitten ties a mouse in a cloth, but he escapes unharmed. Do not imitate this treatment of animals.

excerpt.locator: The Story of Miss Moppet, complete; begins “This is a Pussy called Miss Moppet, she thinks she …” and ends “… is dancing a jig on the top of the cupboard!”.

blocks.text: This is a Pussy called Miss Moppet, she thinks she has heard a mouse!
This is the Mouse peeping out behind the cupboard, and making fun of Miss Moppet. He is not afraid of a kitten.
This is Miss Moppet jumping just too late; she misses the Mouse and hits her own head.
She thinks it is a very hard cupboard!
The Mouse watches Miss Moppet from the top of the cupboard.
Miss Moppet ties up her head in a duster, and sits before the fire.
The Mouse thinks she is looking very ill. He comes sliding down the bell-pull.
Miss Moppet looks worse and worse. The Mouse comes a little nearer.
Miss Moppet holds her poor head in her paws, and looks at him through a hole in the duster. The Mouse comes _very_ close.
And then all of a sudden--Miss Moppet jumps upon the Mouse!
And because the Mouse has teased Miss Moppet--Miss Moppet thinks she will tease the Mouse; which is not at all nice of Miss Moppet.
She ties him up in the duster, and tosses it about like a ball.
But she forgot about that hole in the duster; and when she untied it--there was no Mouse!
He has wriggled out and run away; and he is dancing a jig on the top of the cupboard!

questions.prompt: What happens when Moppet first jumps at the mouse?
facilitatorNotes: She misses the mouse and hits the cupboard. Ask the child to retell the two actions in order.
evidence: she misses the Mouse and hits her own head.

questions.prompt: How does the hole help Moppet first, and help the mouse later?
facilitatorNotes: Moppet peeks through it; later the mouse escapes through the cloth. Accept pointing to the two related moments.
evidence: looks at him through a hole in the duster.

questions.prompt: Does the storyteller approve when Moppet decides to tease the mouse? How can you tell?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator says it is not nice. Invite discussion of both characters teasing without requiring a single moral.
evidence: which is not at all nice of Miss Moppet.

days.title: Seasons
days.challenge: Hold four seasonal pictures and notice the changed final attitude.
days.focus: Seasonal settings shift from outdoor wonder to winter warmth.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “SEASONS.”; opening “IN Spring-time, the Forest,”; ending “And Winter has glee.”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 34, 35.

blocks.text:
IN Spring-time, the Forest,
In Summer, the Sea,
In Autumn, the Mountains,
In Winter,--ah me!

How gay, the old branches
A-swarm with new buds,
The primrose and bluebell
Fresh-blown in the woods,
All green things unfolding,
Where merry birds sing!
I love in the Woodlands
To wander in Spring.

What joy, when the Sea-waves,
In mirth and in might,
Spread purple in shadow,
Flash white into light!
The gale fills the sail,
And the gull flies away;
In crimson and gold
Sets the long Summer Day.

O pride! on the Mountains
To leave earth below;
The great slopes of heather,
One broad purple glow;
The loud-roaring torrent
Leaps, bound after bound,
To plains of gold Autumn,
With mist creeping round

In Spring-time, the Forest,
In Summer, the Sea,
In Autumn, the Mountains,--
And Winter has glee.

questions.prompt: Which place does the opening connect with spring? What new things grow there?
facilitatorNotes: The forest, with new buds, primrose and bluebell. Accept one named plant or bud detail.
evidence:
The primrose and bluebell
      Fresh-blown in the woods,

questions.prompt: What contrast does the winter verse make between daylight and firelight?
facilitatorNotes: Daylight is short while firelight is long. Discuss the feeling of a long cosy evening, without treating fire as something a child should handle.
evidence:
The daylight is short,
      But the firelight is long;

questions.prompt: The first winter line sighs “ah me!” How is winter described at the very end?
facilitatorNotes: Winter has glee. Skating, story and song help explain the more cheerful conclusion.
evidence: And Winter has glee.

days.title: Oh, fair to see
days.challenge: Compare two views of the same kind of tree.
days.focus: Parallel stanzas make blossom and fruit equally worth admiring.
days.context: “Laden” means loaded; “fair” here means beautiful. Listen for what fills each tree.

excerpt.locator:
Oh, fair to see; begins “Oh, fair to see
Bloom-laden cherry tree,”; ends “Oh, fair to see
Fruit-laden cherry tree,
With balls of shining red
Decking a leafy head,
Oh, fair to see!”.

blocks.text:
Oh, fair to see
Bloom-laden cherry tree,
Arrayed in sunny white;
An April day’s delight,
Oh, fair to see!

Oh, fair to see
Fruit-laden cherry tree,
With balls of shining red
Decking a leafy head,
Oh, fair to see!

questions.prompt: What color fills the tree in the first stanza?
facilitatorNotes: The blossoms are imagined as sunny white clothing.
evidence: Arrayed in sunny white;

questions.prompt: What are the shining red balls in the second stanza?
facilitatorNotes: They are cherries, the fruit named at the beginning of that stanza.
evidence: Fruit-laden cherry tree,

questions.prompt: Does the speaker admire just the blossoms or both views?
facilitatorNotes: The same admiring words begin and end both stanzas.
evidence: Oh, fair to see!

days.title: The Bird
days.challenge: Follow repeated offers and refusals and infer the bird’s priorities.
days.focus: A bird prefers freedom and natural surroundings to luxurious gifts.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “THE BIRD.”; opening “"BIRDIE, Birdie, will you pet?”; ending “Good-bye, good-bye to my lady fair!"”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 41.

blocks.text:
"BIRDIE, Birdie, will you pet?
Summer-time is far away yet,
You'll have silken quilts and a velvet bed,
And a pillow of satin for your head!"

"O Birdie, Birdie, will you pet?
Diamond-stones and amber and jet
We'll string for a necklace fair and fine
To please this pretty bird of mine!"

"O thanks for diamonds, and thanks for jet,
But here is something daintier yet,--
A feather-necklace round and round,
That I wouldn't sell for a thousand pound!"

"O Birdie, Birdie, won't you pet?
We'll buy you a dish of silver fret,
A golden cup and an ivory seat,
And carpets soft beneath your feet!"

"Can running water be drunk from gold?
Can a silver dish the forest hold?
A rocking twig is the finest chair,
And the softest paths lie through the air,--
Good-bye, good-bye to my lady fair!"

questions.prompt: Where would the bird rather sleep than in the offered velvet bed?
facilitatorNotes: In the ivy wall, where it hears rain without getting wet. Its own shelter is enough for it.
evidence: I'd rather sleep in the ivy wall;

questions.prompt: What necklace does the bird already have instead of diamonds and jet?
facilitatorNotes: Its feathers form a necklace. Ask the child to imagine feathers circling the neck rather than actual jewellery.
evidence: A feather-necklace round and round,

questions.prompt: Why do the bird’s questions about running water and the forest matter?
facilitatorNotes: They show that rich cups and dishes cannot contain the natural life it values. Accept freedom, movement or outdoor home as supported interpretations.
evidence: Can a silver dish the forest hold?

days.title: The Owl and the Pussy-Cat
days.challenge: Follow a three-part nonsense story and its repeated endings.
days.focus: A missing ring carries two unlikely companions toward a happy ending.
days.context: This is a make-believe animal wedding. A shilling was a coin; “runcible” is Lear’s invented word.

excerpt.locator:
The Owl and the Pussy-Cat; begins “I.

The Owl and the Pussy-Cat went to sea”; ends “And hand in hand, on the edge of the sand,
They danced by the light of the moon,
The moon,
The moon,
They danced by the light of the moon.”.

blocks.text: I.

The Owl and the Pussy-Cat went to sea
In a beautiful pea-green boat:
They took some honey, and plenty of money
Wrapped up in a five-pound note.
The Owl looked up to the stars above,
And sang to a small guitar,
"O lovely Pussy, O Pussy, my love,
What a beautiful Pussy you are,
You are,
You are!
What a beautiful Pussy you are!"
II.

Pussy said to the Owl, "You elegant fowl,
How charmingly sweet you sing!
Oh! let us be married; too long we have tarried:
But what shall we do for a ring?"
They sailed away, for a year and a day,
To the land where the bong-tree grows;
And there in a wood a Piggy-wig stood,
With a ring at the end of his nose,
His nose,
His nose,
With a ring at the end of his nose.
III.

"Dear Pig, are you willing to sell for one shilling
Your ring?" Said the Piggy, "I will."
So they took it away, and were married next day
By the Turkey who lives on the hill.
They dined on mince and slices of quince,
Which they ate with a runcible spoon;
And hand in hand, on the edge of the sand,
They danced by the light of the moon,
The moon,
The moon,
They danced by the light of the moon.

questions.prompt: What color is their boat, and what music travels with them?
facilitatorNotes: Notice the pea-green boat and Owl’s small guitar.
evidence: In a beautiful pea-green boat:

questions.prompt: Why is meeting the Piggy-wig useful to the travelers?
facilitatorNotes: They want a wedding ring, and the pig has one to sell.
evidence: But what shall we do for a ring?

questions.prompt: How does the last part show the pair enjoying being together?
facilitatorNotes: Eating together, holding hands, and dancing all support happiness; invite the child to choose a detail.
evidence: And hand in hand, on the edge of the sand,

days.title: Wishing
days.challenge: Notice how each new wish replaces the last and how the ending changes the desire.
days.focus: Successive wishes broaden a journey before it returns home.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “WISHING.”; opening “RING-TING! I wish I were a Primrose,”; ending “Than any other thing!”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 42, 43.

blocks.text:
RING-TING! I wish I were a Primrose,
A bright yellow Primrose blowing in the Spring!
The stooping boughs above me,
The wandering bee to love me,
The fern and moss to creep across,
And the Elm-tree for our king!

Nay--stay! I wish I were an Elm-tree,
A great lofty Elm-tree, with green leaves gay!
The winds would set them dancing,
The sun and moonshine glancing,
The Birds would house among the boughs,
And sweetly sing!

O--no! I wish I were a Robin,
A Robin or a little Wren, everywhere to go;
Through forest, field, or garden,
And ask no leave or pardon,
Till Winter comes with icy thumbs
To ruffle up our wing.

Well--tell! Where should I fly to,
Where go to sleep in the dark wood or dell?
Before a day was over,
Home comes the rover,
For Mother's kiss,--sweeter this
Than any other thing!

questions.prompt: What living thing does the speaker first wish to become?
facilitatorNotes: A bright yellow primrose in spring. The later tree and bird wishes replace, rather than fulfil, this one.
evidence: I wish I were a Primrose,

questions.prompt: Why might becoming a robin or wren seem exciting after becoming a tree?
facilitatorNotes: A bird can go through forest, field or garden instead of remaining rooted. Accept movement or choice of destinations.
evidence: Through forest, field, or garden,

questions.prompt: What finally draws the wandering speaker home?
facilitatorNotes: Mother’s kiss is called sweeter than anything else. Do not require the child to share the same family arrangement to understand the speaker.
evidence: For Mother's kiss,--sweeter this

days.title: The Table and the Chair
days.challenge: Keep track of a plan, a difficulty, and some unexpected helpers.
days.focus: Everyday furniture becomes adventurous through speech and action.
days.context: This nonsense story gives furniture legs that can walk. Read the two speakers in different voices.

excerpt.locator:
The Table and the Chair; begins “I.

Said the Table to the Chair,”; ends “Dined, and danced upon their heads
Till they toddled to their beds.”.

blocks.text: I.

Said the Table to the Chair,
"You can hardly be aware
How I suffer from the heat
And from chilblains on my feet.
If we took a little walk,
We might have a little talk;
Pray let us take the air,"
Said the Table to the Chair.
II.

Said the Chair unto the Table,
"Now, you _know_ we are not able:
How foolishly you talk,
When you know we _cannot_ walk!"
Said the Table with a sigh,
"It can do no harm to try.
I've as many legs as you:
Why can't we walk on two?"
III.

So they both went slowly down,
And walked about the town
With a cheerful bumpy sound
As they toddled round and round;
And everybody cried,
As they hastened to their side,
"See! the Table and the Chair
Have come out to take the air!"
IV.

But in going down an alley,
To a castle in a valley,
They completely lost their way,
And wandered all the day;
Till, to see them safely back,
They paid a Ducky-quack,
And a Beetle, and a Mouse,
Who took them to their house.
V.

Then they whispered to each other,
"O delightful little brother,
What a lovely walk we've taken!
Let us dine on beans and bacon."
So the Ducky and the leetle
Browny-Mousy and the Beetle
Dined, and danced upon their heads
Till they toddled to their beds.

questions.prompt: Why does the Chair first think walking is impossible?
facilitatorNotes: The Chair says they are not able to walk. It expects ordinary furniture to stay still.
evidence: When you know we _cannot_ walk!

questions.prompt: Which three creatures help the travelers get home?
facilitatorNotes: The duck, beetle, and mouse lead them after they lose their way.
evidence: And a Beetle, and a Mouse,

questions.prompt: How do the Table and Chair include their helpers at the end?
facilitatorNotes: They share dinner and dancing; this makes the ending a celebration together.
evidence: Dined, and danced upon their heads

days.title: I Saw a Little Birdie Fly
days.challenge: Identify speakers and follow a request for payment that is not money.
days.focus: A singing bird asks for a small, friendly response.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “I SAW A LITTLE BIRDIE FLY.”; opening “I SAW a little Birdie fly,”; ending “Fare-you-well, dear Amy!"”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 44.

blocks.text:
"Very sweet you sing," I said;
"Then," quoth he, "to pay me,
Give one little crumb of bread,
A little smile from Amy."

"Just," he sings, "one little smile;
O, a frown would slay me!
Thanks, and now I'm gone awhile,--
Fare-you-well, dear Amy!"

questions.prompt: To whom does the bird say it sings?
facilitatorNotes: Amy. Read the questioning speaker and bird in distinct voices.
evidence: Sing?--I sing to Amy!

questions.prompt: What two small things are requested after the song?
facilitatorNotes: A crumb of bread and a smile from Amy. Discuss the poem’s exchange without turning it into wildlife feeding advice.
evidence: Give one little crumb of bread,

questions.prompt: Does the bird say farewell forever? Which words leave room for another visit?
facilitatorNotes: It says it is gone awhile, which suggests a temporary absence. Avoid claiming a return is promised explicitly.
evidence: Thanks, and now I'm gone awhile,--

days.title: The Wind
days.challenge: Separate what the child observes from questions the child imagines.
days.focus: An unseen force becomes someone the speaker can address.
days.context: The speaker talks directly to the wind. Reread the last stanza as a series of wondering questions.

excerpt.locator:
The Wind; begins “I SAW you toss the kites on high
And blow the birds about the sky;”; ends “O you that are so strong and cold,
O blower, are you young or old?
Are you a beast of field and tree,
Or just a stronger child than me?
O wind, a-blowing all day long,
O wind, that sings so loud a song!”.

blocks.text:
I SAW you toss the kites on high
And blow the birds about the sky;
And all around I heard you pass,
Like ladies' skirts across the grass--
O wind, a-blowing all day long,
O wind, that sings so loud a song!

I saw the different things you did,
But always you yourself you hid.
I felt you push, I heard you call,
I could not see yourself at all--
O wind, a-blowing all day long,
O wind, that sings so loud a song!

O you that are so strong and cold,
O blower, are you young or old?
Are you a beast of field and tree,
Or just a stronger child than me?
O wind, a-blowing all day long,
O wind, that sings so loud a song!

questions.prompt: What two flying things does the wind move in the opening?
facilitatorNotes: Kites and birds show the wind’s strength.
evidence: And blow the birds about the sky;

questions.prompt: Why can the child describe what the wind does without seeing it?
facilitatorNotes: The effects, such as moved things and sound, are noticeable even when the wind itself is invisible.
evidence: I felt you push, I heard you call,

questions.prompt: Does the last stanza answer what the wind is like, or keep wondering?
facilitatorNotes: It asks whether wind is young, old, a beast, or a stronger child; no final answer is supplied.
evidence: Or just a stronger child than me?

days.title: Johnny Town-Mouse, part 1: a journey by mistake
days.challenge: Follow how a comfortable hiding place becomes an unexpected journey.
days.focus: Sound words make the country mouse’s arrival in town feel overwhelming.
days.context: Timmy Willie is a country mouse. A hamper is a large woven basket; a carrier transports goods. The story begins when Timmy climbs into a vegetable hamper.
days.contentNote: A cook calls for a cat and poker, and the frightened mouse runs into a hole; no injury occurs.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Johnny Town-Mouse, paragraphs 1–9; begins “Johnny Town-mouse was born in a cupboard. Timmy Willie was …” and ends “… plate. "Never mind, they don't belong to us," said Johnny.”.

blocks.text: Johnny Town-mouse was born in a cupboard. Timmy Willie was born in a garden. Timmy Willie was a little country mouse who went to town by mistake in a hamper. The gardener sent vegetables to town once a week by carrier; he packed them in a big hamper.

The gardener left the hamper by the garden gate, so that the carrier could pick it up when he passed. Timmy Willie crept in through a hole in the wicker-work, and after eating some peas--Timmy Willie fell fast asleep.

He awoke in a fright, while the hamper was being lifted into the carrier's cart. Then there was a jolting, and a clattering of horse's feet; other packages were thrown in; for miles and miles--jolt--jolt--jolt! and Timmy Willie trembled amongst the jumbled up vegetables.

At last the cart stopped at a house, where the hamper was taken out, carried in, and set down. The cook gave the carrier sixpence; the back door banged, and the cart rumbled away. But there was no quiet; there seemed to be hundreds of carts passing. Dogs barked; boys whistled in the street; the cook laughed, the parlour maid ran up and down-stairs; and a canary sang like a steam engine.
Timmy Willie, who had lived all his life in a garden, was almost frightened to death. Presently the cook opened the hamper and began to unpack the vegetables. Out sprang the terrified Timmy Willie.

Up jumped the cook on a chair, exclaiming "A mouse! a mouse! Call the cat! Fetch me the poker, Sarah!" Timmy Willie did not wait for Sarah with the poker; he rushed along the skirting board till he came to a little hole, and in he popped.

He dropped half a foot, and crashed into the middle of a mouse dinner party, breaking three glasses.--"Who in the world is this?" inquired Johnny Town-mouse. But after the first exclamation of surprise he instantly recovered his manners.

With the utmost politeness he introduced Timmy Willie to nine other mice, all with long tails and white neckties. Timmy Willie's own tail was insignificant. Johnny Town-mouse and his friends noticed it; but they were too well bred to make personal remarks; only one of them asked Timmy Willie if he had ever been in a trap?

The dinner was of eight courses; not much of anything, but truly elegant. All the dishes were unknown to Timmy Willie, who would have been a little afraid of tasting them; only he was very hungry, and very anxious to behave with company manners. The continual noise upstairs made him so nervous, that he dropped a plate. "Never mind, they don't belong to us," said Johnny.

questions.prompt: Why does Timmy enter the hamper before anyone carries it away?
facilitatorNotes: He finds peas, eats, and falls asleep. This ordinary action causes the accidental trip.
evidence: after eating some peas--Timmy Willie fell fast asleep.

questions.prompt: Which sounds help us imagine the uncomfortable ride?
facilitatorNotes: Jolting, clattering, and repeated jolt create movement and noise. Accept any exact sound detail.
evidence: jolt--jolt--jolt!

questions.prompt: How does Johnny react after Timmy crashes into dinner?
facilitatorNotes: He is surprised but quickly becomes polite and introduces the visitor. Discuss how kindness can follow an awkward arrival.
evidence: he instantly recovered his manners.

days.title: Johnny Town-Mouse, part 2: a bed that smells of cat
days.challenge: Notice that a host and a guest can experience the same home differently.
days.focus: Polite hospitality does not make every place comfortable for every visitor.
days.context: Johnny has welcomed Timmy to his town home. Timmy is unused to the sounds, food, and nearby cat. A fender is the guard around a fireplace.
days.contentNote: Mice mention being chased by a cat; the excerpt contains no injury.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Johnny Town-Mouse, paragraphs 10–20; begins “"Why don't those youngsters come back with the dessert?" It …” and ends “… not know that the hamper goes back empty on Saturdays?"”.

blocks.text: "Why don't those youngsters come back with the dessert?" It should be explained that two young mice, who were waiting on the others, went skirmishing upstairs to the kitchen between courses. Several times they had come tumbling in, squeaking and laughing; Timmy Willie learnt with horror that they were being chased by the cat. His appetite failed, he felt faint. "Try some jelly?" said Johnny Town-mouse.
"No? Would you rather go to bed? I will show you a most comfortable sofa pillow."

The sofa pillow had a hole in it. Johnny Town-mouse quite honestly recommended it as the best bed, kept exclusively for visitors. But the sofa smelt of cat. Timmy Willie preferred to spend a miserable night under the fender.

It was just the same next day. An excellent breakfast was provided--for mice accustomed to eat bacon; but Timmy Willie had been reared on roots and salad. Johnny Town-mouse and his friends racketted about under the floors, and came boldly out all over the house in the evening. One particularly loud crash had been caused by Sarah tumbling downstairs with the tea-tray; there were crumbs and sugar and smears of jam to be collected, in spite of the cat.

Timmy Willie longed to be at home in his peaceful nest in a sunny bank. The food disagreed with him; the noise prevented him from sleeping. In a few days he grew so thin that Johnny Town-mouse noticed it, and questioned him. He listened to Timmy Willie's story and inquired about the garden. "It sounds rather a dull place? What do you do when it rains?"

"When it rains, I sit in my little sandy burrow and shell corn and seeds from my Autumn store. I peep out at the throstles and blackbirds on the lawn, and my friend Cock Robin. And when the sun comes out again, you should see my garden and the flowers--roses and pinks and pansies--no noise except the birds and bees, and the lambs in the meadows."

"There goes that cat again!" exclaimed Johnny Town-mouse. When they had taken refuge in the coal-cellar he resumed the conversation; "I confess I am a little disappointed; we have endeavoured to entertain you, Timothy William."
"Oh yes, yes, you have been most kind; but I do feel so ill," said Timmy Willie.
"It may be that your teeth and digestion are unaccustomed to our food; perhaps it might be wiser for you to return in the hamper."
"Oh? Oh!" cried Timmy Willie.
"Why of course for the matter of that we could have sent you back last week," said Johnny rather huffily--"did you not know that the hamper goes back empty on Saturdays?"

questions.prompt: Why does Timmy reject the sofa pillow that Johnny recommends?
facilitatorNotes: It smells of cat, so it does not feel safe to him. Johnny recommends it honestly, showing different viewpoints.
evidence: the sofa smelt of cat.

questions.prompt: What does Timmy miss about his country home?
facilitatorNotes: He mentions his peaceful nest, flowers, birds, and familiar stored seeds. Invite one concrete contrast with town.
evidence: his peaceful nest in a sunny bank.

questions.prompt: What useful fact does Johnny finally tell him about the hamper?
facilitatorNotes: It returns empty on Saturdays, so he can travel home. Notice that Timmy had not known this.
evidence: the hamper goes back empty on Saturdays?

days.title: Johnny Town-Mouse, part 3: the country host
days.challenge: Recognize the reversal when the former visitor becomes the host.
days.focus: A harmless familiar sound can alarm someone who does not know it.
days.context: Timmy has learned how to return home in the vegetable hamper. After the winter, Johnny finally comes to visit him in the country.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Johnny Town-Mouse, paragraphs 21–27; begins “So Timmy Willie said good-bye to his new friends, and …” and ends “… to lie down upon you. How are all our friends?"”.

blocks.text: So Timmy Willie said good-bye to his new friends, and hid in the hamper with a crumb of cake and a withered cabbage leaf; and after much jolting, he was set down safely in his own garden.
Sometimes on Saturdays he went to look at the hamper lying by the gate, but he knew better than to get in again. And nobody got out, though Johnny Town-mouse had half promised a visit.

The winter passed; the sun came out again; Timmy Willie sat by his burrow warming his little fur coat and sniffing the smell of violets and spring grass. He had nearly forgotten his visit to town. When up the sandy path all spick and span with a brown leather bag came Johnny Town-mouse!
Timmy Willie received him with open arms. "You have come at the best of all the year, we will have herb pudding and sit in the sun."
"H'm'm! it is a little damp," said Johnny Town-mouse, who was carrying his tail under his arm, out of the mud.
"What is that fearful noise?" he started violently.
"That?" said Timmy Willie, "that is only a cow; I will beg a little milk, they are quite harmless, unless they happen to lie down upon you. How are all our friends?"

questions.prompt: What does Timmy do differently when he sees the hamper again?
facilitatorNotes: He looks but does not climb in. He remembers the earlier accidental journey.
evidence: he knew better than to get in again.

questions.prompt: How does Timmy welcome Johnny?
facilitatorNotes: He welcomes him warmly and proposes pudding and sitting in the sun. Connect the open arms to his spoken invitation.
evidence: Timmy Willie received him with open arms.

questions.prompt: What noise frightens Johnny, and how does Timmy explain it?
facilitatorNotes: It is a cow. Timmy knows the country sound and treats it as familiar, just as Johnny once accepted town noises.
evidence: that is only a cow

days.title: Johnny Town-Mouse, part 4: a home for each mouse
days.challenge: Separate a narrator’s preference from a rule for everyone.
days.focus: The ending lets different characters prefer different homes.
days.context: Johnny is visiting Timmy’s country home and has just been startled by a cow. He tells Timmy the news from town. On board wages means the cook is paid to look after the empty house.
days.contentNote: Johnny reports in one sentence that the household cat killed the canary; nothing is described.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Johnny Town-Mouse, paragraphs 28–34 (end); begins “Johnny's account was rather middling. He explained why he was …” and ends “… I prefer to live in the country, like Timmy Willie.”.

blocks.text: Johnny's account was rather middling. He explained why he was paying his visit so early in the season; the family had gone to the sea-side for Easter; the cook was doing spring cleaning, on board wages, with particular instructions to clear out the mice. There were four kittens, and the cat had killed the canary.
"They say we did it; but I know better," said Johnny Town-mouse. "Whatever is that fearful racket?"
"That is only the lawn-mower; I will fetch some of the grass clippings presently to make your bed. I am sure you had better settle in the country, Johnny."
"H'm'm--we shall see by Tuesday week; the hamper is stopped while they are at the sea-side."
"I am sure you will never want to live in town again," said Timmy Willie.
But he did. He went back in the very next hamper of vegetables; he said it was too quiet!!
One place suits one person, another place suits another person. For my part I prefer to live in the country, like Timmy Willie.

questions.prompt: Why has Johnny come to the country so early in the year?
facilitatorNotes: The family has gone to the sea-side and the cook is cleaning, with orders to clear out the mice; there are kittens and a cat too. Accept any reason from Johnny’s list.
evidence: with particular instructions to clear out the mice.

questions.prompt: Timmy is sure Johnny will never want to live in town again. Does that come true?
facilitatorNotes: No. Johnny goes back in the very next hamper and says the country is too quiet. The short sentence But he did reverses Timmy’s prediction.
evidence: He went back in the very next hamper of vegetables

questions.prompt: Does the storyteller say everybody should choose country life?
facilitatorNotes: No. The narrator says one place suits one person and another suits another, then states a personal preference. Children may share their own preference and a reason.
evidence: One place suits one person, another place suits another person.

days.title: Yes or No?
days.challenge: Hear the pressure in direct questions and distinguish it from a universal rule.
days.focus: Short opposite choices dramatise an impatient group waiting for a decision.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.
days.contentNote: The old phrase “like a man” links decisiveness with boys or men; adults can explain that anyone can make decisions and ask for thinking time.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “YES OR NO?”; opening “YES or No?”; ending “And follow your nose as fast as you can!”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 53.

blocks.text:
YES or No?
Stay or Go?
He never can tell, he never will know!
We must not wait,
We'll all be late,
While Barnaby puzzles his queer little pate!

What do you say?
Off and away!
Make up your mind to go or to stay.
Fix on your plan,
Step out like a man,
And follow your nose as fast as you can!

questions.prompt: What two choices keep Barnaby puzzled?
facilitatorNotes: Whether to stay or go. The other yes/no question makes the indecision sound repetitive.
evidence: Stay or Go?

questions.prompt: Why are the others impatient while he thinks?
facilitatorNotes: They fear everyone will be late. Ask how a hurried reading differs from a thoughtful pause.
evidence: We'll all be late,

questions.prompt: Does the speaker finally choose stay or go for Barnaby?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker tells him to make up his mind, not one final choice. Note that real children may need time and help with decisions.
evidence: Make up your mind to go or to stay.

days.title: The Land of Counterpane
days.challenge: Match a make-believe landscape to the ordinary objects beneath it.
days.focus: A child confined to bed creates a world through scale and arrangement.
days.context: A counterpane is a bedcover. The poem describes old-fashioned toy soldiers; the child can imagine or draw the landscape.

excerpt.locator:
The Land of Counterpane; begins “WHEN I was sick and lay a-bed,
I had two pillows at my head,”; ends “And sees before him, dale and plain,
The pleasant land of counterpane.”.

blocks.text:
WHEN I was sick and lay a-bed,
I had two pillows at my head,
And all my toys beside me lay
To keep me happy all the day.

And sometimes for an hour or so
I watched my leaden soldiers go,
With different uniforms and drills,
Among the bed-clothes, through the hills;

And sometimes sent my ships in fleets
All up and down among the sheets;
Or brought my trees and houses out,
And planted cities all about.

I was the giant great and still
That sits upon the pillow-hill,
And sees before him, dale and plain,
The pleasant land of counterpane.

questions.prompt: What do the sheets become for the child’s ships?
facilitatorNotes: They become seas along which fleets travel.
evidence: All up and down among the sheets;

questions.prompt: Why might the child call themself a giant?
facilitatorNotes: Compared with the tiny toys and towns, the child is enormous and can look down over them.
evidence: I was the giant great and still

questions.prompt: How does the poem change the feeling of staying in bed?
facilitatorNotes: Play makes it a pleasant landscape despite illness; accept enjoyment alongside any sense of being stuck.
evidence: The pleasant land of counterpane.

days.title: Sleeping
days.challenge: Follow a descending scale of related images.
days.focus: Curtains of different sizes connect nightfall, a room and a child’s eyelids.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.
days.contentNote: Includes a bedtime prayer and angels. Its instruction to sleep only at night is poetic household advice, not a rule against children’s daytime naps.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “SLEEPING.”; opening “DO all your sleeping at night,”; ending “And keep watch round the little one's bed.”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 54, 55.

blocks.text:
DO all your sleeping at night,
For then niddy-noddy is right;
But awake you must keep,
And it won't do to sleep,
In the middle of broad daylight.

The sun at the end of the day
Takes his mighty great candle away;
A curtain on high
Is drawn over the sky,
And the stars peep thro' if they may.

There's the curtain of night over all,
There's our own window-curtain so small,
And least in their size,
Over Emily's eyes
Her fringed little eyelids will fall.

questions.prompt: What enormous object is the sun imagined to take away at day’s end?
facilitatorNotes: A mighty great candle. It is a comparison that makes fading sunlight feel like putting out a room’s light.
evidence: Takes his mighty great candle away;

questions.prompt: What three curtain-like coverings get smaller and smaller?
facilitatorNotes: Night over the sky, the window curtain and Emily’s eyelids. Point to each image while rereading.
evidence:
Over Emily's eyes
    Her fringed little eyelids will fall.

questions.prompt: What shows that Emily is cared for as she settles to sleep?
facilitatorNotes: A kiss and the wish that angels watch over her bed. Accept affection or protection as the feeling, without requiring agreement with the prayer.
evidence: Now, a kiss, my Dear;

days.title: Hurt no living thing
days.challenge: Attend to the distinct movements within a list of small creatures.
days.focus: A broad request is made concrete through several tiny lives.
days.context: Ladybird is another name for ladybug. Read the list with time to picture each creature.

excerpt.locator:
Hurt no living thing; begins “Hurt no living thing:
Ladybird, nor butterfly,”; ends “Nor dancing gnat, nor beetle fat,
Nor harmless worms that creep.”.

blocks.text:
Hurt no living thing:
Ladybird, nor butterfly,
Nor moth with dusty wing,
Nor cricket chirping cheerily,
Nor grasshopper so light of leap,
Nor dancing gnat, nor beetle fat,
Nor harmless worms that creep.

questions.prompt: Which creature is described as chirping?
facilitatorNotes: The cricket chirps cheerily.
evidence: Nor cricket chirping cheerily,

questions.prompt: Which creature leaps, and which ones creep?
facilitatorNotes: The grasshopper leaps and the worms creep; gestures can show the difference.
evidence: Nor grasshopper so light of leap,

questions.prompt: Why list moths, gnats, beetles, and worms after the first request?
facilitatorNotes: The examples include small creatures people might overlook; the opening request applies to them too.
evidence: Hurt no living thing:

days.title: The Bubble
days.challenge: Recognise changing metaphors while following rise, fall and bursting.
days.focus: A fragile bubble is enlarged into a tiny planet and then disappears.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “THE BUBBLE.”; opening “SEE, the pretty Planet!”; ending “As of tears.”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 62.

blocks.text:
SEE, the pretty Planet!
Floating sphere!
Faintest breeze will fan it
Far or near;

Drooping, sinking, failing,
Nigh to earth,
Mounting, whirling, sailing,
Full of mirth;

Life there, welling, flowing,
Waving round;
Pictures coming, going,
Without sound.

Quick now! be this airy
Globe repell'd!
Never can the fairy
Star be held.

Touch'd--it in a twinkle
Disappears!
Leaving but a sprinkle,
As of tears.

questions.prompt: Which huge sky object does the first line compare the bubble to?
facilitatorNotes: A planet. Later moonshine and star images continue that tiny-world fantasy.
evidence: SEE, the pretty Planet!

questions.prompt: Does the bubble only sink, or does it move in other ways too?
facilitatorNotes: It sinks but also mounts, whirls and sails. Choose contrasting movements to act with a hand.
evidence: Mounting, whirling, sailing,

questions.prompt: What happens when the bubble is touched, and what remains?
facilitatorNotes: It vanishes, leaving a sprinkle like tears. The comparison gives a small ending an emotional sound.
evidence:
Leaving but a sprinkle,
        As of tears.

days.title: A Family of Squirrels, part 1: Bobby
days.challenge: Gather describing details into one clear picture.
days.focus: Careful description of movement, tail, ears and paws brings one wild animal to life.
days.context: The children call a wild red squirrel their “pet” because he comes when they whistle, but he lives in the wood. Beech nuts and acorns are tree seeds.

excerpt.locator: Book I, A Family of Squirrels, printed pages 17–18, paragraphs 1–5; begins “We have a pet called Bobby, and we love him …” and ends “… them, and peels off the brown skin with his teeth.”.

blocks.text: We have a pet called Bobby, and we love him very much. He is a little squirrel, living among the beech trees of the wood.
We see him every morning leaping from branch to branch, with his long furry tail stretched out behind. Sometimes he leaps right down on to the ground and runs about picking up beech nuts.
Sometimes he sits bolt upright on a branch, with a nut or acorn in his paws. Then his tail is bent up against his back.

We have known him for two years, and when we whistle to him he comes to us. But if anything frightens him he darts away to the nearest tree. He climbs up in a moment with his sharp claws, and peeps back through the green leaves We see his bright black eyes looking down at us.

His back is covered with a brown red fur, but under his body the fur is white. His lovely red tail is like a brush on his back. His hind legs are long. That is why he can jump so well. On his front paws one toe stands out from the others, almost like our thumb. He uses his paws like hands, when he sits up with a nut in them, and peels off the brown skin with his teeth.

questions.prompt: What two different ways does Bobby hold his tail?
facilitatorNotes: Stretched out behind when he leaps, and bent up against his back when he sits. A hand can show both shapes.
evidence: his long furry tail stretched out behind

questions.prompt: What does Bobby do when something frightens him?
facilitatorNotes: He darts to the nearest tree, climbs fast, and peeps back through the leaves.
evidence: he darts away to the nearest tree

questions.prompt: How does Bobby use his front paws like hands?
facilitatorNotes: He holds a nut and peels off the skin with his teeth; one toe stands out almost like a thumb.
evidence: almost like our thumb.

days.title: A Family of Squirrels, part 2: through the seasons
days.challenge: Track what the squirrels do in each season.
days.focus: The children connect observations across a whole year, and admit what they still do not know.
days.context: Buckley describes British red squirrels. She says they sleep through most of the winter; tree squirrels are now known to stay active, resting in their nests in bad weather. The children notice that Bobby does come out on mild days.
days.contentNote: Squirrels steal birds’ eggs and suck out the yolk.

excerpt.locator: Book I, A Family of Squirrels, printed pages 18–19, paragraphs 6–11 (end of lesson); begins “Sometimes he steals birds' eggs. Then he holds the egg …” and ends “… each found a hole, and curled themselves up to sleep.”.

blocks.text: Sometimes he steals birds' eggs. Then he holds the egg in his paws, cracks the top, and sucks out the yolk.
He has such funny ears! They have long tufts of hair behind them He sometimes comes out of his hole in winter to eat, and we see that the tufts are much longer then than in summer.

But for most of the winter we never see him. He is fast asleep in a hole in a tree. We know where his hole is, for Peter found it once. He had seen Bobby come down one mild day to feed on his store of acorns, buried at the foot of the tree, and he watched him as he went back. Then he climbed up the tree, and in a hole in the trunk he saw Bobby's bushy tail curled round. So he knew that Bobby was snug and cosy in the hole.
Bobby has a little wife, and they always keep near each other. But she is very shy, and will not come to us. In the spring, when there are no nuts, they eat the buds of the trees.

About May they are very busy. They gather leaves, and moss, and twigs. These they weave into a nest in a fork of the tree, far from the ground. Then in June their little ones are born. Paul climbed up and saw four such lovely little squirrels, covered with soft red and white fur. They stayed in the nest for some time, though we often saw them moving about among the branches. The old squirrels took such care of them, and they stayed together all the summer. In the autumn they hid little heaps of nuts and acorns at the foot of the tree, to eat when they should awake in the mild days in winter.
Then we did not see them again. We do not know whether they all crept into one hole, or whether they each found a hole, and curled themselves up to sleep.

questions.prompt: How did Peter find out where Bobby sleeps in winter?
facilitatorNotes: He watched Bobby go back up after feeding, climbed the tree, and saw his bushy tail in a hole in the trunk.
evidence: he saw Bobby's bushy tail curled round.

questions.prompt: What do the squirrels hide in the autumn, and why?
facilitatorNotes: Little heaps of nuts and acorns at the foot of the tree, to eat on mild winter days.
evidence: they hid little heaps of nuts and acorns at the foot of the tree

questions.prompt: At the end, what do the children admit they do not know?
facilitatorNotes: Whether the squirrels share one hole or each find their own. Honest observers say what they have not seen; ask how someone might find out.
evidence: We do not know whether they all crept into one hole

days.title: Where Go the Boats?
days.challenge: Follow a river’s route beyond what the child can see.
days.focus: Colorful observation opens into imagined connection with distant children.
days.context: The boats are small play boats. Read the title as the speaker’s wondering question.

excerpt.locator:
Where Go the Boats?; begins “DARK brown is the river,
Golden is the sand.”; ends “Other little children
Shall bring my boats ashore.”.

blocks.text:
DARK brown is the river,
Golden is the sand.
It flows along for ever,
With trees on either hand.

Green leaves a-floating,
Castles of the foam,
Boats of mine a-boating--
Where will all come home?

On goes the river
And out past the mill,
Away down the valley,
Away down the hill.

Away down the river,
A hundred miles or more,
Other little children
Shall bring my boats ashore.

questions.prompt: What colors does the opening give the river and sand?
facilitatorNotes: Brown and golden make two contrasting parts of the scene.
evidence:
DARK brown is the river,
Golden is the sand.

questions.prompt: What places does the river pass on its way?
facilitatorNotes: It goes past the mill and down the valley and hill; allow two remembered places.
evidence:
Away down the valley,
Away down the hill.

questions.prompt: Who does the speaker imagine finding the boats far away?
facilitatorNotes: Other little children will bring them ashore. This is an imagined future, not an event the speaker has seen.
evidence:
Other little children
Shall bring my boats ashore.

days.title: Nick Spence
days.challenge: Follow the short narrative without inventing motives the speaker does not give.
days.focus: A brisk rhyme tells a sale, a scolding and a proposed change of jobs.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.
days.contentNote: An old farm household calls Nick’s employer “Master” and includes scolding; discuss the printed scene without endorsing harsh treatment.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “NICK SPENCE.”; opening “NICK SPENCE, Nick Spence,”; ending “And Johnny to the fair!”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 65.

blocks.text:
NICK SPENCE, Nick Spence,
Sold the Cow for sixpence!
When his Master scolded him,
Nicky didn't care.
Put him in the farmyard,
