The stableyard, the stackyard,
Send him to the pigsty,
And Johnny to the fair!

questions.prompt: What did Nick sell, and for what amount?
facilitatorNotes: A cow for sixpence, an old money amount. No arithmetic or claim about a present-day price is needed.
evidence: Sold the Cow for sixpence!

questions.prompt: Does the poem tell us that Nick feels sorry when scolded?
facilitatorNotes: No; it says he did not care. Ask the child to distinguish the printed reaction from a possible imagined one.
evidence: Nicky didn't care.

questions.prompt: Who does the speaker suggest sending to the fair instead of Nick?
facilitatorNotes: Johnny. The other lines send Nick to farm work, suggesting a change in who handles the outing.
evidence: And Johnny to the fair!

days.title: If a pig wore a wig
days.challenge: Notice two rhyming word pairs that generate absurd possibilities.
days.focus: Sound makes an ordinary animal part of a comic social scene.
days.context: A tailoress is a woman who sews clothes. In this nonsense poem she can even replace a tail.

excerpt.locator:
If a pig wore a wig; begins “If a pig wore a wig,
What could we say?”; ends “Send him to the tailoress
To get one new.”.

blocks.text:
If a pig wore a wig,
What could we say?
Treat him as a gentleman,
And say “Good day.”
If his tail chanced to fail,
What could we do?—
Send him to the tailoress
To get one new.

questions.prompt: What polite greeting does the speaker suggest for the pig?
facilitatorNotes: “Good day” treats the fancily dressed pig as a gentleman.
evidence: And say “Good day.”

questions.prompt: Which words sound alike in the first line?
facilitatorNotes: Pig and wig rhyme; repeat them orally without asking for reading.
evidence: If a pig wore a wig,

questions.prompt: Why is the visit to the tailoress funny?
facilitatorNotes: A person who sews clothes cannot sew a real replacement tail in this way; the similar words tail and tailoress help the joke.
evidence: Send him to the tailoress

days.title: Ambition
days.challenge: Track increasing size of a wish and question a confident prediction.
days.focus: A seaside building plan expands from a sand house to a city and a crown.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “AMBITION.”; opening “THE Sea! as smooth as silk,”; ending “Perhaps they will make me King?”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 66.

blocks.text:
THE Sea! as smooth as silk,
And the froth of it like new milk,
And the sky a wonderful blue,
The cliff harebells have it too,
And scatter'd all over the shore
A thousand Children or more!

Suppose we join, one-will'd,
A City of Sand to build,
With a rampart broad and strong
From rock to rock along,
Solid and firm enough
To last till the sea grows rough
And the days turn chilly and short,
The end of our seaside sport,
When all must bundle and pack
And swift in the train go back,
Big folk and little folk,
To London lamps and smoke?

Let's draw out our plan to-night,
Begin it with morning light.
We'll bring all the Children together
And build in the sweet sunny weather.
What use in a House of Sand?
But a City--that _would_ be grand!
O yes, I am sure it will stand!
And I, who first thought of the thing,
Perhaps they will make me King?

questions.prompt: What do the children hope to build together on the shore?
facilitatorNotes: A city of sand with a broad strong rampart. Explain a rampart as a protective wall.
evidence: A City of Sand to build,

questions.prompt: What changes in the weather or season might challenge the plan to make it last?
facilitatorNotes: The sea becoming rough and days becoming chilly and short. The poem itself supplies reasons to question the speaker’s confidence.
evidence: To last till the sea grows rough

questions.prompt: What extra reward does the speaker imagine at the very end?
facilitatorNotes: Being made king for having the idea. Accept playful pride or excitement as a reading; the poem does not say the city is actually completed.
evidence: Perhaps they will make me King?

days.title: Block City
days.challenge: Keep the room and the imagined city in mind together.
days.focus: A temporary construction becomes a lasting memory.
days.context: A kirk is a church. The child’s ordinary room supplies the land and water for a block city.

excerpt.locator:
Block City; begins “WHAT are you able to build with your blocks?
Castles and palaces, temples and docks.”; ends “And as long as I live and where'er I may be,
I'll always remember my town by the sea.”.

blocks.text:
WHAT are you able to build with your blocks?
Castles and palaces, temples and docks.
Rain may keep raining, and others go roam,
But I can be happy and building at home.

Let the sofa be mountains, the carpet be sea,
There I'll establish a city for me:
A kirk and a mill and a palace beside,
And a harbour as well where my vessels may ride.

Great is the palace with pillar and wall,
A sort of a tower on the top of it all,
And steps coming down in an orderly way
To where my toy vessels lie safe in the bay.

This one is sailing and that one is moored:
Hark to the song of the sailors on board!
And see on the steps of my palace, the kings
Coming and going with presents and things!

Now I have done with it, down let it go!
All in a moment the town is laid low.
Block upon block lying scattered and free,
What is there left of my town by the sea?

Yet as I saw it, I see it again,
The kirk and the palace, the ships and the men,
And as long as I live and where'er I may be,
I'll always remember my town by the sea.

questions.prompt: What parts of the room become mountains and sea?
facilitatorNotes: The sofa becomes mountains and the carpet becomes sea.
evidence: Let the sofa be mountains, the carpet be sea,

questions.prompt: What happens to the city when play is over?
facilitatorNotes: The town is knocked down and the blocks lie scattered; the speaker chooses to end the building play.
evidence: Now I have done with it, down let it go!

questions.prompt: How can the town remain with the child after it is knocked down?
facilitatorNotes: The child will remember it; the ending distinguishes the physical blocks from the imagined place.
evidence: I'll always remember my town by the sea.

days.title: Ginger and Pickles, part 1: the busy little shop
days.challenge: Listen for the explanation of an unfamiliar word inside a story.
days.focus: A crowded shop may still have an empty cash drawer.
days.context: A cat and a dog keep a village shop for storybook animals. Credit means receiving something now with a promise to pay later; the story explains this practice.
days.contentNote: The shopkeepers joke about eating animal customers; none is eaten in this selection.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Ginger and Pickles, paragraphs 1–18; begins “Once upon a time there was a village shop. The …” and ends “… there is no money in what is called the "till."”.

blocks.text: Once upon a time there was a village shop. The name over the window was "Ginger and Pickles."
It was a little small shop just the right size for Dolls--Lucinda and Jane Doll-cook always bought their groceries at Ginger and Pickles.
The counter inside was a convenient height for rabbits. Ginger and Pickles sold red spotty pocket-handkerchiefs at a penny three farthings.
They also sold sugar, and snuff and galoshes.
In fact, although it was such a small shop it sold nearly everything--except a few things that you want in a hurry--like bootlaces, hair-pins and mutton chops.
Ginger and Pickles were the people who kept the shop. Ginger was a yellow tom-cat, and Pickles was a terrier.
The rabbits were always a little bit afraid of Pickles.
The shop was also patronized by mice--only the mice were rather afraid of Ginger.
Ginger usually requested Pickles to serve them, because he said it made his mouth water.
"I cannot bear," said he, "to see them going out at the door carrying their little parcels."
"I have the same feeling about rats," replied Pickles, "but it would never do to eat our own customers; they would leave us and go to Tabitha Twitchit's."
"On the contrary, they would go nowhere," replied Ginger gloomily.
(Tabitha Twitchit kept the only other shop in the village. She did not give credit.)
Ginger and Pickles gave unlimited credit.
Now the meaning of "credit" is this--when a customer buys a bar of soap, instead of the customer pulling out a purse and paying for it--she says she will pay another time.
And Pickles makes a low bow and says, "With pleasure, madam," and it is written down in a book.
The customers come again and again, and buy quantities, in spite of being afraid of Ginger and Pickles.
But there is no money in what is called the "till."

questions.prompt: How is the shop made convenient for very small customers?
facilitatorNotes: It is doll-sized and its counter suits rabbits. Let the child choose either physical detail.
evidence: The counter inside was a convenient height for rabbits.

questions.prompt: Why do the mice prefer Pickles to serve them?
facilitatorNotes: They fear the cat Ginger. Treat this as an animal-story joke, not a real rule about stores.
evidence: the mice were rather afraid of Ginger.

questions.prompt: What happens instead of money changing hands when a customer buys on credit?
facilitatorNotes: A promise to pay later is written in a book. Reread the explanation and contrast it with paying immediately.
evidence: it is written down in a book.

days.title: Ginger and Pickles, part 2: plenty sold, nothing paid
days.challenge: Connect a repeated phrase about money with the shopkeepers’ problem.
days.focus: Large sales and unpaid bills are different things.
days.context: Customers keep taking goods on credit without paying. A till is a cash drawer. The old money amounts are historical setting; children need not calculate them.
days.contentNote: Historical dog-licence rules appear as story setting; they are not current legal information.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Ginger and Pickles, paragraphs 19–36; begins “The customers came in crowds every day and bought quantities, …” and ends “… all the bills again to everybody 'with comp'ts,'" replied Ginger.”.

blocks.text: The customers came in crowds every day and bought quantities, especially the toffee customers. But there was always no money; they never paid for as much as a pennyworth of peppermints.
But the sales were enormous, ten times as large as Tabitha Twitchit's.
As there was always no money, Ginger and Pickles were obliged to eat their own goods.
Pickles ate biscuits and Ginger ate a dried haddock.
They ate them by candle-light after the shop was closed.
When it came to Jan. 1st there was still no money, and Pickles was unable to buy a dog licence.
"It is very unpleasant, I am afraid of the police," said Pickles.
"It is your own fault for being a terrier; _I_ do not require a licence, and neither does Kep, the Collie dog."

"It is very uncomfortable, I am afraid I shall be summoned. I have tried in vain to get a licence upon credit at the Post Office;" said Pickles. "The place is full of policemen. I met one as I was coming home."
"Let us send in the bill again to Samuel Whiskers, Ginger, he owes 22/9 for bacon."
"I do not believe that he intends to pay at all," replied Ginger.
"And I feel sure that Anna Maria pockets things--Where are all the cream crackers?"
"You have eaten them yourself," replied Ginger.
Ginger and Pickles retired into the back parlour.
They did accounts. They added up sums and sums, and sums.
"Samuel Whiskers has run up a bill as long as his tail; he has had an ounce and three-quarters of snuff since October."
"What is seven pounds of butter at 1/3, and a stick of sealing wax and four matches?"
"Send in all the bills again to everybody 'with comp'ts,'" replied Ginger.

questions.prompt: What keeps happening even though many customers come?
facilitatorNotes: The shop remains without money because customers do not pay. Ask for the repeated contrast, not a business lecture.
evidence: But there was always no money

questions.prompt: Why do Ginger and Pickles eat things from their own shop?
facilitatorNotes: They have no money for other food. They eat biscuits and a dried fish from the stock.
evidence: Ginger and Pickles were obliged to eat their own goods.

questions.prompt: Does Ginger agree that Anna Maria took the crackers?
facilitatorNotes: No; Ginger says Pickles ate them himself. Notice that a worried guess can be mistaken.
evidence: You have eaten them yourself

days.title: Ginger and Pickles, part 3: the silent visitor
days.challenge: Use physical details to check a frightened character’s assumption.
days.focus: An apparently alarming visitor turns out to be a toy, but the bill is real.
days.context: The shopkeepers are worried about unpaid bills. Pickles fears a police officer has arrived. Rates and taxes are bills the shop must pay.
days.contentNote: A character tells the dog to bite the doll, but no attack or injury follows. Explain that this is not an acceptable way to treat visitors.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Ginger and Pickles, paragraphs 37–46; begins “After a time they heard a noise in the shop, …” and ends “… the last straw," said Pickles, "let us close the shop."”.

blocks.text: After a time they heard a noise in the shop, as if something had been pushed in at the door. They came out of the back parlour. There was an envelope lying on the counter, and a policeman writing in a note-book!
Pickles nearly had a fit, he barked and he barked and made little rushes.
"Bite him, Pickles! bite him!" spluttered Ginger behind a sugar-barrel, "he's only a German doll!"
The policeman went on writing in his notebook; twice he put his pencil in his mouth, and once he dipped it in the treacle.
Pickles barked till he was hoarse. But still the policeman took no notice. He had bead eyes, and his helmet was sewed on with stitches.
At length on his last little rush--Pickles found that the shop was empty. The policeman had disappeared.
But the envelope remained.
"Do you think that he has gone to fetch a real live policeman? I am afraid it is a summons," said Pickles.
"No," replied Ginger, who had opened the envelope, "it is the rates and taxes, £3 19 11-3/4."
"This is the last straw," said Pickles, "let us close the shop."

questions.prompt: Which details show that this policeman is a doll?
facilitatorNotes: His bead eyes and sewn-on helmet reveal it. Contrast those clues with Pickles’s barking.
evidence: He had bead eyes, and his helmet was sewed on with stitches.

questions.prompt: What does the visitor do while Pickles barks?
facilitatorNotes: He continues writing and takes no notice. The silence can make the scene funny or make Pickles more nervous; either reading fits.
evidence: But still the policeman took no notice.

questions.prompt: What is actually in the envelope?
facilitatorNotes: A tax bill, not the feared summons. The expense leads Pickles to propose closing the shop.
evidence: it is the rates and taxes

days.title: Ginger and Pickles, part 4: another shop opens
days.challenge: Compare the new shop’s practice with the earlier promise-to-pay system.
days.focus: The village misses a useful service and welcomes a changed version.
days.context: Ginger and Pickles have decided to close their shop. Sally Henny Penny later announces that she will reopen it. A poster advertises what is for sale.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Ginger and Pickles, paragraphs 47–63 (end); begins “They put up the shutters, and left. But they have …” and ends “There is something to please everybody.”.

blocks.text: They put up the shutters, and left. But they have not removed from the neighbourhood. In fact some people wish they had gone further.
Ginger is living in the warren. I do not know what occupation he pursues; he looks stout and comfortable.
Pickles is at present a gamekeeper.
The closing of the shop caused great inconvenience. Tabitha Twitchit immediately raised the price of everything a half-penny; and she continued to refuse to give credit.
Of course there are the trades-men's carts--the butcher, the fish-man and Timothy Baker.
But a person cannot live on "seed wigs" and sponge-cake and butter-buns--not even when the sponge-cake is as good as Timothy's!
After a time Mr. John Dormouse and his daughter began to sell peppermints and candles.
But they did not keep "self-fitting sixes"; and it takes five mice to carry one seven inch candle.
Besides--the candles which they sell behave very strangely in warm weather.
And Miss Dormouse refused to take back the ends when they were brought back to her with complaints.
And when Mr. John Dormouse was complained to, he stayed in bed, and would say nothing but "very snug;" which is not the way to carry on a retail business.

So everybody was pleased when Sally Henny Penny sent out a printed poster to say that she was going to re-open the shop--"Henny's Opening Sale! Grand co-operative Jumble! Penny's penny prices! Come buy, come try, come buy!"
The poster really was most 'ticing.
There was a rush upon the opening day. The shop was crammed with customers, and there were crowds of mice upon the biscuit canisters.
Sally Henny Penny gets rather flustered when she tries to count out change, and she insists on being paid cash; but she is quite harmless.
And she has laid in a remarkable assortment of bargains.
There is something to please everybody.

questions.prompt: Why is closing the shop inconvenient for the village?
facilitatorNotes: The remaining shop raises prices, and other sellers do not offer everything people need. Accept either supported example.
evidence: Tabitha Twitchit immediately raised the price of everything a half-penny

questions.prompt: What makes Sally’s poster sound inviting when read aloud?
facilitatorNotes: Repeated calls such as come buy and come try create a lively invitation. Let the child hear and repeat the pattern.
evidence: Come buy, come try, come buy!

questions.prompt: What does Sally require that Ginger and Pickles did not?
facilitatorNotes: She requires cash payment. Connect that choice to the earlier empty till without requiring a verdict that every kind of credit is bad.
evidence: she insists on being paid cash

days.title: A Riddle
days.challenge: Use several negative and positive clues to suggest a reflection.
days.focus: A moving likeness is described as both real and almost nothing.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Rhymes for the Young Folk aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “A RIDDLE.”; opening “WHAT I say you'll scarce believe,”; ending “--There he is: turn and see!”. Smithsonian witness printed page(s) 75.

blocks.text:
WHAT I say you'll scarce believe,
Yet my words shall not deceive.
I saw what seem'd a little Boy,
With a face of life and joy;
He danced, he ran, he nodded, he smiled,
Just like any other Child;
But could not speak, (how strange was this!)
Or cry, or breathe, nor could I kiss,
To save my life, the cherry red
Of lips, not living and not dead!
He was no picture, statue, doll;
He was not a Child at all;
He was Nothing, as near as could be,
He was as real as you or me.
--There he is: turn and see!

questions.prompt: What can the strange boy seem to do?
facilitatorNotes: Dance, run, nod and smile. These actions suggest a living likeness even before the later clues challenge that thought.
evidence: He danced, he ran, he nodded, he smiled,

questions.prompt: What ordinary living-child actions can this figure not do?
facilitatorNotes: Speak, cry or breathe; the speaker cannot kiss its lips either. Use those clues to distinguish appearance from a separate living person.
evidence: But could not speak, (how strange was this!)

questions.prompt: What could copy a child’s movements but not be a doll, statue or separate child?
facilitatorNotes: A reflection is a strong answer. Invite a safe mirror demonstration; other proposals need to explain all the clues, and the poem never prints a one-word solution.
evidence: He was no picture, statue, doll;

days.title: Foreign Lands
days.challenge: Separate a view from a tree from what the child imagines beyond it.
days.focus: A higher viewpoint makes a familiar neighborhood feel newly discovered.
days.context: “Foreign” here starts with places unfamiliar to the speaker, including the next-door garden.

excerpt.locator: Foreign Lands; begins “UP into the cherry tree”; ends “And all the playthings come alive.”.

blocks.text:
UP into the cherry tree
Who should climb but little me?
I held the trunk with both my hands
And looked abroad on foreign lands.

I saw the next door garden lie,
Adorned with flowers, before my eye,
And many pleasant places more
That I had never seen before.

I saw the dimpling river pass
And be the sky's blue looking-glass;
The dusty roads go up and down
With people tramping in to town.

If I could find a higher tree
Farther and farther I should see,
To where the grown-up river slips
Into the sea among the ships,
To where the roads on either hand
Lead onward into fairy land,
Where all the children dine at five,
And all the playthings come alive.

questions.prompt: What does the child hold while looking out?
facilitatorNotes: Both hands hold the trunk; this fixes the viewpoint inside the tree.
evidence: I held the trunk with both my hands

questions.prompt: Why is the river called the sky's looking-glass?
facilitatorNotes: It reflects the blue sky like a mirror; the child can gesture a sky above a flat reflective surface.
evidence: And be the sky's blue looking-glass;

questions.prompt: Which ending detail could belong to make-believe rather than the actual view?
facilitatorNotes: Living playthings signal fairyland, beyond the gardens and roads actually seen.
evidence: And all the playthings come alive.

days.title: The Horseman
days.challenge: Build an imagined scene from a few sensory details.
days.focus: Pale colours and a still night make a brief sight feel mysterious.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Collected Poems, 1901–1918, Volume II: Peacock Pie aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “THE HORSEMAN”; opening “I HEARD a horseman”; ending “Was of ivory.”. Scan-linked transcript: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Collected_Poems,_1901-1918/Volume_2/The_Horseman

questions.prompt: What does the speaker hear passing over the hill?
facilitatorNotes: A horseman riding. The opening gives a sound before describing the rider.
evidence: I HEARD a horseman

questions.prompt: What is silver, and what is described as ivory?
facilitatorNotes: The helmet is silver; the horse is ivory. Explain helm as helmet and ivory here as a pale material or colour in a fantasy description.
evidence: His helm was silver,

questions.prompt: Does the poem tell us where the rider is going?
facilitatorNotes: No; it leaves the journey unexplained. Invite an imagined destination while clearly distinguishing it from the printed words.
evidence: Ride over the hill;

days.title: Eight o’clock
days.challenge: Listen for changing recipients within a rhythmic count.
days.focus: A knock announces a small burst of household news.
days.context: A postman delivers letters; the poem tells who receives them. The child may use fingers or counters.

excerpt.locator:
Eight o’clock; begins “Eight o’clock;
The postman’s knock!”; ends “And three for dear Mamma.”.

questions.prompt: What sound announces the letters?
facilitatorNotes: The postman’s knock is the second line.
evidence: The postman’s knock!

questions.prompt: Who gets more letters, Papa or Mamma?
facilitatorNotes: Papa gets five and Mamma three; reread both numbers if needed.
evidence: Five letters for Papa;

questions.prompt: Who does the speaker say gets none, and how might that person feel?
facilitatorNotes: The addressed “you” gets none. Disappointment, curiosity, or indifference are possible; the poem supplies no feeling.
evidence: And none for you,

days.title: The Huntsmen
days.challenge: Notice the comic difference between ordinary sleep and horses going upstairs.
days.focus: A repeated group moves from an impossible bedtime to a noisy departure.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Collected Poems, 1901–1918, Volume II: Peacock Pie aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “THE HUNTSMEN”; opening “THREE jolly gentlemen,”; ending “And galloped away.”. Scan-linked transcript: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Collected_Poems,_1901-1918/Volume_2/The_Huntsmen

blocks.text:
THREE jolly gentlemen,
In coats of red,
Rode their horses
Up to bed.

Three jolly gentlemen
Snored till morn,
Their horses champing
The golden corn.

Three jolly gentlemen,
At break of day,
Came clitter-clatter down the stairs
And galloped away.

questions.prompt: How many gentlemen are there, and what colour are their coats?
facilitatorNotes: Three, in red coats. Let three fingers represent them during the rereading.
evidence: Three jolly gentlemen,

questions.prompt: What are the horses doing while the gentlemen snore?
facilitatorNotes: Champing golden corn: chewing it. The different sounds create a funny nighttime scene.
evidence:
Their horses champing
The golden corn.

questions.prompt: Which words make the morning departure sound noisy and quick?
facilitatorNotes: Clitter-clatter and galloped are useful clues. Contrast a quiet snore with the lively final sounds.
evidence:
Came clitter-clatter down the stairs
And galloped away.

days.title: The Quangle Wangle’s Hat
days.challenge: Notice how repeated arrivals change a lonely setting.
days.focus: An enormous hat becomes an unlikely community.
days.context: The Quangle Wangle and many visitors are invented creatures. Treat the names as sounds to enjoy, not spelling work.

excerpt.locator:
The Quangle Wangle’s Hat; begins “I.

On the top of the Crumpetty Tree”; ends “And all were as happy as happy could be,
With the Quangle Wangle Quee.”.

blocks.text: I.

On the top of the Crumpetty Tree
The Quangle Wangle sat,
But his face you could not see,
On account of his Beaver Hat.
For his Hat was a hundred and two feet wide,
With ribbons and bibbons on every side,
And bells, and buttons, and loops, and lace,
So that nobody ever could see the face
Of the Quangle Wangle Quee.
II.

The Quangle Wangle said
To himself on the Crumpetty Tree,
"Jam, and jelly, and bread
Are the best of food for me!
But the longer I live on this Crumpetty Tree
The plainer than ever it seems to me
That very few people come this way
And that life on the whole is far from gay!"
Said the Quangle Wangle Quee.
III.

But there came to the Crumpetty Tree
Mr. and Mrs. Canary;
And they said, "Did ever you see
Any spot so charmingly airy?
May we build a nest on your lovely Hat?
Mr. Quangle Wangle, grant us that!
O please let us come and build a nest
Of whatever material suits you best,
Mr. Quangle Wangle Quee!"
IV.

And besides, to the Crumpetty Tree
Came the Stork, the Duck, and the Owl;
The Snail and the Bumble-Bee,
The Frog and the Fimble Fowl
(The Fimble Fowl, with a Corkscrew leg);
And all of them said, "We humbly beg
We may build our homes on your lovely Hat,--
Mr. Quangle Wangle, grant us that!
Mr. Quangle Wangle Quee!"
V.

And the Golden Grouse came there,
And the Pobble who has no toes,
And the small Olympian bear,
And the Dong with a luminous nose.
And the Blue Baboon who played the flute,
And the Orient Calf from the Land of Tute,
And the Attery Squash, and the Bisky Bat,--
All came and built on the lovely Hat
Of the Quangle Wangle Quee.
VI.

And the Quangle Wangle said
To himself on the Crumpetty Tree,
"When all these creatures move
What a wonderful noise there'll be!"
And at night by the light of the Mulberry moon
They danced to the Flute of the Blue Baboon,
On the broad green leaves of the Crumpetty Tree,
And all were as happy as happy could be,
With the Quangle Wangle Quee.

questions.prompt: Why can nobody see the Quangle Wangle’s face?
facilitatorNotes: The enormous hat and its trimmings hide it.
evidence: For his Hat was a hundred and two feet wide,

questions.prompt: What do the first two visitors ask to build on the hat?
facilitatorNotes: The canaries ask to build a nest.
evidence: May we build a nest on your lovely Hat?

questions.prompt: How has life on the tree changed by the ending?
facilitatorNotes: It begins with loneliness and ends with many creatures enjoying music and company.
evidence: And all were as happy as happy could be,

days.title: Some One
days.challenge: Separate what the speaker is certain of from what remains unknown.
days.focus: A mysterious knock is followed by close attention to ordinary night sounds.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Collected Poems, 1901–1918, Volume II: Peacock Pie aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.
days.contentNote: A nighttime knocking sound remains unexplained.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “SOME ONE”; opening “SOME one came knocking”; ending “At all, at all, at all.”. Scan-linked transcript: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Collected_Poems,_1901-1918/Volume_2/Some_One

blocks.text:
SOME one came knocking
At my wee, small door;
Some one came knocking,
I'm sure — sure — sure;
I listened, I opened,
I looked to left and right,
But nought there was a-stirring
In the still dark night;
Only the busy beetle
Tap-tapping in the wall,
Only from the forest
The screech-owl's call,
Only the cricket whistling
While the dewdrops fall,
So I know not who came knocking,
At all, at all, at all.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker do after hearing the knock?
facilitatorNotes: Listens, opens the door and looks left and right. Follow the exact action sequence with gestures.
evidence:
I listened, I opened,
I looked to left and right,

questions.prompt: Name two creatures the speaker can hear outside or in the wall.
facilitatorNotes: Beetle, screech-owl and cricket are available. Match each named animal to its tap, call or whistle.
evidence: Only the cricket whistling

questions.prompt: Does the poem finally name the person who knocked?
facilitatorNotes: No; the speaker still does not know. The animals offer possible sound clues but the poem does not solve the mystery.
evidence: So I know not who came knocking,

days.title: Windy Nights
days.challenge: Hear repeated beats and distinguish a described rider from an unanswered question.
days.focus: A galloping rhythm makes a stormy night restless.
days.context: Read with a steady hoofbeat rhythm. The poem never tells us the rider's purpose.

excerpt.locator: Windy Nights; begins “WHENEVER the moon and stars are set,”; ends “By he comes back at the gallop again.”.

blocks.text:
WHENEVER the moon and stars are set,
Whenever the wind is high,
All night long in the dark and wet,
A man goes riding by.
Late in the night when the fires are out,
Why does he gallop and gallop about?

Whenever the trees are crying aloud,
And ships are tossed at sea,
By, on the highway, low and loud,
By at the gallop goes he.
By at the gallop he goes, and then
By he comes back at the gallop again.

questions.prompt: What is the night like when the rider passes?
facilitatorNotes: It is dark, wet, and windy; the sky's lights are set.
evidence: All night long in the dark and wet,

questions.prompt: Which repeated word sounds like the horse's movement?
facilitatorNotes: Gallop returns several times. Tap gently to hear its beat.
evidence: Why does he gallop and gallop about?

questions.prompt: Do we learn why the rider keeps coming back?
facilitatorNotes: No; the speaker asks why, and the last line repeats the return without answering.
evidence: By he comes back at the gallop again.

days.title: Bread and Cherries
days.challenge: Combine a spoken call with the buyers’ expressions to infer interest.
days.focus: Bright colours and a seller’s call bring a tiny market scene alive.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Collected Poems, 1901–1918, Volume II: Peacock Pie aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “BREAD AND CHERRIES”; opening “"CHERRIES, ripe cherries!"”; ending “To eat with their bread.”. Scan-linked transcript: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Collected_Poems,_1901-1918/Volume_2/Bread_and_Cherries

blocks.text:
"CHERRIES, ripe cherries!"
The old woman cried,
In her snowy white apron,
And basket beside;
And the little boys came,
Eyes shining, cheeks red,
To buy bags of cherries
To eat with their bread.

questions.prompt: What fruit is the woman selling?
facilitatorNotes: Ripe cherries. Repeat her opening call with a cheerful market voice.
evidence: ripe cherries!

questions.prompt: What colour is her apron, and what colour are the boys’ cheeks?
facilitatorNotes: The apron is snowy white; their cheeks are red. Ask the child to picture both colours.
evidence: Eyes shining, cheeks red,

questions.prompt: What do the boys’ shining eyes and red cheeks make you imagine about their feelings?
facilitatorNotes: They may be eager, pleased, or excited to buy the cherries. The poem gives visible details rather than naming a feeling, so accept another feeling supported by those details.
evidence: Eyes shining, cheeks red,

days.title: Wrens and robins
days.challenge: Attend to four different bird actions inside a compact scene.
days.focus: A short list makes a hedge feel crowded with life.
days.context: Read twice and invite a different small hand motion for each bird action.

excerpt.locator: Wrens and robins; begins “Wrens and robins in the hedge,”; ends “Everywhere!”.

blocks.text:
Wrens and robins in the hedge,
Wrens and robins here and there;
Building, perching, pecking, fluttering,
Everywhere!

questions.prompt: Which two kinds of birds fill this hedge?
facilitatorNotes: Wrens and robins are repeated in the first two lines.
evidence: Wrens and robins in the hedge,

questions.prompt: Which action might help the birds make a home?
facilitatorNotes: Building suggests nest-making; the poem does not describe the nests themselves.
evidence: Building, perching, pecking, fluttering,

questions.prompt: Why end with “Everywhere!” instead of naming one more place?
facilitatorNotes: It makes the birds seem abundant all around the speaker; the exclamation can sound delighted or surprised.
evidence: Everywhere!

days.title: The Skylark and Her Enemy, part 1: up before the lark
days.challenge: Notice how a well-known saying is tested by real watching.
days.focus: An early-morning experiment and a close look describe the skylark’s song and body.
days.context: A skylark is a small brown bird that sings while rising high over fields. To be “up with the lark” is an old saying for getting up very early. Gay here means brightly coloured.
days.contentNote: The children catch a lark to look at it and then let it go.

excerpt.locator: Book I, The Skylark and Her Enemy, printed pages 19–20, paragraphs 1–5; begins “There are a great many larks near our home. They …” and ends “… on the ground, except when he rises up to sing.”.

blocks.text: There are a great many larks near our home. They sing so gaily in the morning as we go to school. But they sing much earlier than that.

We wanted once to try if we could get up before the lark. So we agreed to meet at five o'clock in the morning, in the meadow where one has been singing all this year. We heard him before we got out of the lane. There he was, rising up into the air, going a little to the right, and then a little to the left, rising and singing all the time, as if he wanted to wake all the world with joy.
We watched him till he was quite a tiny speck in the sky. Then he came down again. When he was only a few feet from the ground he shut his wings and dropped into the grass.

The next morning we went at four o'clock. That lark was not singing, but one in the next field was rising up as gay as a lark could be. Then our mothers said we must not get up any earlier. So we could not rise before the larks.

We caught a lark once to look at it, and then let it fly away again. It is not a gay bird. It has brown wings marked with dark streaks. Its breast and throat are a dull white, dotted with brown spots, and it has a white streak above its eye. Its feet are curious. The toes lie flat on the ground, and the hind toe has a very long claw. If you watch a lark you will see that he runs, he does not hop. Neither does he perch in the trees, and only sometimes on a low bush. He lives on the ground, except when he rises up to sing.

questions.prompt: What did the children try to do, and did they manage it?
facilitatorNotes: To get up before the lark. They did not: a lark was already singing at five, and another at four o’clock.
evidence: We wanted once to try if we could get up before the lark.

questions.prompt: How does the lark move while it sings?
facilitatorNotes: It rises into the air, going a little right and a little left, then drops into the grass. A hand can trace the path.
evidence: rising and singing all the time

questions.prompt: The children say the lark “is not a gay bird,” even though it sings so gaily. What do they mean?
facilitatorNotes: Its feathers are dull brown and streaked rather than bright. Talk about how one word can mean bright-coloured or cheerful.
evidence: It is not a gay bird.

days.title: The Skylark and Her Enemy, part 2: the hawk overhead
days.challenge: Explain how an animal’s behaviour protects it.
days.focus: Nest-hiding, landing away from the nest, and a sudden drop all keep larks safe from the hawk.
days.context: A sparrow-hawk is a bird that hunts smaller birds. A rut is a groove in the ground, such as a wheel track.
days.contentNote: A hawk tries to catch a lark; the lark escapes.

excerpt.locator: Book I, The Skylark and Her Enemy, printed pages 20–23, paragraphs 6–10 (end of lesson); begins “In the winter, as we go to school, we see …” and ends “… safe, and got back to his wife and little ones.”.

blocks.text: In the winter, as we go to school, we see large flocks of larks in the fields, looking for insects, and seeds of wheat and oats. When we come near them, they get up, a few at a time, and fly away a little further. Then they wheel round and settle down to feed.
In the winter they scarcely ever sing. It is in the spring, when they pair, that they sing so beautifully.

About March we can often find a lark's nest hidden in the grass. They build in a rut, or a little hollow in the ground, often in the middle of the field. They line the nest with dry grass, and lay four or five eggs in it. The eggs are a dirty grey colour with brown spots on them, and they lie very snugly in the thick tufts of grass.

When the lark comes down after singing he does not drop close to the nest but a little way off. Then he runs up to the nest through the grass. This is because he is afraid that the sparrow-hawk might see the nest, and pounce on the little ones.

The sparrow-hawk is the lark's great enemy. One day we were looking at a lark rising up, and all at once we saw a sparrow-hawk just going to pounce upon it. The lark saw him too, and darted up faster than the hawk could soar. Then the hawk flew away a little and hovered about till the lark was tired and was obliged to come down. Then once more the hawk tried to pounce. But the lark was too clever for him. He closed his wings and dropped right down into the thick grass, and the hawk could not find him. We were glad the little lark was safe, and got back to his wife and little ones.

questions.prompt: Where does the lark build its nest?
facilitatorNotes: On the ground, in a rut or little hollow in the grass, often in the middle of a field.
evidence: They build in a rut, or a little hollow in the ground

questions.prompt: Why does the lark land a little way from its nest?
facilitatorNotes: So the sparrow-hawk will not see where the nest is and catch the young birds.
evidence: he is afraid that the sparrow-hawk might see the nest

questions.prompt: How does the lark escape the hawk the second time?
facilitatorNotes: He closes his wings and drops into thick grass where the hawk cannot find him. Compare this with his first escape, flying up faster than the hawk.
evidence: He closed his wings and dropped right down into the thick grass

days.title: Old Shellover
days.challenge: Infer a time of day and notice how two voices answer each other.
days.focus: Nighttime conversation invites small garden creatures into view.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Collected Poems, 1901–1918, Volume II: Peacock Pie aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.
days.contentNote: “Horny” here means hardened or tough, as with a gardener’s hands; explain that older sense only if needed.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “OLD SHELLOVER”; opening “"COME!" said Old Shellover.”; ending “"Ay!" said Creep.”. Scan-linked transcript: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Collected_Poems,_1901-1918/Volume_2/Old_Shellover

questions.prompt: Why is the garden quiet enough for this invitation?
facilitatorNotes: The gardener is asleep and the thrush has gone to its nest. These are stated circumstances; do not invent a chase.
evidence: The horny old Gardener's fast asleep;

questions.prompt: Who peeps out of a hole, and what shines in the moonlight?
facilitatorNotes: Sallie Worm peeps out; dew shines. Invite a low, close-to-the-ground view of the garden.
evidence: Old Sallie Worm from her hole doth peep;

questions.prompt: Does Creep agree to come at the end?
facilitatorNotes: Yes: Ay means yes here. Read Shellover’s invitation and Creep’s response in two voices.
evidence: "Ay!" said Creep.

days.title: Four-leaved clover
days.challenge: Follow the speaker's excited search through commands to a meadow.
days.focus: A hoped-for discovery turns grass and insects into participants.
days.context: This untitled “Garden Songs” poem begins “Oh, I'd search the world over.” A four-leaved clover is less common than one with three leaflets.

excerpt.locator: Four-leaved clover; begins “OH, I'd search the world over”; ends “There's one hidden somewhere, I know.”.

blocks.text:
OH, I'd search the world over
For one four-leaved clover!
Bend low, pretty grass, bend low!
Jump, little crickets! and tumble, you bees!
Green little grasshoppers, limber your knees!
There's one hidden somewhere, I know.

questions.prompt: What special plant is the speaker hoping to find?
facilitatorNotes: The poem names one four-leaved clover.
evidence: For one four-leaved clover!

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker ask the grass to bend low?
facilitatorNotes: Lower grass would make it easier to search beneath or among it; this is a playful request to a plant.
evidence: Bend low, pretty grass, bend low!

questions.prompt: What words show the speaker has not given up?
facilitatorNotes: The final claim insists that a clover is hidden somewhere; it conveys confidence without reporting a find.
evidence: There's one hidden somewhere, I know.

days.title: The Little Bird
days.challenge: Follow the change from crowded noise to quiet arrival.
days.focus: A lively household celebration ends with a surprising first-person image.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Collected Poems, 1901–1918, Volume II: Peacock Pie aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “THE LITTLE BIRD”; opening “MY dear Daddie bought a mansion”; ending “Wee small bird: and that was Me.”. Scan-linked transcript: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Collected_Poems,_1901-1918/Volume_2/The_Little_Bird

blocks.text:
MY dear Daddie bought a mansion
For to bring my Mammie to,
In a hat with a long feather,
And a trailing gown of blue;
And a company of fiddlers
And a rout of maids and men
Danced the clock round to the morning,
In a gay house-warming then.
And when all the guests were gone, and
All was still as still can be,
In from the dark ivy hopped a
Wee small bird: and that was Me.

questions.prompt: What makes music while the visitors dance?
facilitatorNotes: A company of fiddlers. A fiddle is a violin; the text does not name other instruments.
evidence: And a company of fiddlers

questions.prompt: When does the little bird hop in: during the party or after everyone has gone?
facilitatorNotes: After the guests are gone, when all is still. The quiet is a clear contrast with the long dancing.
evidence: And when all the guests were gone, and

questions.prompt: Why is ‘and that was Me’ a surprising ending after the little bird hops in?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker suddenly identifies with the tiny quiet visitor after the grand, noisy party. It can suggest a child’s arrival in a family through a bird image. Let the child explain the surprise without treating a person becoming a bird as a fact.
evidence: Wee small bird: and that was Me.

days.title: A Good Play
days.challenge: Keep pretend voyage-time separate from ordinary household time.
days.focus: Chairs and food turn a room into a sailing adventure.
days.context: The poem recalls a pretend game. Read without asking children to copy its use of tools or stairs.

excerpt.locator: A Good Play; begins “WE built a ship upon the stairs”; ends “So there was no one left but me.”.

blocks.text:
WE built a ship upon the stairs
All made of the back-bedroom chairs,
And filled it full of sofa pillows
To go a-sailing on the billows.

We took a saw and several nails,
And water in the nursery pails;
And Tom said, 'Let us also take
An apple and a slice of cake;'--
Which was enough for Tom and me
To go a-sailing on till tea.

We sailed along for days and days,
And had the very best of plays;
But Tom fell out and hurt his knee,
So there was no one left but me.

questions.prompt: What furniture becomes the ship?
facilitatorNotes: Chairs from the back bedroom supply the imagined ship.
evidence: All made of the back-bedroom chairs,

questions.prompt: How long will their food last in real household time?
facilitatorNotes: They say it is enough until tea, even though their game imagines sailing for days.
evidence: To go a-sailing on till tea.

questions.prompt: What event changes the game at the end?
facilitatorNotes: Tom falls out and hurts his knee, leaving the speaker alone; the injury is brief and undescribed.
evidence: But Tom fell out and hurt his knee,

days.title: Miss T.
days.challenge: Follow a long food list back to the repeated idea of one person.
days.focus: A playful list turns eating into a small everyday wonder.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Collected Poems, 1901–1918, Volume II: Peacock Pie aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “MISS T.”; opening “IT'S a very odd thing —”; ending “Turns into Miss T.”. Scan-linked transcript: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Collected_Poems,_1901-1918/Volume_2/Miss_T.

blocks.text:
IT'S a very odd thing —
As odd as can be —
That whatever Miss T. eats
Turns into Miss T.;
Porridge and apples,
Mince, muffins and mutton,
Jam, junket, jumbles —
Not a rap, not a button
It matters; the moment
They're out of her plate,
Though shared by Miss Butcher
And sour Mr. Bate;
Tiny and cheerful,
And neat as can be,
Whatever Miss T. eats
Turns into Miss T.

questions.prompt: Which two foods are named together just after the first mention of Miss T.?
facilitatorNotes: Porridge and apples. Invite the child to echo that pair before following the longer list.
evidence: Porridge and apples,

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say all the different foods turn into?
facilitatorNotes: Miss T. The poem makes the body’s use of food sound magical without explaining digestion.
evidence: Turns into Miss T.;

questions.prompt: What words describe Miss T. herself near the ending?
facilitatorNotes: Tiny, cheerful and neat. Contrast the many foods with this small, recognisable person.
evidence:
Tiny and cheerful,
And neat as can be,

days.title: The Tailor of Gloucester, part 1: one missing skein
days.challenge: Follow detailed description to identify the one missing material.
days.focus: Rich fabrics contrast with the tailor’s own poverty.
days.context: A tailor makes clothes. A skein is a small bundle of thread; twist is strong twisted silk. Gloucester is an English city. Adults may explain unfamiliar fabric words briefly rather than demand memorization.

excerpt.locator: The Tailor of Gloucester (New York: Warne, copyright 1903), narrative paragraphs 1–12; begins “IN the time of swords and periwigs and full-skirted coats …” and ends “… run all over the town without going into the streets.”.

blocks.text: IN the time of swords and periwigs and full-skirted coats with flowered lappets—when gentlemen wore ruffles, and gold-laced waistcoats of paduasoy and taffeta—there lived a tailor in Gloucester.
He sat in the window of a little shop in Westgate Street, cross-legged on a table from morning till dark.

All day long while the light lasted he sewed and snippetted, piecing out his satin, and pompadour, and lutestring; stuffs had strange names, and were very expensive in the days of the Tailor of Gloucester.
But although he sewed fine silk for his neighbours, he himself was very, very poor—a little old man in spectacles, with a pinched face, old crooked fingers, and a suit of threadbare clothes.

He cut his coats without waste; according to his embroidered cloth, they were very small ends and snippets that lay about upon the table—"Too narrow breadths for nought—except waistcoats for mice," said the tailor.

One bitter cold day near Christmas-time the tailor began to make a coat (a coat of cherry-coloured corded silk embroidered with pansies and roses) and a cream-coloured satin waistcoat (trimmed with gauze and green worsted chenille) for the Mayor of Gloucester.

The tailor worked and worked, and he talked to himself. He measured the silk, and turned it round and round, and trimmed it into shape with his shears; the table was all littered with cherry-coloured snippets.
"No breadth at all, and cut on the cross; it is no breadth at all; tippets for mice and ribbons for mobs! for mice!" said the Tailor of Gloucester.
When the snow-flakes came down against the small leaded window-panes and shut out the light, the tailor had done his day's work; all the silk and satin lay cut out upon the table.

There were twelve pieces for the coat and four pieces for the waistcoat; and there were pocket-flaps and cuffs and buttons, all in order. For the lining of the coat there was fine yellow taffeta, and for the buttonholes of the waistcoat there was cherry-coloured twist. And everything was ready to sew together in the morning, all measured and sufficient—except that there was wanting just one single skein of cherry-coloured twisted silk.

The tailor came out of his shop at dark, for he did not sleep there at nights; he fastened the window and locked the door, and took away the key. No one lived there at nights but little brown mice, and they ran in and out without any keys!

For behind the wooden wainscots of all the old houses in Gloucester, there are little mouse staircases and secret trap-doors; and the mice run from house to house through those long, narrow passages; they can run all over the town without going into the streets.

questions.prompt: How are the clothes the tailor makes different from the clothes he wears?
facilitatorNotes: He works with expensive fine silk, but his own clothes are worn. Use the contrast, not an assumption about his worth.
evidence: a suit of threadbare clothes.

questions.prompt: What tiny use does he imagine for the leftover cloth?
facilitatorNotes: Waistcoats or little garments for mice. The small scraps introduce a possibility important later.
evidence: except waistcoats for mice

questions.prompt: What is missing when the coat pieces are ready?
facilitatorNotes: One skein of cherry-colored twisted silk. Almost everything is ready, so this small shortage matters.
evidence: one single skein of cherry-coloured twisted silk.

days.title: The Tailor of Gloucester, part 2: tapping under a cup
days.challenge: Use a repeated sound to anticipate a hidden discovery.
days.focus: The tailor’s careful listening uncovers an unexpected guest.
days.context: The tailor has gone home and sent his cat Simpkin to buy food and sewing silk with his last coin. Wainscot means wooden wall paneling.

excerpt.locator: The Tailor of Gloucester (New York: Warne, copyright 1903), narrative paragraphs 13–27; begins “But the tailor came out of his shop and shuffled …” and ends “… hopped away down off the dresser, and under the wainscot.”.

blocks.text: But the tailor came out of his shop and shuffled home through the snow; he lived quite near by in College Court, next the doorway to College Green. And although it was not a big house, the tailor was so poor he only rented the kitchen.
He lived alone with his cat; it was called Simpkin.
Now all day long while the tailor was out at work, Simpkin kept house by himself; and he also was fond of the mice, though he gave them no satin for coats!
"Miaw?" said the cat when the tailor opened the door, "miaw?"

The tailor replied: "Simpkin, we shall make our fortune, but I am worn to a ravelling. Take this groat (which is our last fourpence), and, Simpkin, take a china pipkin, buy a penn'orth of bread, a penn'orth of milk, and a penn'orth of sausages. And oh, Simpkin, with the last penny of our fourpence buy me one penn'orth of cherry-coloured silk. But do not lose the last penny of the fourpence, Simpkin, or I am undone and worn to a thread-paper, for I have NO MORE TWIST."
Then Simpkin again said "Miaw!" and took the groat and the pipkin, and went out into the dark.
The tailor was very tired and beginning to be ill. He sat down by the hearth and talked to himself about that wonderful coat.

"I shall make my fortune—to be cut bias—the Mayor of Gloucester is to be married on Christmas Day in the morning, and he hath ordered a coat and an embroidered waistcoat—to be lined with yellow taffeta—and the taffeta sufficeth; there is no more left over in snippets than will serve to make tippets for mice——"
Then the tailor started; for suddenly, interrupting him, from the dresser at the other side of the kitchen came a number of little noises—
Tip tap, tip tap, tip tap tip!
"Now what can that be?" said the Tailor of Gloucester, jumping up from his chair. The dresser was covered with crockery and pipkins, willow pattern plates, and tea-cups and mugs.
The tailor crossed the kitchen, and stood quite still beside the dresser, listening, and peering through his spectacles. Again from under a teacup came those funny little noises—
Tip tap, tip tap, tip tap tip!
"This is very peculiar," said the Tailor of Gloucester, and he lifted up the tea-cup which was upside down.
Out stepped a little live lady mouse, and made a courtesy to the tailor! Then she hopped away down off the dresser, and under the wainscot.

questions.prompt: What does the tailor ask Simpkin to remember with the last penny?
facilitatorNotes: The cherry-colored silk. His repeated worry explains why the errand matters.
evidence: buy me one penn'orth of cherry-coloured silk.

questions.prompt: Where does the mysterious tapping come from?
facilitatorNotes: The dresser, then specifically beneath an upside-down teacup. Invite the child to trace how the search becomes more precise.
evidence: from under a teacup came those funny little noises

questions.prompt: How does the little mouse behave after the tailor lifts the cup?
facilitatorNotes: She makes a courtesy (an old spelling of curtsy, a polite bow) and hops away. This polite human action signals the tale’s fantasy.
evidence: made a courtesy to the tailor!

days.title: The Tailor of Gloucester, part 3: a chorus of cups
days.challenge: Notice how one repeated event grows into many.
days.focus: The released mice hear the tailor’s need and begin to respond.
days.context: One mouse has escaped from beneath a teacup. The tailor returns to worrying about his unfinished coat; then more cups begin to tap.

excerpt.locator: The Tailor of Gloucester (New York: Warne, copyright 1903), narrative paragraphs 28–39; begins “The tailor sat down again by the fire, warming his …” and ends “… kitchen when Simpkin came back with the pipkin of milk!”.

blocks.text: The tailor sat down again by the fire, warming his poor cold hands, and mumbling to himself:—

"The waistcoat is cut out from peach-coloured satin—tambour stitch and rose-buds in beautiful floss silk! Was I wise to entrust my last fourpence to Simpkin? One-and-twenty buttonholes of cherry-coloured twist!"
But all at once, from the dresser, there came other little noises—
Tip tap, tip tap, tip tap tip!
"This is passing extraordinary!" aid the Tailor of Gloucester, and turned over another tea-cup, which was upside down.
Out stepped a little gentleman mouse, and made a bow to the tailor!
And then from all over the dresser came a chorus of little tappings, all sounding together, and answering one another, like watch-beetles in an old worm-eaten window-shutter—
Tip tap, tip tap, tip tap tip!
And out from under tea-cups and from under bowls and basins, stepped other and more little mice, who hopped away down off the dresser and under the wainscot.

The tailor sat down, close over the fire, lamenting: "One-and-twenty buttonholes of cherry-coloured silk! To be finished by noon of Saturday: and this is Tuesday evening. Was it right to let loose those mice, undoubtedly the property of Simpkin? Alack, I am undone, for I have no more twist!"

The little mice came out again and listened to the tailor; they took notice of the pattern of that wonderful coat. They whispered to one another about the taffeta lining and about little mouse tippets.

And then suddenly they all ran away together down the passage behind the wainscot, squeaking and calling to one another as they ran from house to house; and not one mouse was left in the tailor's kitchen when Simpkin came back with the pipkin of milk!

questions.prompt: How does the tapping change as more mice appear?
facilitatorNotes: It becomes a chorus of taps answering one another. The repetition grows from one hidden mouse to a whole group.
evidence: a chorus of little tappings

questions.prompt: What deadline worries the tailor?
facilitatorNotes: The coat must be done by noon Saturday, and it is Tuesday evening. Children can understand soon without calculating the days.
evidence: To be finished by noon of Saturday: and this is Tuesday evening.

questions.prompt: What shows that the mice pay attention to his sewing problem?
facilitatorNotes: They listen, notice the coat pattern, and whisper about its materials. These actions suggest a plan, though the passage does not state it yet.
evidence: they took notice of the pattern of that wonderful coat.

days.title: The Tailor of Gloucester, part 4: two missing things
days.challenge: Recognize that the cat and tailor want different things.
days.focus: Simpkin’s hidden parcel creates a problem the sick tailor cannot solve.
days.context: Simpkin returns to find the mice gone. The tailor needs sewing silk, while Simpkin expected mice for supper. The story mentions that intention but no mouse is eaten.
days.contentNote: The cat wants mice for supper, but the mice are safe elsewhere. The tailor becomes ill; later excerpts show recovery.

excerpt.locator: The Tailor of Gloucester (New York: Warne, copyright 1903), narrative paragraphs 40–51; begins “Simpkin opened the door and bounced in, with an angry …” and ends “… dinner for Simpkin and the poor old tailor of Gloucester.”.

blocks.text: Simpkin opened the door and bounced in, with an angry "G-r-r-miaw!" like a cat that is vexed; for he hated the snow, and there was snow in his ears, and snow in his collar at the back of his neck. He put down the loaf and the sausages upon the dresser, and sniffed.
"Simpkin," said the tailor, "where is my twist?"
But Simpkin set down the pipkin of milk upon the dresser, and looked suspiciously at the tea-cups. He wanted his supper of little fat mouse!
"Simpkin," said the tailor, "where is my twist?"
But Simpkin hid a little parcel privately in the tea-pot, and spit and growled at the tailor; and if Simpkin had been able to talk, he would have asked: "Where is my Mouse?"
"Alack, I am undone!" said the Tailor of Gloucester, and went sadly to bed.

All that night long Simpkin hunted and searched through the kitchen, peeping into cupboards and under the wainscot, and into the tea-pot where he had hidden that twist; but still he found never a mouse!
And whenever the tailor muttered and talked in his sleep, Simpkin said: "Miaw-ger-r-w-s-s-ch!" and made strange, horrid noises, as cats do at night.
For the poor old tailor was very ill with a fever, tossing and turning in his four-post bed; and still in his dreams he mumbled: "No more twist! no more twist!"

All that day he was ill, and the next day, and the next; and what should become of the cherry-coloured coat? In the tailor's shop in Westgate Street the embroidered silk and satin lay cut out upon the table—one-and-twenty buttonholes—and who should come to sew them, when the window was barred, and the door was fast locked?
But that does not hinder the little brown mice; they run in and out without any keys through all the old houses in Gloucester!

Out-of-doors the market folks went trudging through the snow to buy their geese and turkeys, and to bake their Christmas pies; but there would be no Christmas dinner for Simpkin and the poor old tailor of Gloucester.

questions.prompt: What does the tailor keep asking Simpkin to give him?
facilitatorNotes: His twist, or sewing silk. He asks the same question twice, and Simpkin answers only with suspicious looks and growls.
evidence: where is my twist?

questions.prompt: Where does Simpkin put the parcel instead?
facilitatorNotes: He hides it in the teapot. The reader knows something the tailor does not.
evidence: hid a little parcel privately in the tea-pot

questions.prompt: Why can the mice enter the locked workshop when people cannot?
facilitatorNotes: They have small passages through the old houses and need no keys. This practical detail opens a possible solution.
evidence: they run in and out without any keys

days.title: The Tailor of Gloucester, part 5: the city finds a voice
days.challenge: Distinguish the story’s magical night from ordinary animal sounds.
days.focus: A quiet snowy city changes into a chorus heard by Simpkin.
days.context: The tailor is ill on Christmas Eve. The narrator introduces an old-story belief that animals can speak that night; it is a fantasy tradition, not a factual claim.

excerpt.locator: The Tailor of Gloucester (New York: Warne, copyright 1903), narrative paragraphs 52–66; begins “The tailor lay ill for three days and nights; and …” and ends “… ears as if he had a bee in his bonnet.”.

blocks.text: The tailor lay ill for three days and nights; and then it was Christmas Eve, and very late at night. The moon climbed up over the roofs and chimneys, and looked down over the gateway into College Court. There were no lights in the windows, nor any sound in the houses; all the city of Gloucester was fast asleep under the snow.
And still Simpkin wanted his mice, and mewed as he stood beside the four-post bed.

But it is in the old story that all the beasts can talk in the night between Christmas Eve and Christmas Day in the morning (though there are very few folk that can hear them, or know what it is that they say).
When the Cathedral clock struck twelve there was an answer—like an echo of the chimes—and Simpkin heard it, and came out of the tailor's door, and wandered about in the snow.

From all the roofs and gables and old wooden houses in Gloucester came a thousand merry voices singing the old Christmas rhymes—all the old songs that ever I heard of, and some that I don't know, like Whittington's bells.
First and loudest the cocks cried out: "Dame, get up, and bake your pies!"
"Oh, dilly, dilly, dilly!" sighed Simpkin.
And now in a garret there were lights and sounds of dancing, and cats came from over the way.
"Hey, diddle, diddle, the cat and the fiddle! All the cats in Gloucester—except me," said Simpkin

Under the wooden eaves the starlings and sparrows sang of Christmas pies; the jackdaws woke up in the Cathedral tower; and although it was the middle of the night the throstles and robins sang; the air was quite full of little twittering tunes.
But it was all rather provoking to poor hungry Simpkin.

Particularly he was vexed with some little shrill voices from behind a wooden lattice. I think that they were bats, because they always have very small voices—especially in a black frost, when they talk in their sleep, like the Tailor of Gloucester.
They said something mysterious that sounded like—

"Buzz, quoth the blue fly; hum, quoth the bee;
Buzz and hum they cry, and so do we!"
and Simpkin went away shaking his ears as if he had a bee in his bonnet.

questions.prompt: What makes the city seem quiet before midnight?
facilitatorNotes: Dark windows, sleeping houses, and snow create stillness. Accept one sound or sight detail.
evidence: all the city of Gloucester was fast asleep under the snow.

questions.prompt: What surprising thing does the old story say animals can do?
facilitatorNotes: Speak during the night before Christmas morning. Ask the child to distinguish the tale’s rule from real life.
evidence: all the beasts can talk

questions.prompt: Does all the singing make Simpkin cheerful?
facilitatorNotes: No; he is hungry and finds it provoking. The happy city sounds different from his unhappy viewpoint.
evidence: it was all rather provoking to poor hungry Simpkin.

days.title: The Tailor of Gloucester, part 6: busy voices behind shutters
days.challenge: Use sounds to infer work that the viewpoint character cannot fully see.
days.focus: Song rhythms and sewing sounds reveal the mice’s activity.
days.context: Simpkin approaches the tailor’s workshop. The mice are inside, and the door is locked. Read the nursery-rhyme passages with their pauses and repeated sounds.
days.contentNote: One traditional rhyme jokes that a cat would bite off the mice’s heads; it is a line in a song, and no one is hurt.

excerpt.locator: The Tailor of Gloucester (New York: Warne, copyright 1903), narrative paragraphs 67–82; begins “From the tailor's shop in Westgate came a glow of …” and ends “"No more twist! No more twist!"”.

blocks.text: From the tailor's shop in Westgate came a glow of light; and when Simpkin crept up to peep in at the window it was full of candles. There was a snippeting of scissors, and snappeting of thread; and little mouse voices sang loudly and gaily:

"Four-and-twenty tailors
Went to catch a snail,
The best man amongst them
Durst not touch her tail;
She put out her horns
Like a little kyloe cow.
Run, tailors, run! or she'll have you all e'en now!"
Then without a pause the little mouse voices went on again:

"Sieve my lady's oatmeal,
Grind my lady's flour,
Put it in a chestnut,
Let it stand an hour——"
"Mew! Mew!" interrupted Simpkin, and he scratched at the door. But the key was under the tailor's pillow; he could not get in.
The little mice only laughed, and tried another tune—

"Three little mice sat down to spin,
Pussy passed by and she peeped in.
What are you at, my fine little men?
Making coats for gentlemen.
Shall I come in and cut off your threads?
Oh, no, Miss Pussy, you'd bite off our heads!"
"Mew! Mew!" cried Simpkin.
"Hey diddle dinketty!" answered the little mice—

"Hey diddle dinketty, poppetty pet!
The merchants of London they wear scarlet;
Silk in the collar, and gold in the hem,
So merrily march the merchantmen!"
They clicked their thimbles to mark the time, but none of the songs pleased Simpkin; he sniffed and mewed at the door of the shop.

"And then I bought
A pipkin and a popkin,
A slipkin and a slopkin,
All for one farthing——
and upon the kitchen dresser!" added the rude little mice.

"Mew! scratch! scratch!" scuffled Simpkin on the window-sill; while the little mice inside sprang to their feet, and all began to shout at once in little twittering voices: "No more twist! No more twist!" And they barred up the window-shutters and shut out Simpkin.
But still through the nicks in the shutters he could hear the click of thimbles, and little mouse voices singing:
"No more twist! No more twist!"

questions.prompt: What sounds suggest that someone is sewing inside?
facilitatorNotes: Scissors, thread, thimbles, and mouse voices. Ask for a work sound as well as a song sound.
evidence: a snippeting of scissors, and snappeting of thread

questions.prompt: Why can Simpkin not get through the door?
facilitatorNotes: The key is under the tailor’s pillow. The locked door gives the mice a protected workspace.
evidence: the key was under the tailor's pillow

questions.prompt: Which worried phrase from the tailor do the mice call out?
facilitatorNotes: No more twist. Its return connects the mysterious sewing to the earlier shortage of silk.
evidence: No more twist! No more twist!

days.title: The Tailor of Gloucester, part 7: the nearly finished coat
days.challenge: Join earlier clues to explain a kindness never directly shown being completed.
days.focus: Tiny stitches and one missing buttonhole reveal the unseen helpers.
days.context: Simpkin has heard the busy mice in the workshop. The tailor is recovering as Christmas morning arrives. Listen for what changes in the cat’s choices.

excerpt.locator: The Tailor of Gloucester (New York: Warne, copyright 1903), narrative paragraphs 83–101 (end); begins “Simpkin came away from the shop and went home considering …” and ends “… looked as if they had been made by little mice!”.

blocks.text: Simpkin came away from the shop and went home considering in his mind. He found the poor old tailor without fever, sleeping peacefully.
Then Simpkin went on tip-toe and took a little parcel of silk out of the tea-pot; and looked at it in the moonlight; and he felt quite ashamed of his badness compared with those good little mice!
When the tailor awoke in the morning, the first thing which he saw, upon the patchwork quilt, was a skein of cherry-coloured twisted silk, and beside his bed stood the repentant Simpkin!
"Alack, I am worn to a ravelling," said the tailor of Gloucester, "but I have my twist!"
The sun was shining on the snow when the tailor got up and dressed, and came out into the street with Simpkin running before him.
The starlings whistled on the chimney stacks, and the throstles and robins sang—but they sang their own little noises, not the words they had sung in the night.

"Alack," said the tailor, "I have my twist; but no more strength—nor time—than will serve to make me one single buttonhole; for this is Christmas Day in the Morning! The Mayor of Gloucester shall be married by noon —and where is his cherry-coloured coat?"
He unlocked the door of the little shop in Westgate Street, and Simpkin ran in, like a cat that expects something.
But there was no one there! Not even one little brown mouse!
The boards were swept and clean; the little ends of thread and the little silk snippets were all tidied away, and gone from off the floor.

But upon the table—oh joy! the tailor gave a shout—there, where he had left plain cuttings of silk there lay the most beautifullest coat and embroidered satin waistcoat that ever were worn by a Mayor of Gloucester!
There were roses and pansies upon the facings of the coat; and the waistcoat was worked with poppies and corn-flowers.
Everything was finished except just one single cherry-coloured buttonhole, and where that buttonhole was wanting there was pinned a scrap of paper with these words—in little teeny weeny writing—
NO MORE TWIST.
And from then began the luck of the Tailor of Gloucester; he grew quite stout, and he grew quite rich.
He made the most wonderful waistcoats for all the rich merchants of Gloucester, and for all the fine gentlemen of the country round.
Never were seen such ruffles, or such embroidered cuffs and lappets! But his buttonholes were the greatest triumph of it all.
The stitches of those buttonholes were so neat—so neat—I wonder how they could be stitched by an old man in spectacles, with crooked old fingers, and a tailor's thimble.
The stitches of those buttonholes were so small—so small—they looked as if they had been made by little mice!

questions.prompt: What does Simpkin do after feeling ashamed?
facilitatorNotes: He retrieves the silk and leaves it by the tailor’s bed. This action repairs his earlier concealment.
evidence: took a little parcel of silk out of the tea-pot

questions.prompt: What single piece of work is still unfinished on the beautiful coat?
facilitatorNotes: One cherry-coloured buttonhole, with a note saying no more twist. The shortage exactly matches the earlier problem.
evidence: except just one single cherry-coloured buttonhole

questions.prompt: Why does the narrator wonder whether mice made the buttonholes?
facilitatorNotes: The stitches are extraordinarily tiny, and earlier clues showed mice sewing. Invite evidence-based inference rather than insisting the text directly shows every stitch.
evidence: they looked as if they had been made by little mice!

days.title: If all were rain
days.challenge: Compare two opposite imagined weather conditions.
days.focus: Parallel statements show that either single condition is insufficient for a rainbow.
days.context: “Bow” here means rainbow. Draw a sun, rain, and rainbow while rereading.

excerpt.locator: If all were rain; begins “If all were rain and never sun,”; ends “There’d be no rainbow still.”.

blocks.text:
If all were rain and never sun,
No bow could span the hill;
If all were sun and never rain,
There’d be no rainbow still.

questions.prompt: What is missing in the first imagined world?
facilitatorNotes: There is rain but never sun.
evidence: If all were rain and never sun,

questions.prompt: What is missing in the second imagined world?
facilitatorNotes: There is sun but never rain.
evidence: If all were sun and never rain,

questions.prompt: Why do both halves end without a rainbow?
facilitatorNotes: The poem brings together the need for rain and sunlight; explain that sunlight and water droplets can make a rainbow visible.
evidence: There’d be no rainbow still.

days.title: The Cupboard
days.challenge: Track a refrain while identifying the person who controls the cupboard.
days.focus: A repeated wish for treats circles around a grandmother and her key.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Collected Poems, 1901–1918, Volume II: Peacock Pie aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.
days.contentNote: The poem links sweets with being “good” and describes a grandmother’s body. Treat those as this speaker’s historical language, not rules about food or people’s worth.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “THE CUPBOARD”; opening “I KNOW a little cupboard,”; ending “For me, me, me.”. Scan-linked transcript: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Collected_Poems,_1901-1918/Volume_2/The_Cupboard

blocks.text:
I KNOW a little cupboard,
With a teeny tiny key,
And there's a jar of Lollypops
For me, me, me.

It has a little shelf, my dear,
As dark as dark can be,
And there's a dish of Banbury Cakes
For me, me, me.

I have a small fat grandmamma,
With a very slippery knee,
And she's Keeper of the Cupboard,
With a key, key, key.

And when I'm very good, my dear,
As good as good can be,
There's Banbury Cakes, and Lollypops
For me, me, me.

questions.prompt: Which two kinds of treats are kept in the cupboard?
facilitatorNotes: Lollypops and Banbury Cakes. Explain the latter as a named kind of cake or pastry.
evidence: And there's a dish of Banbury Cakes

questions.prompt: Who keeps the key?
facilitatorNotes: The grandmother, called Keeper of the Cupboard. The capital letters make her ordinary role sound grand.
evidence: And she's Keeper of the Cupboard,

questions.prompt: What phrase keeps reminding us whose eager voice we hear?
facilitatorNotes: For me, me, me. Invite a rhythmic echo and discuss how repetition shows eagerness.
evidence: For me, me, me.

days.title: Looking-Glass River
days.challenge: Follow a reflected picture as the water changes.
days.focus: A temporary disturbance creates suspense and then reassurance.
days.context: A looking-glass is a mirror; “wimple” is a small ripple. These are observations from beside the river.

excerpt.locator:
Looking-Glass River; begins “SMOOTH it slides upon its travel,”; ends “The stream and all in it
Will clear by-and-by.”.

blocks.text:
SMOOTH it slides upon its travel,
Here a wimple, there a gleam--
O the clean gravel!
O the smooth stream!

Sailing blossoms, silver fishes,
Paven pools as clear as air--
How a child wishes
To live down there!

We can see our coloured faces
Floating on the shaken pool
Down in cool places,
Dim and very cool;

Till a wind or water wrinkle,
Dipping marten, plumping trout,
Spreads in a twinkle
And blots all out.

See the rings pursue each other;
All below grows black as night,
Just as if mother
Had blown out the light!

Patience, children, just a minute--
See the spreading circles die;
The stream and all in it
Will clear by-and-by.

questions.prompt: What familiar shapes can the children see floating in the pool?
facilitatorNotes: Their colored faces appear as reflections.
evidence: We can see our coloured faces

questions.prompt: What happens when a trout or a dip in the water makes ripples?
facilitatorNotes: Spreading circles blot out the clear reflection.
evidence:
Spreads in a twinkle
And blots all out.

questions.prompt: Why does the last stanza ask for patience?
facilitatorNotes: The circles will subside and the stream will look clear again; the disappearance is temporary.
evidence: See the spreading circles die;

days.title: Hide and Seek
days.challenge: Hear a recurring game phrase and follow the final change of speaker.
days.focus: Natural hiding places lead into the private experience of falling asleep.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Collected Poems, 1901–1918, Volume II: Peacock Pie aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “HIDE AND SEEK”; opening “HIDE and seek, says the Wind,”; ending “Into the dream of Sleep.”. Scan-linked transcript: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Collected_Poems,_1901-1918/Volume_2/Hide_and_Seek

questions.prompt: Where does the wind seem to play hide and seek?
facilitatorNotes: In the shade of the woods. Imagine leaves and shade moving without claiming that wind is a person.
evidence: In the shade of the woods;

questions.prompt: Which sky visitors speak the same game words after the wind?
facilitatorNotes: The Moon and the Cloud. The repeated phrase connects different parts of the scene.
evidence: Hide and seek, says the Moon,

questions.prompt: Where does the speaker go at the end instead of into the woods or sea?
facilitatorNotes: From Wake into Sleep. The ending turns the game into an image of falling asleep.
evidence:
Out of the dream of Wake
Into the dream of Sleep.

days.title: O wind, where have you been
days.challenge: Connect an invisible scent with a named flower and season.
