days.focus: A question to the wind makes the spring air carry a story.
days.context: Turf means grassy ground; honeysuckle and violets are flowering plants.

excerpt.locator: O wind, where have you been; begins “O wind, where have you been,”; ends “Make the turf so sweet.”.

blocks.text:
O wind, where have you been,
That you blow so sweet?
Among the violets
Which blossom at your feet.

The honeysuckle waits
For Summer and for heat.
But violets in the chilly Spring
Make the turf so sweet.

questions.prompt: What makes the speaker describe the wind as sweet?
facilitatorNotes: The wind has passed among violets, whose scent fills the air.
evidence: Among the violets

questions.prompt: Which flower waits for hotter weather?
facilitatorNotes: Honeysuckle waits for summer and heat.
evidence: The honeysuckle waits

questions.prompt: How can the spring be chilly and still be pleasant in this poem?
facilitatorNotes: Violets make the grass smell sweet before summer warmth arrives.
evidence: But violets in the chilly Spring

days.title: Master of All Masters: too many special names
days.challenge: Remember a set of substituted words long enough to decode a message.
days.focus: The ending tests the usefulness of a character’s elaborate private vocabulary.
days.context: A girl begins working in a household whose owner has invented names for ordinary objects. Read the repeated questions slowly; the final warning combines the names.
days.contentNote: The story ends with a warning about a spark on a cat’s tail and possible house fire; no injury is described. In a real emergency tell a nearby adult clearly.

excerpt.locator: Master of All Masters, 1922 edition pp. 333–334, complete; begins “A girl once went to the fair to hire herself …” and ends “That's all!!”.

blocks.text: A girl once went to the fair to hire herself for servant. At last a funny-looking old gentleman engaged her, and took her home to his house. When she got there, he told her that he had something to teach her, for that in his house he had his own names for things.
He said to her, "What will you call me?"
"Master or mister, or whatever you please, sir," says she.
He said, "You must call me 'master of all masters.' And what would you call this?" pointing to his bed.
"Bed or couch, or whatever you please, sir."
"No, that's my 'barnacle.' And what do you call these?" said he, pointing to his pantaloons.
"Breeches or trousers, or whatever you please, sir."
"You must call them 'squibs and crackers.' And what would you call her?" pointing to the cat.
"Cat or kit, or whatever you please, sir."
"You must call her 'white-faced simminy.' And this now," showing the fire, "what would you call this?"
"Fire or flame, or whatever you please, sir."
"You must call it 'hot cockalorum,' and what this?" he went on, pointing to the water.
"Water or wet, or whatever you please, sir."
"No, 'pondalorum' is its name. And what do you call all this?" asked he, as he pointed to the house.
"House or cottage, or whatever you please, sir."
"You must call it 'high topper mountain.'"

That very night the servant woke her master up in a fright and said, "Master of all masters, get out of your barnacle and put on your squibs and crackers. For white-faced simminy has got a spark of hot cockalorum on its tail, and unless you get some pondalorum high topper mountain will be all on hot cockalorum." ...
That's all!!

questions.prompt: Which invented name stands for the bed?
facilitatorNotes: Barnacle. Reread the girl’s ordinary question and the master’s special answer.
evidence: that's my 'barnacle.

questions.prompt: What does white-faced simminy mean?
facilitatorNotes: The cat. Let the child use the earlier dialogue as a key rather than guessing from sound alone.
evidence: white-faced simminy

questions.prompt: Why might the final warning be easier to act on in ordinary words?
facilitatorNotes: It says the cat has a spark on its tail and water is needed before the house burns. Many unusual names make an urgent warning hard to understand.
evidence: all on hot cockalorum

days.title: The Window
days.challenge: Compare what the speaker can see with what passers-by cannot see.
days.focus: A hidden watcher notices a world that does not notice the watcher.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Collected Poems, 1901–1918, Volume II: Peacock Pie aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “THE WINDOW”; opening “BEHIND the blinds I sit and watch”; ending “Nor will guess when I am gone.”. Scan-linked transcript: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Collected_Poems,_1901-1918/Volume_2/The_Window

blocks.text:
BEHIND the blinds I sit and watch
The people passing — passing by;
And not a single one can see
My tiny watching eye.

questions.prompt: Where is the speaker sitting while watching people pass?
facilitatorNotes: Behind the blinds. That covering helps explain why the watcher is unseen.
evidence: BEHIND the blinds I sit and watch

questions.prompt: What colour does the sunlight make the little room?
facilitatorNotes: Yellow. Shaded sunlight suggests filtered light rather than an electric lamp.
evidence: All yellowed with the shaded sun;

questions.prompt: Do the people outside know when the speaker leaves?
facilitatorNotes: No; the final line says they will not guess. The poem keeps the speaker’s small private world separate from the passing crowd.
evidence: Nor will guess when I am gone.

days.title: From a Railway Carriage
days.challenge: Follow fast-changing sights while hearing a strong rhythmic beat.
days.focus: Rapid lists imitate the experience of looking out of a moving train.
days.context: “Brambles” are thorny berry bushes; the poem uses “tramp” for a person traveling on foot without a settled home.

excerpt.locator: From a Railway Carriage; begins “FASTER than fairies, faster than witches,”; ends “Each a glimpse and gone forever!”.

questions.prompt: Name two things that flash past near the beginning.
facilitatorNotes: Bridges, houses, hedges, and ditches are all supplied.
evidence: Bridges and houses, hedges and ditches;

questions.prompt: What is the child outside the train doing?
facilitatorNotes: The child climbs and scrambles while gathering brambles.
evidence: All by himself and gathering brambles;

questions.prompt: Why does the poem give us just a glimpse of each scene?
facilitatorNotes: The train moves quickly, so each sight is left behind before the speaker can linger.
evidence: Each a glimpse and gone forever!

days.title: Full Moon
days.challenge: Follow a gradual arrival and departure through light and movement.
days.focus: Moonlight becomes a quiet visitor beside a sleepy child.
days.context: An adult reads this complete poem from Collected Poems, 1901–1918, Volume II: Peacock Pie aloud, then rereads it with pauses for the child to point, speak or act. No independent decoding is expected.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “FULL MOON”; opening “ONE night as Dick lay half asleep,”; ending “She vanished, and was gone.”. Scan-linked transcript: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Collected_Poems,_1901-1918/Volume_2/Full_Moon

blocks.text:
ONE night as Dick lay half asleep,
Into his drowsy eyes
A great still light began to creep
From out the silent skies.

It was the lovely moon's, for when
He raised his dreamy head,
Her surge of silver filled the pane
And streamed across his bed.

So, for awhile, each gazed at each —
Dick and the solemn moon —
Till, climbing slowly on her way,
She vanished, and was gone.

questions.prompt: What first enters Dick’s drowsy eyes?
facilitatorNotes: A great still light from the skies. The next stanza identifies it as moonlight.
evidence: A great still light began to creep

questions.prompt: Where does the silver light travel after filling the windowpane?
facilitatorNotes: Across Dick’s bed. Invite a slow sweeping hand gesture to follow its path.
evidence: And streamed across his bed.

questions.prompt: Who leaves at the end: Dick or the moon?
facilitatorNotes: The moon moves on and vanishes from view. The poem presents them as gazing at each other, giving the moon a personlike presence.
evidence:
Till, climbing slowly on her way,
She vanished, and was gone.

days.title: On the grassy banks
days.challenge: Contrast the movement of young animals with the adults watching them.
days.focus: Woolly family language makes a lively scene affectionate.
days.context: Lambkins means little lambs, and bleating is the sound sheep make.

excerpt.locator:
On the grassy banks; begins “On the grassy banks
Lambkins at their pranks;”; ends “Watch by them and bleat.”.

blocks.text:
On the grassy banks
Lambkins at their pranks;
Woolly sisters, woolly brothers
Jumping off their feet
While their woolly mothers
Watch by them and bleat.

questions.prompt: Which animals jump off their feet?
facilitatorNotes: The lambs are the playful “woolly sisters” and “woolly brothers.”
evidence: Jumping off their feet

questions.prompt: What do their mothers do while the lambs play?
facilitatorNotes: They stay nearby, watching and bleating.
evidence: Watch by them and bleat.

questions.prompt: How does repeating “woolly” connect the lambs and mothers?
facilitatorNotes: All share the same soft woolly appearance and are described as a family.
evidence: While their woolly mothers

days.title: Under the Window
days.challenge: Infer affection from what the speaker notices and hopes for.
days.focus: An early-rising speaker imagines companionship with flowers and a robin.
days.context: A child looks from home into a small garden. ‘Betimes’ means early, and ‘durst’ means dared. Listen for the difference between seeing a bird and imagining a conversation.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAGE 15”; opening “UNDER the window is my garden,”; ending “And perhaps he’d chat—if he durst.”.

blocks.text:
UNDER the window is my garden,
Where sweet, sweet flowers grow;
And in the pear-tree dwells a robin,
The dearest bird I know.

Tho’ I peep out betimes in the morning,
Still the flowers are up the first;
Then I try and talk to the robin,
And perhaps he’d chat—if he durst.

questions.prompt: Where does the robin live?
facilitatorNotes: In the pear-tree in the garden. Let the child point above an imagined garden rather than needing a picture.
evidence: And in the pear-tree dwells a robin,

questions.prompt: Who is already up when the speaker looks out early?
facilitatorNotes: The flowers are up first. The poem talks as if flowers wake up like people.
evidence: Still the flowers are up the first;

questions.prompt: Has the robin actually answered the speaker?
facilitatorNotes: No; perhaps it would chat if it dared. Explain durst as dared and keep the wish separate from a reported conversation.
evidence: And perhaps he’d chat—if he durst.

days.title: The Jumblies
days.challenge: Use the recurring chorus to stay oriented through a longer imaginary voyage.
days.focus: Impossible equipment and repeated confidence carry a nonsense adventure.
days.context: A sieve has holes for draining liquid. Invite the child to join “Far and few” each time; pause briefly between sections.
days.contentNote: The imaginary voyage includes warnings about drowning and a tobacco-pipe used as a mast. Its impossible boat is make-believe.

excerpt.locator:
The Jumblies; begins “I.

They went to sea in a sieve, they did;”; ends “And every one said, "If we only live,
We, too, will go to sea in a sieve,
To the hills of the Chankly Bore."
Far and few, far and few,
Are the lands where the Jumblies live:
Their heads are green, and their hands are blue;
And they went to sea in a sieve.”.

blocks.text: I.

They went to sea in a sieve, they did;
In a sieve they went to sea:
In spite of all their friends could say,
On a winter's morn, on a stormy day,
In a sieve they went to sea.
And when the sieve turned round and round,
And every one cried, "You'll all be drowned!"
They called aloud, "Our sieve ain't big;
But we don't care a button, we don't care a fig:
In a sieve we'll go to sea!"
Far and few, far and few,
Are the lands where the Jumblies live:
Their heads are green, and their hands are blue
And they went to sea in a sieve.
II.

They sailed away in a sieve, they did,
In a sieve they sailed so fast,
With only a beautiful pea-green veil
Tied with a ribbon, by way of a sail,
To a small tobacco-pipe mast.
And every one said who saw them go,
"Oh! won't they be soon upset, you know?
For the sky is dark, and the voyage is long;
And, happen what may, it's extremely wrong
In a sieve to sail so fast."
Far and few, far and few,
Are the lands where the Jumblies live:
Their heads are green, and their hands are blue;
And they went to sea in a sieve.
III.

The water it soon came in, it did;
The water it soon came in:
So, to keep them dry, they wrapped their feet
In a pinky paper all folded neat;
And they fastened it down with a pin.
And they passed the night in a crockery-jar;
And each of them said, "How wise we are!
Though the sky be dark, and the voyage be long,
Yet we never can think we were rash or wrong,
While round in our sieve we spin."
Far and few, far and few,
Are the lands where the Jumblies live:
Their heads are green, and their hands are blue;
And they went to sea in a sieve.
IV.

And all night long they sailed away;
And when the sun went down,
They whistled and warbled a moony song
To the echoing sound of a coppery gong,
In the shade of the mountains brown.
"O Timballoo! How happy we are
When we live in a sieve and a crockery-jar!
And all night long, in the moonlight pale,
We sail away with a pea-green sail
In the shade of the mountains brown."
Far and few, far and few,
Are the lands where the Jumblies live:
Their heads are green, and their hands are blue;
And they went to sea in a sieve.
V.

They sailed to the Western Sea, they did,--
To a land all covered with trees:
And they bought an owl, and a useful cart,
And a pound of rice, and a cranberry-tart,
And a hive of silvery bees;
And they bought a pig, and some green jackdaws,
And a lovely monkey with lollipop paws,
And forty bottles of ring-bo-ree,
And no end of Stilton cheese.
Far and few, far and few,
Are the lands where the Jumblies live:
Their heads are green, and their hands are blue;
And they went to sea in a sieve.
VI.

And in twenty years they all came back,--
In twenty years or more;
And every one said, "How tall they've grown!
For they've been to the Lakes, and the Torrible Zone,
And the hills of the Chankly Bore."
And they drank their health, and gave them a feast
Of dumplings made of beautiful yeast;
And every one said, "If we only live,
We, too, will go to sea in a sieve,
To the hills of the Chankly Bore."
Far and few, far and few,
Are the lands where the Jumblies live:
Their heads are green, and their hands are blue;
And they went to sea in a sieve.

questions.prompt: Why do the friends think a sieve is a worrying boat?
facilitatorNotes: Water can enter its holes; the poem later confirms water comes in.
evidence: The water it soon came in, it did;

questions.prompt: Which strange purchase would you most like to picture?
facilitatorNotes: The child can choose a named purchase and explain its strangeness; a monkey’s lollipop paws are clearly fanciful.
evidence: And a lovely monkey with lollipop paws,

questions.prompt: Do the people welcome the travelers home? What happens that tells you?
facilitatorNotes: They give them a feast and want to make a similar journey, changing the earlier worried response.
evidence: And they drank their health, and gave them a feast

days.title: You See, Merry Phillis
days.challenge: Connect several setting details to a pleasant mood.
days.focus: A garden tea party is pictured through food, shade and a watching bird.
days.context: Two friends meet for tea in a garden. A ‘spray’ is a small leafy branch, and ‘gay’ here means cheerful. Picture the setting while the adult reads.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAGE 17”; opening “YOU see, merry Phillis, that dear little maid,”; ending “No wonder the blackbird is gay!”.

blocks.text:
YOU see, merry Phillis, that dear little maid,
Has invited Belinda to tea;
Her nice little garden is shaded by trees,—
What pleasanter place could there be?

There’s a cake full of plums, there are strawberries too,
And the table is set on the green;
I’m fond of a carpet all daisies and grass,—
Could a prettier picture be seen?

A blackbird (yes, blackbirds delight in warm weather,)
Is flitting from yonder high spray;
He sees the two little ones talking together,—
No wonder the blackbird is gay!

questions.prompt: Who has invited Belinda to tea?
facilitatorNotes: Phillis. Say the two names distinctly so listeners can follow host and guest.
evidence: Has invited Belinda to tea;

questions.prompt: What is the garden’s carpet made of?
facilitatorNotes: Daisies and grass, not woven cloth. The comparison makes the outdoor ground feel like a furnished room.
evidence: I’m fond of a carpet all daisies and grass,—

questions.prompt: What does the blackbird see the two children doing?
facilitatorNotes: Talking together. Gay here means cheerful; the speaker imagines that their happy meeting pleases the bird.
evidence: He sees the two little ones talking together,—

days.title: Winter-Time
days.challenge: Connect several fanciful comparisons with physical winter sensations.
days.focus: The speaker makes cold weather visible and tangible through images.
days.context: A comforter here is a warm scarf. The sun is described as sleepy because winter daylight is brief.

excerpt.locator: Winter-Time; begins “LATE lies the wintry sun a-bed,”; ends “Are frosted like a wedding-cake.”.

blocks.text:
LATE lies the wintry sun a-bed,
A frosty, fiery sleepy-head;
Blinks but an hour or two; and then,
A blood-red orange, sets again.

Before the stars have left the skies,
At morning in the dark I rise;
And shivering in my nakedness,
By the cold candle, bathe and dress.

Close by the jolly fire I sit
To warm my frozen bones a bit;
Or with a reindeer-sled, explore
The colder countries round the door.

When to go out, my nurse doth wrap
Me in my comforter and cap:
The cold wind burns my face, and blows
Its frosty pepper up my nose.

questions.prompt: What fruit does the setting sun resemble?
facilitatorNotes: A blood-red orange gives its shape and color.
evidence: A blood-red orange, sets again.

questions.prompt: What might “frosty pepper” help you imagine feeling?
facilitatorNotes: Sharp cold air stings the nose as pepper might; the wind carries no real pepper.
evidence: Its frosty pepper up my nose.

questions.prompt: What do the landscape and a wedding cake have in common at the end?
facilitatorNotes: A pale coating covers trees, houses, hills, and the lake, resembling frosting.
evidence: Are frosted like a wedding-cake.

days.title: As I Stepped Out to Hear the News
days.challenge: Follow a small description and hear the comic final detail.
days.focus: A meeting draws attention from a girl’s shoes to the ordinary surprise inside them.
days.context: A speaker goes outside hoping to hear news and notices a girl passing. Pause before the last line to hear the small surprise.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAGE 18”; opening “AS I stepped out to hear the news,”; ending “She’d a nice little pair of feet inside them!”.

blocks.text:
AS I stepped out to hear the news,
I met a lass in socks and shoes;
She’d shoes with strings, and a friend had tied them,
She’d a nice little pair of feet inside them!

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker first step out?
facilitatorNotes: To hear the news. The poem soon turns from that purpose to a girl’s appearance.
evidence: AS I stepped out to hear the news,

questions.prompt: Who has tied the girl’s shoe strings?
facilitatorNotes: A friend. She’d here means she had; explain the shortened form orally if needed.
evidence: and a friend had tied them,

questions.prompt: What is inside the shoes at the end, and why might that answer make us smile?
facilitatorNotes: Her feet. It is exactly what one expects, but the poem announces it as a pleasing discovery.
evidence: She’d a nice little pair of feet inside them!

days.title: Rushes in a watery place
days.challenge: Compare two kinds of movement and then notice a change over time.
days.focus: Six lines join habitat, motion, and seasonal growth.
days.context: Rushes and reeds are plants that grow in wet places. Pause after each pair of lines.

excerpt.locator: Rushes in a watery place; begins “Rushes in a watery place,”; ends “Ripe fruit to follow.”.

questions.prompt: What kinds of places hold the rushes and reeds?
facilitatorNotes: A watery place and a hollow are named, suggesting low wet ground.
evidence: And reeds in a hollow;

questions.prompt: How do the skylark and swallow move differently?
facilitatorNotes: One soars and one darts; invite a broad motion and a quick one.
evidence:
A soaring skylark in the sky,
A darting swallow;

questions.prompt: What will be found where blossoms used to hang?
facilitatorNotes: Ripe fruit follows the earlier blossoms, so the ending moves ahead in time.
evidence: Ripe fruit to follow.

days.title: Jemima Puddle-Duck, part 1: looking for a nesting place
days.challenge: Separate a character’s strong wish from other characters’ opinions of her.
days.focus: Determination sets an independent journey in motion.
days.context: Jemima wants to hatch her own eggs. A poke bonnet is a hat with a deep brim. This animal fantasy gives a duck human clothing and conversation.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Jemima Puddle-Duck, paragraphs 1–14; begins “What a funny sight it is to see a brood …” and ends “… nesting-place. She rather fancied a tree-stump amongst some tall fox-gloves.”.

blocks.text: What a funny sight it is to see a brood of ducklings with a hen!
--Listen to the story of Jemima Puddle-duck, who was annoyed because the farmer's wife would not let her hatch her own eggs.

Her sister-in-law, Mrs. Rebeccah Puddle-duck, was perfectly willing to leave the hatching to some one else--"I have not the patience to sit on a nest for twenty-eight days; and no more have you, Jemima. You would let them go cold; you know you would!"
"I wish to hatch my own eggs; I will hatch them all by myself," quacked Jemima Puddle-duck.
She tried to hide her eggs; but they were always found and carried off.
Jemima Puddle-duck became quite desperate. She determined to make a nest right away from the farm.
She set off on a fine spring afternoon along the cart-road that leads over the hill.
She was wearing a shawl and a poke bonnet.
When she reached the top of the hill, she saw a wood in the distance.
She thought that it looked a safe quiet spot.
Jemima Puddle-duck was not much in the habit of flying. She ran downhill a few yards flapping her shawl, and then she jumped off into the air.
She flew beautifully when she had got a good start.
She skimmed along over the tree-tops until she saw an open place in the middle of the wood, where the trees and brushwood had been cleared.
Jemima alighted rather heavily, and began to waddle about in search of a convenient dry nesting-place. She rather fancied a tree-stump amongst some tall fox-gloves.

questions.prompt: What does Jemima want to do herself?
facilitatorNotes: Sit on and hatch her eggs. Repeat her own statement before discussing other characters’ opinions.
evidence: I wish to hatch my own eggs

questions.prompt: Why does she decide to leave the farm?
facilitatorNotes: Her hidden eggs are repeatedly found and taken away. The repeated frustration explains the journey.
evidence: they were always found and carried off.

questions.prompt: What makes the distant wood attractive to Jemima?
facilitatorNotes: She thinks it looks safe and quiet. That is her judgment at this point, not a guarantee from the narrator.
evidence: She thought that it looked a safe quiet spot.

days.title: Jemima Puddle-Duck, part 2: the polite stranger
days.challenge: Notice clues that a character overlooks.
days.focus: Courteous speech and suspicious physical details point in different directions.
days.context: Jemima has arrived in a wood to find a dry nest. Civil means polite. Faggots here means bundles of sticks used for building; earth can mean an animal’s den.
days.contentNote: A fox disguises his dangerous intentions with politeness; later excerpts show Jemima being rescued.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Jemima Puddle-Duck, paragraphs 15–33; begins “But--seated upon the stump, she was startled to find an …” and ends “… be proud to see a fine nestful in his wood-shed.”.

blocks.text: But--seated upon the stump, she was startled to find an elegantly dressed gentleman reading a newspaper.
He had black prick ears and sandy coloured whiskers.
"Quack?" said Jemima Puddle-duck, with her head and her bonnet on one side--"Quack?"
The gentleman raised his eyes above his newspaper and looked curiously at Jemima--
"Madam, have you lost your way?" said he. He had a long bushy tail which he was sitting upon, as the stump was somewhat damp.
Jemima thought him mighty civil and handsome. She explained that she had not lost her way, but that she was trying to find a convenient dry nesting-place.
"Ah! is that so? indeed!" said the gentleman with sandy whiskers, looking curiously at Jemima. He folded up the newspaper, and put it in his coat-tail pocket.
Jemima complained of the superfluous hen.
"Indeed! how interesting! I wish I could meet with that fowl. I would teach it to mind its own business!"

"But as to a nest--there is no difficulty: I have a sackful of feathers in my wood-shed. No, my dear madam, you will be in nobody's way. You may sit there as long as you like," said the bushy long-tailed gentleman.
He led the way to a very retired, dismal-looking house amongst the fox-gloves.
It was built of faggots and turf, and there were two broken pails, one on top of another, by way of a chimney.
"This is my summer residence; you would not find my earth--my winter house--so convenient," said the hospitable gentleman.
There was a tumble-down shed at the back of the house, made of old soap-boxes. The gentleman opened the door, and showed Jemima in.
The shed was almost quite full of feathers--it was almost suffocating; but it was comfortable and very soft.
Jemima Puddle-duck was rather surprised to find such a vast quantity of feathers. But it was very comfortable; and she made a nest without any trouble at all.
When she came out, the sandy whiskered gentleman was sitting on a log reading the newspaper--at least he had it spread out, but he was looking over the top of it.
He was so polite, that he seemed almost sorry to let Jemima go home for the night. He promised to take great care of her nest until she came back again next day.
He said he loved eggs and ducklings; he should be proud to see a fine nestful in his wood-shed.

questions.prompt: What features suggest what kind of animal the gentleman is?
facilitatorNotes: Pointed ears, sandy whiskers, and a bushy tail suggest a fox. The text lets listeners infer this before calling him foxy later.
evidence: He had black prick ears and sandy coloured whiskers.

questions.prompt: Why does Jemima like the shed?
facilitatorNotes: It has soft feathers, so making a nest is easy. Invite the child also to wonder why there are so many feathers.
evidence: she made a nest without any trouble at all.

questions.prompt: What suggests that the gentleman is watching Jemima rather than reading?
facilitatorNotes: His newspaper is spread out, but he looks over the top. This detail invites suspicion without proving everything he plans.
evidence: he was looking over the top of it.

days.title: Jemima Puddle-Duck, part 3: an attentive listener
days.challenge: Compare a disguised warning sign with a careful listener’s questions.
days.focus: The narrator supplies a clue that the main character misses.
days.context: Jemima returns each afternoon to the fox’s shed. An omelette is an egg dish; herbs such as sage and thyme flavor food. The fox’s slips in speech matter.
days.contentNote: The narrator calls Jemima a simpleton. Discuss how deception works without blaming someone for being deceived; Kep seeks help.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Jemima Puddle-Duck, paragraphs 34–45; begins “Jemima Puddle-duck came every afternoon; she laid nine eggs in …” and ends “… fox-hound puppies who were out at walk with the butcher.”.

blocks.text: Jemima Puddle-duck came every afternoon; she laid nine eggs in the nest. They were greeny white and very large. The foxy gentleman admired them immensely. He used to turn them over and count them when Jemima was not there.

At last Jemima told him that she intended to begin to sit next day--"and I will bring a bag of corn with me, so that I need never leave my nest until the eggs are hatched. They might catch cold," said the conscientious Jemima.
"Madam, I beg you not to trouble yourself with a bag; I will provide oats. But before you commence your tedious sitting, I intend to give you a treat. Let us have a dinner-party all to ourselves!

"May I ask you to bring up some herbs from the farm-garden to make a savoury omelette? Sage and thyme, and mint and two onions, and some parsley. I will provide lard for the stuff--lard for the omelette," said the hospitable gentleman with sandy whiskers.
Jemima Puddle-duck was a simpleton: not even the mention of sage and onions made her suspicious.
She went round the farm-garden, nibbling off snippets of all the different sorts of herbs that are used for stuffing roast duck.
And she waddled into the kitchen, and got two onions out of a basket.
The collie-dog Kep met her coming out, "What are you doing with those onions? Where do you go every afternoon by yourself, Jemima Puddle-duck?"
Jemima was rather in awe of the collie; she told him the whole story.
The collie listened, with his wise head on one side; he grinned when she described the polite gentleman with sandy whiskers.
He asked several questions about the wood, and about the exact position of the house and shed.
Then he went out, and trotted down the village. He went to look for two fox-hound puppies who were out at walk with the butcher.

questions.prompt: What does the fox do with the eggs when Jemima is away?
facilitatorNotes: He turns them over and counts them. This private behavior suggests an interest different from merely offering shelter.
evidence: turn them over and count them when Jemima was not there.

questions.prompt: Why is the list of herbs an alarming clue?
facilitatorNotes: The narrator says they are used for stuffing roast duck. Explain that the fox may plan to eat Jemima, while she thinks he plans a friendly meal.
evidence: herbs that are used for stuffing roast duck.

questions.prompt: How does Kep respond after listening to Jemima?
facilitatorNotes: He asks exactly where the house is and goes to find help. Focus on gathering useful information rather than mocking Jemima’s mistake.
evidence: He asked several questions about the wood

days.title: Jemima Puddle-Duck, part 4: a rescue with a sad cost
days.challenge: Recognize that a story can end with both relief and loss.
days.focus: The fox’s changed voice confirms earlier clues, while the ending resists a perfectly happy resolution.
days.context: Kep has learned where Jemima’s nest is and found two young dogs to help. Jemima returns carrying herbs, still expecting a dinner invitation.
days.contentNote: Non-graphic animal peril: a fight is heard outside, dogs have minor injuries, and the eggs are eaten. Jemima survives and later hatches ducklings. Preview this sad ending for sensitive listeners.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Jemima Puddle-Duck, paragraphs 46–61 (end); begins “Jemima Puddle-duck went up the cart-road for the last time, …” and ends “… her nerves; but she had always been a bad sitter.”.

blocks.text: Jemima Puddle-duck went up the cart-road for the last time, on a sunny afternoon. She was rather burdened with bunches of herbs and two onions in a bag.
She flew over the wood, and alighted opposite the house of the bushy long-tailed gentleman.
He was sitting on a log; he sniffed the air, and kept glancing uneasily round the wood. When Jemima alighted he quite jumped.
"Come into the house as soon as you have looked at your eggs. Give me the herbs for the omelette. Be sharp!"
He was rather abrupt. Jemima Puddle-duck had never heard him speak like that.
She felt surprised, and uncomfortable.
While she was inside she heard pattering feet round the back of the shed. Some one with a black nose sniffed at the bottom of the door, and then locked it.
Jemima became much alarmed.
A moment afterwards there were most awful noises--barking, baying, growls and howls, squealing and groans.
And nothing more was ever seen of that foxy-whiskered gentleman.
Presently Kep opened the door of the shed, and let out Jemima Puddle-duck.
Unfortunately the puppies rushed in and gobbled up all the eggs before he could stop them.
He had a bite on his ear and both the puppies were limping.
Jemima Puddle-duck was escorted home in tears on account of those eggs.
She laid some more in June, and she was permitted to keep them herself: but only four of them hatched.
Jemima Puddle-duck said that it was because of her nerves; but she had always been a bad sitter.

questions.prompt: How has the fox’s manner changed?
facilitatorNotes: He is abrupt and uneasy instead of courteous. Jemima notices this change and feels uncomfortable.
evidence: Jemima Puddle-duck had never heard him speak like that.

questions.prompt: Who releases Jemima from the shed?
facilitatorNotes: Kep opens the door. The noises outside have ended before she is released; the text does not show the fight directly.
evidence: Kep opened the door of the shed

questions.prompt: Why is Jemima still crying after she is safe?
facilitatorNotes: The puppies ate her eggs. A rescue can be welcome while a real loss remains; do not require a cheerful response.
evidence: in tears on account of those eggs.

days.title: Three Tabbies Took Out Their Cats to Tea
days.challenge: Separate the realistic animal sounds from the fanciful tea-party setting.
days.focus: A polite visit mixes human habits with unmistakable cat sounds.
days.context: Imagine a very polite tea visit with cats. The ending borrows an old saying; enjoy the joke orally rather than treating it as a multiplication exercise.
days.contentNote: “Tabbies” is old language for the women taking their cats out. The final riddle invokes the fictional saying that cats have nine lives; real animals have one life.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAGE 19”; opening “THREE tabbies took out their cats to tea,”; ending “How many lives had these cats between them?”.

blocks.text:
THREE tabbies took out their cats to tea,
As well-behaved tabbies as well could be:
Each sat in the chair that each preferred,
They mewed for their milk, and they sipped and purred.
Now tell me this (as these cats you’ve seen them)—
How many lives had these cats between them?

questions.prompt: What do the cats ask for by mewing?
facilitatorNotes: Milk. The text makes their mews into requests at a formal visit.
evidence: They mewed for their milk,

questions.prompt: Which sounds suggest the cats are comfortable after drinking?
facilitatorNotes: Purring. Compare a soft contented purr with the earlier asking mew.
evidence: and they sipped and purred.

questions.prompt: Why does the last line ask about lives instead of cups of tea?
facilitatorNotes: It plays on the old saying that cats have nine lives. Explain the saying as make-believe; no multiplication answer is required.
evidence: How many lives had these cats between them?

days.title: The Hayloft
days.challenge: Trace the meadow grass into a new imagined landscape.
days.focus: Harvested hay becomes mountains through a child's perspective.
days.context: A hayloft stores dried grass. Scythes are old harvesting tools; this describes a remembered setting.

excerpt.locator: The Hayloft; begins “THROUGH all the pleasant meadow-side”; ends “The happy hills of hay.”.

blocks.text:
THROUGH all the pleasant meadow-side
The grass grew shoulder-high,
Till the shining scythes went far and wide
And cut it down to dry.

These green and sweetly smelling crops
They led in waggons home;
And they piled them here in mountain tops
For mountaineers to roam.

Here is Mount Clear, Mount Rusty-Nail,
Mount Eagle and Mount High;--
The mice that in these mountains dwell,
No happier are than I!

O what a joy to clamber there,
O what a place for play,
With the sweet, the dim, the dusty air,
The happy hills of hay.

questions.prompt: What happens to the tall grass before it reaches the loft?
facilitatorNotes: It is cut and left to dry, then carried home in wagons.
evidence: And cut it down to dry.

questions.prompt: Why does the child give parts of the hay names beginning with “Mount”?
facilitatorNotes: The piled hay looks like mountain tops to climb and explore.
evidence: And they piled them here in mountain tops

questions.prompt: Which senses besides sight help the poem describe the loft?
facilitatorNotes: Smell is explicit; dusty air can also suggest touch or breathing. Ask the child to pick an actual phrase.
evidence: With the sweet, the dim, the dusty air,

days.title: Margery Brown
days.challenge: Notice how one repeated setting holds three different actions.
days.focus: Repeated questions reveal looking, listening and uncertain waiting.
days.context: Read the questions and Margery’s replies in two voices. Picture her on a hill outside London, hearing distant sounds whose meaning remains uncertain.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAGE 22”; opening ““MARGERY BROWN, on the top of the hill,”; ending “For the bells ring strangely in London town.””.

blocks.text:
“MARGERY BROWN, on the top of the hill,
Why are you standing, idle still?”
“Oh, I’m looking over to London town;
Shall I see the horsemen if I go down?”

“Margery Brown, on the top of the hill,
Why are you standing, listening still?”
“Oh, I hear the bells of London ring,
And I hear the men and the maidens sing.”

“Margery Brown, on the top of the hill,
Why are you standing, waiting still?”
“Oh, a knight is there, but I can’t go down,
For the bells ring strangely in London town.”

questions.prompt: Where does Margery remain during all three exchanges?
facilitatorNotes: On the top of the hill. The repeated opening anchors each conversation in the same place.
evidence: on the top of the hill,

questions.prompt: Name two sounds she hears from London.
facilitatorNotes: Bells ringing and men and maidens singing. Ask the child to distinguish the instrument sound from human voices.
evidence: And I hear the men and the maidens sing.

questions.prompt: Does the poem explain exactly why the bells sound strange to her?
facilitatorNotes: No. It reports that they sound strange and that she cannot go down, leaving the reason unclear. Avoid supplying a battle or emergency as fact.
evidence: For the bells ring strangely in London town.

days.title: Good Mistress Sundial
days.challenge: Notice a practical limitation inside a make-believe conversation.
days.focus: A sun-dependent instrument sends a questioner to a flower.
days.context: This untitled “Garden Songs” poem gives voices to a sundial and a four-o'clock flower. Such flowers often open late in the day, but are not precise clocks.

excerpt.locator: Good Mistress Sundial; begins “"GOOD Mistress Sundial, what's the hour?"”; ends “_She_ carries the time o' day in her heart."”.

blocks.text:
"GOOD Mistress Sundial, what's the hour?"
"Alack! to tell you I haven't power.
It rains; and I only can work, you see,
When the sun is casting his light upon me.
I'm nothing at all but a senseless block
Whenever his beautiful rays depart;
But ask my neighbor, the Four-o'clock;
_She_ carries the time o' day in her heart."

questions.prompt: Why can't the sundial tell the hour right now?
facilitatorNotes: It is raining and sunlight is unavailable to cast the needed shadow.
evidence: It rains; and I only can work, you see,

questions.prompt: Whom does the sundial suggest asking instead?
facilitatorNotes: Its neighbor is the Four-o'clock flower, named like a time.
evidence: But ask my neighbor, the Four-o'clock;

questions.prompt: What makes the ending a playful answer rather than an exact clock reading?
facilitatorNotes: No hour is supplied; a flower is imagined to carry time in its heart.
evidence: _She_ carries the time o' day in her heart.

days.title: Little Wind
days.challenge: Hear repeated address and opposing direction words.
days.focus: A four-line request makes wind an imagined helper that changes the weather.
days.context: The speaker makes four requests to the wind as though it could listen. A plain is a broad, fairly flat stretch of land; trace the changes in direction with a hand.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAGE 23”; opening “LITTLE wind, blow on the hill-top,”; ending “Little wind, blow off the rain.”.

blocks.text:
LITTLE wind, blow on the hill-top,
Little wind, blow down the plain;
Little wind, blow up the sunshine,
Little wind, blow off the rain.

questions.prompt: Where does the speaker first ask the wind to blow?
facilitatorNotes: On the hill-top, then down the plain. Show a high hill and a low flat area with hands.
evidence: LITTLE wind, blow on the hill-top,

questions.prompt: Which weather does the speaker want brought in?
facilitatorNotes: Sunshine. The matching last line asks for rain to be taken away.
evidence: Little wind, blow up the sunshine,

questions.prompt: How does saying “Little wind” four times make this sound like speaking to someone?
facilitatorNotes: It repeatedly calls the wind by name before giving a request. Accept an impression of coaxing or chanting, without claiming wind can actually obey.
evidence: Little wind, blow off the rain.

days.title: Nuts and Nut-Eaters, part 1: from catkins to nuts
days.challenge: Follow a change that happens slowly over many weeks.
days.focus: Watching the same bushes through the year shows how flowers become nuts.
days.context: Hazel bushes grow wild nuts in Britain. Catkins are dangling flower clusters; the “yellow dust” is pollen. A nuthatch is a small bird.

excerpt.locator: Book I, Nuts and Nut-Eaters, printed pages 23–26, paragraphs 1–6; begins “We pass through a small nut-wood on our way to …” and ends “… and the little birds called Nuthatches, carry them all away.”.

blocks.text: We pass through a small nut-wood on our way to school. In the winter, when there are no leaves on the trees, we see the grey clusters which we call "lambs-tails" hanging on the nut-bushes, Paul says their real name is "catkins."

We often look at them to see how they grow. At first they are only like little grey buds on the branch. Then they grow larger and hang down. By degrees they become very loose, like tassels, and under the grey scales come some little bags of yellow dust.
Then in March, still before the leaves are on the trees, the wind shakes the tree and blows the yellow dust about.

By this time we find small flowers, growing near the end of the branches. You have to look well to find them. But they are very pretty. Each flower has two tiny red horns, and there are many flowers in one green cup.

We know that these red flowers grow into nuts, for we find the nuts just in that place in September. When the wind blows the yellow dust out of the lambs-tails, some of it falls on the red horns of the flowers, and this makes the nut grow.
In the autumn we look out well to see when the nuts are ripe. We want to get some before the Squirrels, and the little birds called Nuthatches, carry them all away.

questions.prompt: What do the children call the grey clusters, and what does Paul say their real name is?
facilitatorNotes: Lambs-tails; catkins. Both names describe the same thing.
evidence: which we call "lambs-tails"

questions.prompt: How do the catkins change as spring comes?
facilitatorNotes: From small grey buds, they grow larger, hang down, and become loose like tassels full of yellow dust.
evidence: like tassels

questions.prompt: According to the children, what has to happen for a red flower to grow into a nut?
facilitatorNotes: Yellow dust from the catkins must fall on its red horns. Let the child retell the steps.
evidence: some of it falls on the red horns of the flowers

days.title: Nuts and Nut-Eaters, part 2: who gets the nuts?
days.challenge: Use a small clue to explain something hidden.
days.focus: A tiny hole reveals the weevil’s life inside the nut, and the lesson ends by counting all the nut-eaters.
days.context: A kernel is the part of the nut we eat. A weevil is a tiny beetle with a long snout; its young is a grub, or maggot.

excerpt.locator: Book I, Nuts and Nut-Eaters, printed pages 26–29, paragraphs 7–13 (end of lesson); begins “Peggy is in such a hurry that she picks them …” and ends “… and some the weevil grub gets, before they are ripe.”.

blocks.text: Peggy is in such a hurry that she picks them sometimes before they are ripe. This is foolish, for then there is only a very small watery kernel inside. The rest of the shell is filled with white soft stuff.
Paul says this white stuff is the food which the nut uses to make itself large and firm. When the nuts are ripe they drop quite easily out of the brown leafy cup in which they sit.
Sometimes when we pick the nuts we find one with a little hole in the shell. Then we know that the nut is a bad one, and we shall most likely find a maggot inside.
It is so curious! Paul tells us that this maggot is a young beetle. It does not look like one. But many beetles when they are young have no legs and are only grubs.

This nut-beetle is called a Weevil. When the nut is quite young and soft, the mother weevil comes and lays an egg in it. She is a very small beetle and has a long snout. With her snout she makes a hole in the soft green nutshell, and then lays a tiny egg in the hole. By-and-by the egg hatches into a maggot. It grows fat by feeding on the nut. So when we gather it, the nut is half eaten, and the maggot is curled up inside.
If we had not picked the nut, the maggot would have eaten a large hole in the nutshell with its horny mouth, and then have crept out of its maggot skin as a little weevil with wings.

So the yellow dust and the red flowers make nuts. Some of these nuts we get. Some the squirrels get. Some the nuthatch gets. Some fall to the ground and grow up into young nut trees, and some the weevil grub gets, before they are ripe.

questions.prompt: Why is it foolish to pick nuts before they are ripe?
facilitatorNotes: The kernel is still small and watery, and the shell is full of soft white stuff the nut uses to grow.
evidence: there is only a very small watery kernel inside.

questions.prompt: What tiny clue tells the children that a nut has a maggot inside?
facilitatorNotes: A little hole in the shell, made when the mother weevil laid her egg.
evidence: one with a little hole in the shell.

questions.prompt: At the end, who gets the nuts?
facilitatorNotes: The children, the squirrels, the nuthatch, the weevil grub, and the ground, where some grow into new trees. Children may say which seems fairest.
evidence: Some the squirrels get.

days.title: Farewell to the Farm
days.challenge: Follow a departure through repeated farewells and a shrinking view.
days.focus: A chorus gathers the ordinary places that matter to the children.
days.context: A coach is a horse-drawn carriage. Invite the child to join each farewell.

excerpt.locator:
Farewell to the Farm; begins “THE coach is at the door at last;”; ends “Last, round the woody turn we swing:
Good-bye, good-bye, to everything!”.

blocks.text:
THE coach is at the door at last;
The eager children, mounting fast
And kissing hands, in chorus sing:
Good-bye, good-bye, to everything!

To house and garden, field and lawn,
The meadow-gates we swang upon,
To pump and stable, tree and swing,
Good-bye, good-bye, to everything!

And fare you well for evermore,
O ladder at the hayloft door,
O hayloft where the cobwebs cling,
Good-bye, good-bye, to everything!

questions.prompt: What is ready at the beginning that makes the children hurry?
facilitatorNotes: The coach has reached the door, so departure is imminent.
evidence: THE coach is at the door at last;

questions.prompt: Why might they say goodbye to a pump, gate, and ladder as well as people?
facilitatorNotes: These objects belong to the place and its remembered play; the poem gives the surroundings affectionate attention.
evidence: To pump and stable, tree and swing,

questions.prompt: Why do the trees and houses look smaller near the end?
facilitatorNotes: The coach is moving away, so the view recedes; the objects do not actually shrink.
evidence: The trees and houses smaller grow;

days.title: Indeed It Is True
days.challenge: Distinguish a confident storytelling voice from evidence that a claim is real.
days.focus: Repeated certainty introduces a fantastical story about the moon.
days.context: A playful speaker insists on a story about the moon. ‘Bide’ means live or stay, and ‘cross’ means grumpy. Listen to how strongly the speaker asks to be believed.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAGE 24”; opening “INDEED it is true, it is perfectly true;”; ending “And he’s cross as a bundle of sticks.”.

questions.prompt: Who does the speaker say lives in the moon?
facilitatorNotes: An old man and his dog. Explain bide as live or stay.
evidence: An old man and his dog bide up there in the moon,

questions.prompt: Does this imagined man sound friendly or grumpy?
facilitatorNotes: Grumpy: cross means bad-tempered here. The bundle-of-sticks comparison is playful and need not be literally explained.
evidence: And he’s cross as a bundle of sticks.

questions.prompt: Does saying “true” twice prove the moon story is a fact?
facilitatorNotes: No. The insistence is part of the playful voice; listeners can enjoy a make-believe claim without believing it.
evidence: INDEED it is true, it is perfectly true;

days.title: There is but one May
days.challenge: Connect a disappointing description of weather with a positive result.
days.focus: The second stanza discovers value in even a cold, rainy May.
days.context: Read both stanzas before discussing whether the speaker likes this month.

excerpt.locator: There is but one May; begins “There is but one May in the year,”; ends “Bring up the flowers.”.

blocks.text:
There is but one May in the year,
And sometimes May is wet and cold;
There is but one May in the year
Before the year grows old.

Yet though it be the chilliest May,
With least of sun and most of showers,
Its wind and dew, its night and day,
Bring up the flowers.

questions.prompt: What might May be like besides warm and sunny?
facilitatorNotes: It can be wet and cold.
evidence: And sometimes May is wet and cold;

questions.prompt: What arrives because of its wind, dew, night, and day?
facilitatorNotes: Flowers grow even in the chilliest version of May.
evidence: Bring up the flowers.

questions.prompt: How does the second stanza change the feeling of the first?
facilitatorNotes: “Yet” turns attention from limited, possibly unpleasant weather toward what the month makes grow.
evidence: Yet though it be the chilliest May,

days.title: As I Was Walking Up the Street
days.challenge: Track how a flower links the faraway encounter to Mary.
days.focus: A journey gathers sounds and brings a small gift back home.
days.context: This short journey begins near ringing bells and passes into fairyland. Follow who speaks, who picks a flower, and who carries it home.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAGE 27”; opening “AS I was walking up the street,”; ending “I’ve brought it home for Mary.”.

blocks.text:
AS I was walking up the street,
The steeple bells were ringing;
As I sat down at Mary’s feet,
The sweet, sweet birds were singing.

As I walked far into the world,
I met a little fairy;
She plucked this flower, and, as it’s sweet,
I’ve brought it home for Mary.

questions.prompt: What two sounds does the speaker hear before meeting the fairy?
facilitatorNotes: Ringing steeple bells and singing birds. Echo the two sound words in turn.
evidence: The steeple bells were ringing;

questions.prompt: Who picks the flower?
facilitatorNotes: The fairy. Keep the fairy’s action distinct from the speaker’s later carrying action.
evidence: She plucked this flower,

questions.prompt: For whom does the speaker bring the flower home?
facilitatorNotes: Mary. The journey ends with a gift for a named person, rather than with staying beside the fairy.
evidence: I’ve brought it home for Mary.

days.title: My Kingdom
days.challenge: Notice scale changing between an outdoor game and returning home.
days.focus: A child's small kingdom feels vast until ordinary adult surroundings return.
days.context: Dell means a small hollow; heather and gorse are flowering shrubs. The kingdom is a game.

excerpt.locator: My Kingdom; begins “DOWN by a shining water well”; ends “How great and cool the rooms!”.

blocks.text:
DOWN by a shining water well
I found a very little dell,
No higher than my head.
The heather and the gorse about
In summer bloom were coming out,
Some yellow and some red.

And all about was mine, I said,
The little sparrows overhead,
The little minnows too.
This was the world and I was king;
For me the bees came by to sing,
For me the swallows flew.

I played there were no deeper seas,
Nor any wider plains than these,
Nor other kings than me.
At last I heard my mother call
Out from the house at evenfall,
To call me home to tea.

And I must rise and leave my dell,
And leave my dimpled water well,
And leave my heather blooms.
Alas! and as my home I neared,
How very big my nurse appeared,
How great and cool the rooms!

questions.prompt: What does the child rename a sea?
facilitatorNotes: The little pool becomes a sea in the imagined kingdom.
evidence: I called the little pool a sea;

questions.prompt: What ends the child's time as king?
facilitatorNotes: Mother calls from the house at evening, inviting the child home to tea.
evidence: At last I heard my mother call

questions.prompt: Why do the nurse and rooms seem so big after the game?
facilitatorNotes: The child has spent time imagining a tiny place as a whole world; returning changes the scale.
evidence: How very big my nurse appeared,

days.title: The Bogey-Beast, part 1: a pot beside the road
days.challenge: Separate what an object is from the uses someone imagines for it.
days.focus: A cheerful voice turns a modest find into a grand possibility.
days.context: A poor woman earns food by doing errands for neighbors. A sup is a small drink, and a shawl is a wrap. A bogey-beast is a mischievous creature from folklore.

excerpt.locator: The Bogey-Beast, 1922 edition pp. 268–269, paragraphs 1–9; begins “There was once a woman who was very, very cheerful, …” and ends “… to it and drag it behind her like a go-cart.”.

blocks.text: There was once a woman who was very, very cheerful, though she had little to make her so; for she was old, and poor, and lonely. She lived in a little bit of a cottage and earned a scant living by running errands for her neighbours, getting a bite here, a sup there, as reward for her services. So she made shift to get on, and always looked as spry and cheery as if she had not a want in the world.
Now one summer evening, as she was trotting, full of smiles as ever, along the high road to her hovel, what should she see but a big black pot lying in the ditch!
"Goodness me!" she cried, "that would be just the very thing for me if I only had something to put in it! But I haven't! Now who could have left it in the ditch?"
And she looked about her expecting the owner would not be far off; but she could see nobody.
"Maybe there is a hole in it," she went on, "and that's why it has been cast away. But it would do fine to put a flower in for my window; so I'll just take it home with me."
And with that she lifted the lid and looked inside. "Mercy me!" she cried, fair amazed. "If it isn't full of gold pieces. Here's luck!"
And so it was, brimful of great gold coins. Well, at first she simply stood stock-still, wondering if she was standing on her head or her heels. Then she began saying:
"Lawks! But I do feel rich. I feel awful rich!"

After she had said this many times, she began to wonder how she was to get her treasure home. It was too heavy for her to carry, and she could see no better way than to tie the end of her shawl to it and drag it behind her like a go-cart.

questions.prompt: What useful purpose does she imagine before opening the pot?
facilitatorNotes: She could put a flower in it even if it has a hole. Her first thought is practical and small.
evidence: put a flower in for my window

questions.prompt: How does her reaction change when she sees inside?
facilitatorNotes: She is astonished and feels rich because it holds gold. Ask the child to compare her two exclamations.
evidence: If it isn't full of gold pieces.

questions.prompt: How does she solve the problem of carrying something too heavy?
facilitatorNotes: She ties her shawl to it and drags it. The comparison to a go-cart helps the listener picture the movement.
evidence: drag it behind her like a go-cart.

days.title: The Bogey-Beast, part 2: less gold, less worry
days.challenge: Compare a surprising event with the character’s unexpected reaction.
days.focus: Speech reveals a habit of finding advantages in a loss.
days.context: The woman is dragging home what she believes is a pot of gold. She imagines possible uses for it before she stops to rest.

excerpt.locator: The Bogey-Beast, 1922 edition pp. 269–270, paragraphs 10–14; begins “"It will soon be dark," she said to herself as …” and ends “… death o' me, and with this great lump of silver--"”.

blocks.text: "It will soon be dark," she said to herself as she trotted along. "So much the better! The neighbours will not see what I'm bringing home, and I shall have all the night to myself, and be able to think what I'll do! Mayhap I'll buy a grand house and just sit by the fire with a cup o' tea and do no work at all like a queen. Or maybe I'll bury it at the garden-foot and just keep a bit in the old china teapot on the chimney-piece. Or maybe--Goody! Goody! I feel that grand I don't know myself."
By this time she was a bit tired of dragging such a heavy weight, and, stopping to rest a while, turned to look at her treasure.
And lo! it wasn't a pot of gold at all! It was nothing but a lump of silver.
She stared at it and rubbed her eyes and stared at it again.

"Well! I never," she said at last. "And me thinking it was a pot of gold! I must have been dreaming. But this is luck! Silver is far less trouble--easier to mind, and not so easy stolen. Them gold pieces would have been the death o' me, and with this great lump of silver--"

questions.prompt: What two different plans does she imagine for the gold?
facilitatorNotes: Buying a house and relaxing, or hiding most of it while keeping some in a teapot. Different possibilities show her excitement.
evidence: just keep a bit in the old china teapot

questions.prompt: What does she actually see when she looks behind her?
facilitatorNotes: A lump of silver. The short announcement interrupts her long plans.
evidence: nothing but a lump of silver.

questions.prompt: Why does she call silver good luck?
facilitatorNotes: She thinks it will be easier to look after and less likely to be stolen. Her own priorities explain a reaction others might not share.
evidence: Silver is far less trouble

days.title: The Bogey-Beast, part 3: the useful stone
days.challenge: Track two changes while the character’s repeated attitude stays steady.
days.focus: Repeated words create comic surprise instead of increasing disappointment.
days.context: The woman’s treasure has already changed from gold to silver. She drags it farther toward home, stopping whenever she is tired.

excerpt.locator: The Bogey-Beast, 1922 edition pp. 270–271, paragraphs 15–19; begins “So she went off again planning what she would do, …” and ends “… it lying there, douce and peaceable as a stone should.”.

blocks.text: So she went off again planning what she would do, and feeling as rich as rich, until becoming a bit tired again she stopped to rest and gave a look round to see if her treasure was safe; and she saw nothing but a great lump of iron!

"Well! I never!" says she again. "And I mistaking it for silver! I must have been dreaming. But this is luck! It's real convenient. I can get penny pieces for old iron, and penny pieces are a deal handier for me than your gold and silver. Why! I should never have slept a wink for fear of being robbed. But a penny piece comes in useful, and I shall sell that iron for a lot and be real rich--rolling rich."

So on she trotted full of plans as to how she would spend her penny pieces, till once more she stopped to rest and looked round to see if her treasure was safe. And this time she saw nothing but a big stone.

"Well! I never!" she cried, full of smiles. "And to think I mistook it for iron. I must have been dreaming. But here's luck indeed, and me wanting a stone terrible bad to stick open the gate. Eh my! but it's a change for the better! It's a fine thing to have good luck."

So, all in a hurry to see how the stone would keep the gate open she trotted off down the hill till she came to her own cottage. She unlatched the gate and then turned to unfasten her shawl from the stone which lay on the path behind her. Aye! it was a stone sure enough. There was plenty light to see it lying there, douce and peaceable as a stone should.

questions.prompt: What does she plan to do when the treasure becomes iron?
facilitatorNotes: Sell it for pennies. She imagines small coins as useful and easier to manage.
evidence: I can get penny pieces for old iron

questions.prompt: What job does she find for the stone?
facilitatorNotes: Holding her gate open. This is a specific need at her own cottage.
evidence: to stick open the gate.

questions.prompt: Which repeated phrase helps us hear her unchanging attitude?
facilitatorNotes: I must have been dreaming or Well! I never! returns after each surprise. Invite the child to compare the changing objects with her cheerful voice.
evidence: I must have been dreaming.

days.title: The Bogey-Beast, part 4: a treasure in the telling
days.challenge: Consider a form of good fortune that cannot be kept in a pot.
days.focus: A lively transformation changes treasure into a memorable experience.
days.context: The woman has reached home with what now looks like a stone. This final section explains the title. Listen for the many movement and sound words.

excerpt.locator: The Bogey-Beast, 1922 edition p. 271, paragraphs 20–25 (end); begins “So she bent over it to unfasten the shawl end, …” and ends “… cottage and spent the evening chuckling over her good luck.”.

blocks.text: So she bent over it to unfasten the shawl end, when--
"Oh my!"

All of a sudden it gave a jump, a squeal, and in one moment was as big as a haystack. Then it let down four great lanky legs and threw out two long ears, flourished a great long tail and romped off, kicking and squealing and whinnying and laughing like a naughty mischievous boy!
The old woman stared after it till it was fairly out of sight, then she burst out laughing too.

"Well!" she chuckled, "I am in luck! Quite the luckiest body hereabouts. Fancy my seeing the Bogey-Beast all to myself; and making myself so free with it too! My goodness! I do feel that uplifted--that GRAND!"--
So she went into her cottage and spent the evening chuckling over her good luck.

questions.prompt: How does the quiet stone change when she bends over it?
facilitatorNotes: It jumps, grows huge, gains legs and ears, and runs away. Invite a retelling using two of the movement words.
evidence: gave a jump, a squeal

questions.prompt: Does the creature’s departure make the woman miserable?
facilitatorNotes: No; she laughs. Her response continues the pattern even after she has no object left.
evidence: she burst out laughing too.

questions.prompt: What does she now count as her good luck?
facilitatorNotes: Seeing the rare creature herself and sharing an extraordinary experience. Children may think this is lucky, disappointing, or both if they explain why.
evidence: Fancy my seeing the Bogey-Beast all to myself

days.title: Five Little Sisters
days.challenge: Hold matching quantities and arrangements while noticing differing details.
days.focus: Parallel verses compare a row of children with a row of flowers.
days.context: A pelisse is a coat, and a muff is a hand-warmer. Read the two stanzas while listening for a new group that takes the place of the sisters.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAGE 28”; opening “FIVE little sisters walking in a row;”; ending “A bright yellow flower, and a new red pot.”.

blocks.text:
FIVE little sisters walking in a row;
Now, isn’t that the best way for little girls to go?
Each had a round hat, each had a muff,
And each had a new pelisse of soft green stuff.

Five little marigolds standing in a row;
Now, isn’t that the best way for marigolds to grow?
Each with a green stalk, and all the five had got
A bright yellow flower, and a new red pot.

questions.prompt: How are both the sisters and the marigolds arranged?
facilitatorNotes: In a row, with five in each group. No written counting is needed; five fingers can support listening.
evidence: Five little marigolds standing in a row;

questions.prompt: Which clothing colour matches the colour of the flowers’ stalks?
facilitatorNotes: Green: the sisters’ pelisses, or coats, are green, like the stalks. Explain muff as a hand-warmer only if needed.
evidence: And each had a new pelisse of soft green stuff.

questions.prompt: What bright colours appear in the last line?
facilitatorNotes: Yellow flowers and red pots. The repeated structure links the two groups, while those details belong to the plants.
evidence: A bright yellow flower, and a new red pot.

days.title: Hopping frog
days.challenge: Compare how the speaker addresses two animals with different movements.
days.focus: A promise of noninterference extends from a bright frog to a less admired toad.
days.context: “Pelt” means throw things at; the speaker promises not to do that. “Plod” means move slowly and steadily.

excerpt.locator: Hopping frog; begins “Hopping frog, hop here and be seen,”; ends “You won’t hurt me, and I won’t hurt you.”.

blocks.text:
Hopping frog, hop here and be seen,
I’ll not pelt you with stick or stone:
Your cap is laced and your coat is green;
Good bye, we’ll let each other alone.

Plodding toad, plod here and be looked at,
You the finger of scorn is crooked at:
But though you’re lumpish, you’re harmless too;
You won’t hurt me, and I won’t hurt you.

questions.prompt: What color does the speaker give the frog’s coat?
facilitatorNotes: The green coat is an imagined garment for the frog’s skin.
evidence: Your cap is laced and your coat is green;

questions.prompt: How is the toad’s movement different from the frog’s?
facilitatorNotes: The frog hops while the toad plods; small gestures can make the comparison.
evidence: Plodding toad, plod here and be looked at,

questions.prompt: What promise is shared by the ending and the first stanza?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker will leave the animals unharmed and expects peaceful coexistence.
evidence: You won’t hurt me, and I won’t hurt you.

days.title: In Go-cart So Tiny
days.challenge: Contrast a journey imagined with a journey actually begun.
days.focus: An ambitious promise meets the familiar habit of postponing a start.
days.context: A go-cart here is a little cart someone pulls. ‘Drew’ means pulled, not made a picture. Listen for the difference between a grand promise and what has happened so far.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAGE 29”; opening “IN go-cart so tiny”; ending “Put off till to-morrow.”.

blocks.text:
IN go-cart so tiny
My sister I drew;
And I’ve promised to draw her
The wide world through.

We have not yet started—
I own it with sorrow—
Because our trip’s always
Put off till to-morrow.

questions.prompt: Whom does the speaker pull in the little cart?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker’s sister. Drew means pulled here, not made a picture.
evidence: My sister I drew;

questions.prompt: How far does the speaker promise to take her?
facilitatorNotes: Through the wide world. That enormous promise contrasts with the tiny cart.
evidence: The wide world through.

questions.prompt: Have they begun this grand trip? What keeps delaying it?
facilitatorNotes: No; it is always put off until tomorrow. The speaker admits feeling sorry about that.
evidence: Put off till to-morrow.

days.title: The Little Land
days.challenge: Hold a miniature imagined world in mind through a longer poem.
days.focus: Changing the speaker's size transforms a lawn into a landscape.
days.context: Adults read slowly with a pause between the little world and the return to the room. The child can trace or draw the tiny journey.

excerpt.locator: The Little Land; begins “WHEN at home alone I sit”; ends “Late at night to go to bed.”.

blocks.text:
WHEN at home alone I sit
And am very tired of it,
I have just to shut my eyes
To go sailing through the skies--
To go sailing far away
To the pleasant Land of Play;
To the fairy land afar
Where the Little People are;
Where the clover-tops are trees,
And the rain-pools are the seas,
And the leaves like little ships
Sail about on tiny trips;
And above the daisy tree
Through the grasses,
High o'erhead the Bumble Bee
Hums and passes.

In that forest to and fro
I can wander, I can go;
See the spider and the fly,
And the ants go marching by
Carrying parcels with their feet
Down the green and grassy street.
I can in the sorrel sit
Where the ladybird alit.

I can climb the jointed grass;
And on high
See the greater swallows pass
In the sky,
And the round sun rolling by
Heeding no such things as I.

Through that forest I can pass
Till, as in a looking-glass,
Humming fly and daisy tree
And my tiny self I see,
Painted very clear and neat
On the rain-pool at my feet.

Should a leaflet come to land
Drifting near to where I stand,
Straight I'll board that tiny boat
Round the rain-pool sea to float.

Little thoughtful creatures sit
On the grassy coasts of it;
Little things with lovely eyes
See me sailing with surprise.
Some are clad in armour green--
(These have sure to battle been!)--

Some are pied with ev'ry hue,
Black and crimson, gold and blue;
Some have wings and swift are gone;--
But they all look kindly on.

When my eyes I once again
Open, and see all things plain:
High bare walls, great bare floor;
Great big knobs on drawer and door;
Great big people perched on chairs,
Stitching tucks and mending tears,
Each a hill that I could climb,
And talking nonsense all the time--

O dear me,
That I could be
A sailor on the rain-pool sea,
A climber in the clover tree,
And just come back, a sleepy-head,
Late at night to go to bed.

questions.prompt: What becomes a sea when the speaker imagines being small?
facilitatorNotes: Rain pools become seas; ordinary leaves can then serve as ships.
evidence: And the rain-pools are the seas,

questions.prompt: How does the speaker know the picture in the pool is a reflection?
facilitatorNotes: The tiny self appears with the fly and daisy as in a looking-glass.
evidence: And my tiny self I see,

questions.prompt: What does opening the eyes change near the end?
facilitatorNotes: The room, furniture, and people look huge again; the child wants to return to the imagined small world.
evidence: Great big knobs on drawer and door;

days.title: Look Over the Wall
days.challenge: Distinguish what can be seen from what can be heard.
days.focus: A passing royal procession combines bright clothes, movement and sound.
days.context: A crowd is waiting for a royal procession. The Court is the royal household and its attendants. Read so the waving banners and drumming can be imagined without a picture.
days.contentNote: Describes an old royal procession and attendants who never refuse commands. This is a historical story detail, not a rule that children must always obey adults.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAGE 34”; opening “LOOK over the wall, and I’ll tell you why,—”; ending “You’ll see a great deal, if you do not see all.”.

blocks.text:
LOOK over the wall, and I’ll tell you why,—
The King and the Queen will soon pass by;
Madams and masters, look this way,
The King and his Court ride past to-day.

The Queen has a robe that is gold and red,
She is stately, and sits with a crown on her head,
And four very little boys after her go,
To do as she bids them,—they never say “No.”

The banners are waving, the soldiers are drumming;
’Tis indeed a fine sight that, I tell you, is coming!
So, if you look long enough over the wall,
You’ll see a great deal, if you do not see all.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker ask everyone to look over the wall?
facilitatorNotes: The King, Queen and Court are about to pass. The invitation prepares listeners to watch.
evidence: The King and the Queen will soon pass by;

questions.prompt: What two colours are in the Queen’s robe?
facilitatorNotes: Gold and red. Her crown is another visible detail, but its colour is not stated.
evidence: The Queen has a robe that is gold and red,

questions.prompt: Which moving detail and which sound make the procession lively?
facilitatorNotes: Waving banners and drumming soldiers. The final lines suggest the wall may prevent seeing everything.
evidence: The banners are waving, the soldiers are drumming;

days.title: An emerald is as green as grass
days.challenge: Compare beauty and usefulness across two stanzas about stones.
days.focus: The ending gives an ordinary-looking stone an unexpected importance.
days.context: An emerald, ruby, sapphire, diamond, and opal are gemstones. Flint can make sparks when struck appropriately; this is a reading, not an experiment.

excerpt.locator: An emerald is as green as grass; begins “An emerald is as green as grass;”; ends “But a flint holds fire.”.

questions.prompt: Which stone is compared with the blue sky?
facilitatorNotes: The sapphire shines as blue as heaven, here meaning the sky.
evidence: A sapphire shines as blue as heaven;

questions.prompt: Where is the flint first found, unlike the shining gems?
facilitatorNotes: It lies in the mud, an unglamorous setting.
evidence: A flint lies in the mud.

questions.prompt: How does the last line change our view of the muddy flint?
facilitatorNotes: It can help produce real fire, unlike an opal’s merely fiery-looking sparkle; usefulness adds another kind of value.
evidence: But a flint holds fire.

days.title: Which Is the Way to Somewhere Town?
days.challenge: Recognise the difference between imaginary directions and a real route.
days.focus: Question-and-answer directions lead to an impossible destination.
days.context: These are make-believe travel directions. Read each question and answer, then picture where an ordinary road would need to go to follow them.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAGE 38”; opening “WHICH is the way to Somewhere Town?”; ending “That is the way, quite clearly.”.

blocks.text:
WHICH is the way to Somewhere Town?
Oh, up in the morning early;
Over the tiles and the chimney-pots,
That is the way, quite clearly.

And which is the door to Somewhere Town?
Oh, up in the morning early;
The round red sun is the door to go through,
That is the way, quite clearly.

questions.prompt: When does the answer say the journey should begin?
facilitatorNotes: Early in the morning. The same time phrase appears in both verses.
evidence: Oh, up in the morning early;

questions.prompt: What is the supposed door into Somewhere Town?
facilitatorNotes: The round red sun. Its impossible role tells us these are fantasy directions.
evidence: The round red sun is the door to go through,

questions.prompt: Why would these directions be hard to follow on an ordinary walk?
facilitatorNotes: They go over roofs and through the sun. Explain that this is an imagined journey, not an invitation to climb on a roof.
evidence: Over the tiles and the chimney-pots,

days.title: My Shadow
days.challenge: Distinguish the child's playful explanation from an observed change in light.
days.focus: Treating a shadow as a companion makes familiar behavior seem strange.
days.context: The speaker teases the shadow. Explain that a shadow needs light blocked by an object; it is not a separate child.

excerpt.locator: My Shadow; begins “I HAVE a little shadow that goes in and out with me,”; ends “Had stayed at home behind me and was fast asleep in bed.”.

blocks.text:
I HAVE a little shadow that goes in and out with me,
And what can be the use of him is more than I can see.
He is very, very like me from the heels up to the head;
And I see him jump before me, when I jump into my bed.

The funniest thing about him is the way he likes to grow--
Not at all like proper children, which is always very slow;
For he sometimes shoots up taller like an india-rubber ball,
And sometimes gets so little that there's none of him at all.

He hasn't got a notion of how children ought to play,
And can only make a fool of me in every sort of way.
He stays so close beside me, he's a coward you can see;
I'd think shame to stick to nursie as that shadow sticks to me!

One morning, very early, before the sun was up,
I rose and found the shining dew on every buttercup;
But my lazy little shadow, like an arrant sleepy-head,
Had stayed at home behind me and was fast asleep in bed.

questions.prompt: How does the shadow grow differently from a real child?
facilitatorNotes: It can become tall or disappear very quickly, unlike children's slow growth.
evidence: And sometimes gets so little that there's none of him at all.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker call the shadow a coward?
facilitatorNotes: It stays close instead of playing independently. This is the speaker's imagined judgment, not a fact about shadows or people.
evidence: He stays so close beside me,

questions.prompt: What detail explains why a sun-cast shadow is missing in the last stanza?
facilitatorNotes: The child goes out before sunrise. The joke says the shadow stayed asleep.
evidence: One morning, very early, before the sun was up,

days.title: Pipe Thee High
days.challenge: Hear contrast in pitch and encouragement in the ending.
days.focus: A short chant connects changing musical notes to lively movement.
days.context: ‘Pipe’ means make musical notes here. The speaker encourages a little trumpet player; the adult can model a comfortable high hum and low hum before rereading.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAGE 40”; opening “PIPE thee high, and pipe thee low,”; ending “Well done, little master!”.

blocks.text:
PIPE thee high, and pipe thee low,
Let the little feet go faster;
Blow your penny trumpet,—blow!
Well done, little master!

questions.prompt: What two kinds of notes does the first line ask for?
facilitatorNotes: High and low. An adult can demonstrate with comfortable humming, then reread the words.
evidence: PIPE thee high, and pipe thee low,

questions.prompt: What does the music encourage the little feet to do?
facilitatorNotes: Go faster, suggesting dancing or stepping. The text says feet move; dancing is a reasonable interpretation.
evidence: Let the little feet go faster;

questions.prompt: How does the last line show the player is being encouraged?
facilitatorNotes: It says Well done. The ending praises the effort after the repeated request to blow the trumpet.
evidence: Well done, little master!

days.title: Timmy Tiptoes, part 1: a store of nuts
days.challenge: Understand a practical worry hidden inside a cozy scene.
days.focus: Dialogue plants a question about getting stored food back out.
