days.context: Timmy and Goody are storybook squirrels gathering nuts for the winter. A thicket is a clump of bushes; a commotion is a noisy disturbance.
days.contentNote: The squirrels expect to sleep all winter; real tree squirrels stay active through the winter. A quarrel over buried nuts is mentioned briefly.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Timmy Tiptoes, paragraphs 1–10; begins “Once upon a time there was a little fat comfortable …” and ends “… other squirrels began to dig,--the whole wood was in commotion!”.

blocks.text: Once upon a time there was a little fat comfortable grey squirrel, called Timmy Tiptoes. He had a nest thatched with leaves in the top of a tall tree; and he had a little squirrel wife called Goody.

Timmy Tiptoes sat out, enjoying the breeze; he whisked his tail and chuckled--"Little wife Goody, the nuts are ripe; we must lay up a store for winter and spring." Goody Tiptoes was busy pushing moss under the thatch--"The nest is so snug, we shall be sound asleep all winter." "Then we shall wake up all the thinner, when there is nothing to eat in spring-time," replied prudent Timothy.
When Timmy and Goody Tiptoes came to the nut thicket, they found other squirrels were there already.
Timmy took off his jacket and hung it on a twig; they worked away quietly by themselves.
Every day they made several journeys and picked quantities of nuts. They carried them away in bags, and stored them in several hollow stumps near the tree where they had built their nest.
When these stumps were full, they began to empty the bags into a hole high up a tree, that had belonged to a wood-pecker; the nuts rattled down--down--down inside.
"How shall you ever get them out again? It is like a money-box!" said Goody.
"I shall be much thinner before spring-time, my love," said Timmy Tiptoes, peeping into the hole.
They did collect quantities--because they did not lose them! Squirrels who bury their nuts in the ground lose more than half, because they cannot remember the place.

The most forgetful squirrel in the wood was called Silvertail. He began to dig, and he could not remember. And then he dug again and found some nuts that did not belong to him; and there was a fight. And other squirrels began to dig,--the whole wood was in commotion!

questions.prompt: What job is Goody doing while Timmy talks about nuts?
facilitatorNotes: She is putting moss under the leaf roof. Her work makes the home snug while his plan concerns food.
evidence: Goody Tiptoes was busy pushing moss under the thatch

questions.prompt: Where do they put nuts after the hollow stumps are full?
facilitatorNotes: Into a former woodpecker hole high in a tree. Ask the child to imagine the nuts falling inside.
evidence: a hole high up a tree, that had belonged to a wood-pecker

questions.prompt: Why does Goody compare the hole to a money-box?
facilitatorNotes: Nuts go in easily, but she worries about getting them out. Accept any explanation linking the narrow opening to retrieval.
evidence: How shall you ever get them out again? It is like a money-box!

days.title: Timmy Tiptoes, part 2: a song taken the wrong way
days.challenge: Separate what the bird meant from what the squirrels thought it meant.
days.focus: A misunderstood song leads to an unfair accusation.
days.context: The squirrels who buried their nuts cannot find them, and the wood is in an uproar. The little birds’ songs put real bird calls into words. To confess is to admit doing something wrong.
days.contentNote: The other squirrels attack Timmy and squeeze him into a small hole, where he lies stunned. He recovers in the next part.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Timmy Tiptoes, paragraphs 11–24; begins “Unfortunately, just at this time a flock of little birds …” and ends “"Timmy Tiptoes! Timmy Tiptoes! Oh, where is Timmy Tiptoes?"”.

blocks.text: Unfortunately, just at this time a flock of little birds flew by, from bush to bush, searching for green caterpillars and spiders. There were several sorts of little birds, twittering different songs.
The first one sang--"Who's bin digging-up _my_ nuts? Who's-been-digging-up _my_ nuts?"
And another sang--"Little bita bread and-_no_-cheese! Little bit-a-bread an'-_no_-cheese!"

The squirrels followed and listened. The first little bird flew into the bush where Timmy and Goody Tiptoes were quietly tying up their bags, and it sang--"Who's-bin digging-up _my_ nuts? Who's been digging-up _my_-nuts?"
Timmy Tiptoes went on with his work without replying; indeed, the little bird did not expect an answer. It was only singing its natural song, and it meant nothing at all.

But when the other squirrels heard that song, they rushed upon Timmy Tiptoes and cuffed and scratched him, and upset his bag of nuts. The innocent little bird which had caused all the mischief, flew away in a fright!
Timmy rolled over and over, and then turned tail and fled towards his nest, followed by a crowd of squirrels shouting--"Who's-been digging-up _my_-nuts?"

They caught him and dragged him up the very same tree, where there was the little round hole, and they pushed him in. The hole was much too small for Timmy Tiptoes' figure. They squeezed him dreadfully, it was a wonder they did not break his ribs. "We will leave him here till he confesses," said Silvertail Squirrel, and he shouted into the hole--
"Who's-been-digging-up _my_-nuts?"
Timmy Tiptoes made no reply; he had tumbled down inside the tree, upon half a peck of nuts belonging to himself. He lay quite stunned and still.
Goody Tiptoes picked up the nut bags and went home. She made a cup of tea for Timmy; but he didn't come and didn't come.
Goody Tiptoes passed a lonely and unhappy night. Next morning she ventured back to the nut-bushes to look for him; but the other unkind squirrels drove her away.
She wandered all over the wood, calling--
"Timmy Tiptoes! Timmy Tiptoes! Oh, where is Timmy Tiptoes?"

questions.prompt: Did the little bird mean to blame Timmy? How do you know?
facilitatorNotes: No. The narrator says it was only singing its natural song and meant nothing at all. Let the child repeat the song and decide how it might sound to an angry listener.
evidence: It was only singing its natural song, and it meant nothing at all.

questions.prompt: What do the other squirrels think the song means, and what do they do?
facilitatorNotes: They think Timmy dug up their nuts, so they rush at him, upset his bag, and push him into the hole. Ask whether they checked first; the text shows they did not.
evidence: they rushed upon Timmy Tiptoes

questions.prompt: How do we know Goody misses Timmy?
facilitatorNotes: She makes him tea, spends a lonely night, and searches the wood calling his name. Accept any action from the text.
evidence: She made a cup of tea for Timmy; but he didn't come and didn't come.

days.title: Timmy Tiptoes, part 3: a second household below
days.challenge: Connect a mysterious sound with a hidden neighbor.
days.focus: Two stores of nuts reveal two linked underground homes.
days.context: Timmy has been pushed into the hole in the tree and has fallen onto his own store of nuts. Goody does not know where he is. A chipmunk is a small striped squirrel; ’ticed means enticed, or coaxed.
days.contentNote: Timmy is sore after the attack. The story laughs at him growing fat; talk about choices and comfort rather than judging bodies.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Timmy Tiptoes, paragraphs 25–34; begins “In the meantime Timmy Tiptoes came to his senses. He …” and ends “… could," said the Chipmunk, "but my husband, Chippy Hackee, bites!"”.

blocks.text: In the meantime Timmy Tiptoes came to his senses. He found himself tucked up in a little moss bed, very much in the dark, feeling sore; it seemed to be under ground. Timmy coughed and groaned, because his ribs hurted him. There was a chirpy noise, and a small striped Chipmunk appeared with a night light, and hoped he felt better?
It was most kind to Timmy Tiptoes; it lent him its night-cap; and the house was full of provisions.

The Chipmunk explained that it had rained nuts through the top of the tree--"Besides, I found a few buried!" It laughed and chuckled when it heard Timmy's story. While Timmy was confined to bed, it 'ticed him to eat quantities--"But how shall I ever get out through that hole unless I thin myself? My wife will be anxious!" "Just another nut--or two nuts; let me crack them for you," said the Chipmunk. Timmy Tiptoes grew fatter and fatter!

Now Goody Tiptoes had set to work again by herself. She did not put any more nuts into the woodpecker's hole, because she had always doubted how they could be got out again. She hid them under a tree root; they rattled down, down, down. Once when Goody emptied an extra big bagful, there was a decided squeak; and next time Goody brought another bagful, a little striped Chipmunk scrambled out in a hurry.

"It is getting perfectly full-up down-stairs; the sitting-room is full, and they are rolling along the passage; and my husband, Chippy Hackee, has run away and left me. What is the explanation of these showers of nuts?"

"I am sure I beg your pardon; I did not know that anybody lived here," said Mrs. Goody Tiptoes; "but where is Chippy Hackee? My husband, Timmy Tiptoes, has run away too." "I know where Chippy is; a little bird told me," said Mrs. Chippy Hackee.
She led the way to the woodpecker's tree, and they listened at the hole.
Down below there was a noise of nut crackers, and a fat squirrel voice and a thin squirrel voice were singing together--

"My little old man and I fell out,
How shall we bring this matter about?
Bring it about as well as you can,
And get you gone, you little old man!"
"You could squeeze in, through that little round hole," said Goody Tiptoes. "Yes, I could," said the Chipmunk, "but my husband, Chippy Hackee, bites!"

questions.prompt: What does the chipmunk do to make Timmy more comfortable?
facilitatorNotes: It gives him a moss bed, a night-cap, and food. Invite one care detail without praising the pressure to keep eating.
evidence: it lent him its night-cap

questions.prompt: What tells Goody that her new nut-storage place is occupied?
facilitatorNotes: A squeak and then a chipmunk emerging reveal someone below. Link the sound to the discovery.
evidence: there was a decided squeak

questions.prompt: How does Goody explain the falling nuts to Mrs. Chippy Hackee?
facilitatorNotes: She apologizes and says she did not know anyone lived there. Discuss a mistake causing trouble without intention.
evidence: I did not know that anybody lived here

days.title: Timmy Tiptoes, part 4: a larger way out
days.challenge: Compare two characters’ different reasons for leaving the tree.
days.focus: Weather solves one problem while a possible danger changes another character’s mind.
days.context: Goody and Mrs. Chippy Hackee are listening at the hole. Timmy and Chippy Hackee are inside, cracking nuts and singing. A fortnight is two weeks.
days.contentNote: A bear appears but does not attack. This is fantasy; animals do not use padlocks or umbrellas.

excerpt.locator: The Tale of Timmy Tiptoes, paragraphs 35–47 (end); begins “Down below there was a noise of cracking nuts and …” and ends “… sings--"Who's-been-digging-up _my_-nuts? Who's been digging-up _my_-nuts?" But nobody ever answers!”.

blocks.text: Down below there was a noise of cracking nuts and nibbling; and then the fat squirrel voice and the thin squirrel voice sang--

"For the diddlum day
Day diddle dum di!
Day diddle diddle dum day!"
Then Goody peeped in at the hole, and called down--"Timmy Tiptoes! Oh fie, Timmy Tiptoes!" And Timmy replied, "Is that you, Goody Tiptoes? Why, certainly!"
He came up and kissed Goody through the hole; but he was so fat that he could not get out.
Chippy Hackee was not too fat, but he did not want to come; he stayed down below and chuckled.
And so it went on for a fortnight; till a big wind blew off the top of the tree, and opened up the hole and let in the rain.
Then Timmy Tiptoes came out, and went home with an umbrella.
But Chippy Hackee continued to camp out for another week, although it was uncomfortable.
At last a large bear came walking through the wood. Perhaps he also was looking for nuts; he seemed to be sniffing around.
Chippy Hackee went home in a hurry!
And when Chippy Hackee got home, he found he had caught a cold in his head; and he was more uncomfortable still.
And now Timmy and Goody Tiptoes keep their nut-store fastened up with a little padlock.
And whenever that little bird sees the Chipmunks, he sings--"Who's-been-digging-up _my_-nuts? Who's been digging-up _my_-nuts?" But nobody ever answers!

questions.prompt: What changes the hole so Timmy can get out?
facilitatorNotes: A strong wind removes the top of the tree. Explain that the opening changes rather than Timmy suddenly shrinking.
evidence: a big wind blew off the top of the tree

questions.prompt: Why does Chippy finally hurry home?
facilitatorNotes: A large bear appears and sniffs nearby. The narrator only guesses what the bear wants, so do not claim it definitely seeks Chippy.
evidence: Perhaps he also was looking for nuts

questions.prompt: What do Timmy and Goody change about storing nuts afterward?
facilitatorNotes: They use a padlock. The fantasy solution shows that the experience changes their later plan.
evidence: keep their nut-store fastened up with a little padlock.

days.title: The peacock has a score of eyes
days.challenge: Notice familiar words that mean something different when attached to objects.
days.focus: Contradictions make a playful catalogue of double meanings.
days.context: A score means twenty. A cod’s “sound” is its swim bladder; dandelion “clocks” are seed heads; cat’s-cradle is a string game.

excerpt.locator: The peacock has a score of eyes; begins “The peacock has a score of eyes,”; ends “Nor foxglove fit the fox.”.

questions.prompt: Why can’t a peacock see with the “eyes” on its feathers?
facilitatorNotes: They are eye-shaped markings, not seeing organs.
evidence: With which he cannot see;

questions.prompt: What makes the cod’s “silent sound” a word joke?
facilitatorNotes: “Sound” names part of the fish rather than a noise. The adult should supply the unusual meaning.
evidence: The cod-fish has a silent sound,

questions.prompt: Which name at the end sounds as though it belongs to an animal but does not?
facilitatorNotes: Cat’s-cradle and foxglove both qualify. Explain a string figure or flower and let the child choose.
evidence: Nor foxglove fit the fox.

days.title: Bowl Away!
days.challenge: Connect action words with the speaker’s wish for a successful turn.
days.focus: Repeated calls make a rolling game sound quick and competitive.
days.context: This old game involves rolling a hoop and keeping it upright. Hear the quick beat of the cheering words; no equipment or picture is needed to discuss the encouragement.
days.contentNote: The historical game is hoop bowling. “Beat” means win, and “He is my man” is the speaker’s old-fashioned cheer, not a limit on who may play.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAGE 42”; opening “BOWL away! bowl away!”; ending “Beat, beat them all!”.

blocks.text:
BOWL away! bowl away!
Fast as you can;
He who can fastest bowl,
He is my man!

Up and down, round about,—
Don’t let it fall;
Ten times, or twenty times,
Beat, beat them all!

questions.prompt: Does the speaker want slow or fast movement?
facilitatorNotes: Fast: the word appears twice near the start. Read the opening with a quick but clear beat.
evidence: Fast as you can;

questions.prompt: What does the speaker want the player to avoid?
facilitatorNotes: Letting it fall. The historical illustration shows hoop bowling; explain rolling a hoop if the child needs the setting.
evidence: Don’t let it fall;

questions.prompt: What does “Beat, beat them all!” mean in this game?
facilitatorNotes: Win against the others, not hit people. The surrounding calls about speed and repeated turns support the game meaning.
evidence: Beat, beat them all!

days.title: Summer Sun
days.challenge: Trace light through several small openings and interpret a final comparison.
days.focus: The sun is imagined as an active visitor and gardener.
days.context: A parlour is a sitting room. The poem's sun has fingers and a face in make-believe.

excerpt.locator: Summer Sun; begins “GREAT is the sun, and wide he goes”; ends “The gardener of the World, he goes.”.

blocks.text:
GREAT is the sun, and wide he goes
Through empty heaven without repose;
And in the blue and glowing days
More thick than rain he showers his rays

Though closer still the blinds we pull
To keep the shady parlour cool,
Yet he will find a chink or two
To slip his golden fingers through.

The dusty attic spider-clad
He, through the keyhole, maketh glad;
And through the broken edge of tiles,
Into the laddered hayloft smiles.

Meantime his golden face around
He bares to all the garden ground,
And sheds a warm and glittering look
Among the ivy's inmost nook.

Above the hills, along the blue,
Round the bright air with footing true,
To please the child, to paint the rose,
The gardener of the World, he goes.

questions.prompt: Can closed blinds keep every sunbeam out of the room?
facilitatorNotes: No; the sun finds small chinks to enter.
evidence: Yet he will find a chink or two

questions.prompt: Name one other little opening that admits sunlight.
facilitatorNotes: A keyhole or broken edge of roof tiles lets the light in.
evidence: He, through the keyhole, maketh glad;

questions.prompt: Why might the poet call the sun a gardener?
facilitatorNotes: It warms and lights the growing world, including roses and ivy; “paint the rose” imagines its role in their beauty.
evidence: To please the child, to paint the rose,

days.title: I Saw a Ship That Sailed the Sea
days.challenge: Follow a shift in feeling without assuming the same ship returns.
days.focus: A farewell changes from sadness to expectation of a future arrival.
days.context: Some watchers stand on shore as a ship heads toward London. Listen for how the last two lines change the feeling of watching it leave.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAGE 47”; opening “I SAW a ship that sailed the sea,”; ending “Some other ship—some other day.”.

blocks.text:
I SAW a ship that sailed the sea,
It left me as the sun went down;
The white birds flew, and followed it
To town,—to London town.

Right sad were we to stand alone,
And see it pass so far away;
And yet we knew some ship would come—
Some other ship—some other day.

questions.prompt: What time of day is it when the ship leaves?
facilitatorNotes: Sunset: the sun goes down. The light helps establish the departure scene.
evidence: It left me as the sun went down;

questions.prompt: Who follows the ship toward London?
facilitatorNotes: White birds. The people remain behind and feel sad.
evidence: The white birds flew, and followed it

questions.prompt: Do the watchers expect this very ship to come back, or simply some other ship?
facilitatorNotes: The ending says some other ship on some other day. It offers hope without promising this exact ship’s return.
evidence: Some other ship—some other day.

days.title: The Ant-Hill, part 1: a busy heap
days.challenge: Compare what is seen at different times of day.
days.focus: Repeated visits show that a still heap is a busy home.
days.context: These are British wood ants, which build big mounds of leaves and sticks. A grain of barley is about the size of a small seed. A gamekeeper looked after birds on a country estate.
days.contentNote: The ants bite, and the children watch them pull apart a dead worm.

excerpt.locator: Book I, The Ant-Hill, printed pages 32–33, paragraphs 1–5; begins “There is a big ant-hill in the wood on the …” and ends “… shut up in silk bags, and they are called "cocoons."”.

blocks.text: There is a big ant-hill in the wood on the way to school. It is at the foot of the old oak tree, near the path, and is almost as tall as Peter. It looks like a loose heap of leaves, mixed with sticks and earth. It is broad at the bottom, and round at the top.

When we come home in the evening all is quiet on the ant-hill. We cannot see even one ant outside. It looks as if no one lived there. But when we pass in the morning, and the sun is warm and bright, we can see the ants creeping out of the cracks and running about the heap.

They are as big as a grain of barley, and have a tiny knob in the middle of their body. They have long feelers and strong jaws. They bite hard if you touch them. But they do not sting with their tails, as our house ants do.

At dinner-time we find them still more busy. They have opened many holes in the hill, and hurry to and fro. Some fetch bits of leaves and sticks, and add them to the heap. Others bring in food. One day Paul saw a number of ants pulling a dead worm to pieces. Then each ant carried a tiny bit in her jaws to the hill, and went in at a hole.

Sometimes the ants bring some little white lumps in their mouths out of the hill. Peggy's father, the gamekeeper, gives these white lumps to his birds to eat. He calls them ant-eggs. But Paul says they are not eggs. They are baby ants shut up in silk bags, and they are called "cocoons."

questions.prompt: How does the ant-hill look in the evening, and how is it different in the morning?
facilitatorNotes: In the evening it is quiet and seems empty; on a warm morning ants run all over it.
evidence: It looks as if no one lived there.

questions.prompt: What jobs do the ants do at dinner-time?
facilitatorNotes: They open holes, fetch bits of leaves and sticks, and bring in food, such as pieces of a worm.
evidence: Some fetch bits of leaves and sticks

questions.prompt: The gamekeeper calls the white lumps ant-eggs. Why does Paul disagree?
facilitatorNotes: Paul says they are baby ants shut up in silk bags, called cocoons. Two people can name the same thing differently; ask how Paul could check.
evidence: But Paul says they are not eggs.

days.title: The Ant-Hill, part 2: nurses and cocoons
days.challenge: Put the stages of an ant’s growth in order.
days.focus: The lesson explains how nursing ants raise the young and repair their home.
days.context: A grub is a young insect with no legs. A cocoon is a silk bag. Nursing ants are worker ants that care for the young.
days.contentNote: Paul pokes a hole in the ant-hill with a stick; the ants bite the children and carry their young away.

excerpt.locator: Book I, The Ant-Hill, printed pages 33–35, paragraphs 6–10 (end of lesson); begins “Real ant-eggs are much smaller. When the baby ant comes …” and ends “… ants. The ants without wings are the nurses and workers.”.

blocks.text: Real ant-eggs are much smaller. When the baby ant comes out of the egg it is blind and has no legs. It is called a grub. The nursing ants feed it with honey, and it puts a silk thread out of its mouth and spins a bag round itself.

When the bag is done, the nurses cannot feed the grub any more. So they take care of it. They carry it up to the sunshine by day, and down below at night. Inside the bag, the grub grows into a real ant, with eyes and legs. Then the nurses help it out of its prison, and it begins work.

One day Paul poked a hole in the ant-hill with his stick. We saw in the ground, under the leaves, a hollow place full of white cocoons. The ants were very angry. Some bit us, others picked up the cocoons in their jaws and ran away, for fear we should hurt their babies.
When we came back in the evening the ants had mended the hill. Every hole was closed, and all the cocoons were safe inside.
One day in summer we saw a number of ants with wings, flying over the ant-hill. Paul says these are the father and mother ants. The ants without wings are the nurses and workers.

questions.prompt: What do the nurses do with the cocoons by day and by night?
facilitatorNotes: They carry them up to the sunshine by day and down below at night.
evidence: They carry it up to the sunshine by day

questions.prompt: What do the ants do when Paul pokes the hill?
facilitatorNotes: They are angry, bite, and carry the cocoons away. Children may say whether poking the hill was kind.
evidence: for fear we should hurt their babies.

questions.prompt: What had the ants done by the evening?
facilitatorNotes: They had mended the hill, closed every hole, and kept the cocoons safe.
evidence: the ants had mended the hill.

days.title: A pin has a head
days.challenge: Interpret body-part words used for objects.
days.focus: A chain of riddling contrasts plays with ordinary vocabulary.
days.context: Read in small groups of lines. Explain unfamiliar terms such as a fly’s trunk, meaning its feeding tube, and ash keys, meaning winged fruits containing seeds.

excerpt.locator: A pin has a head; begins “A pin has a head, but has no hair;”; ends “And baby crows, without being a cock.”.

questions.prompt: Why can a needle have an eye and still not see?
facilitatorNotes: Its eye is the hole for thread, not a living eye.
evidence: Needles have eyes, but they cannot see;

questions.prompt: What do a watch’s hands lack that yours have?
facilitatorNotes: They have no thumbs or fingers because they are pointers on a clock face.
evidence: A watch has hands, but no thumb or finger

questions.prompt: Choose the boot, river, or saw: how does its familiar word have a second meaning?
facilitatorNotes: The boot’s tongue is a flap, a river runs by flowing, and a saw’s teeth are cutting points. Let the child explain one with adult support.
evidence: A saw has teeth, but it does not eat;

days.title: It Was Tommy Who Said
days.challenge: Use sight and sound details to understand a cheerful question.
days.focus: A springtime observer addresses a bird as a fellow happy creature.
days.context: Tommy notices spring and speaks to a lark high in the sky. Read his words cheerfully, leaving a pause after the question at the end.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAGE 49”; opening “IT was Tommy who said,”; ending “Is it you, sir, or I?””.

blocks.text:
IT was Tommy who said,
“The sweet spring-time is come;
I see the birds flit,
And I hear the bees hum.

“Oho! Mister Lark,
Up aloft in the sky,
Now, which is the happiest,—
Is it you, sir, or I?”

questions.prompt: What does Tommy see, and what does he hear?
facilitatorNotes: He sees birds flit and hears bees hum. Point to eyes and ears while rereading those lines.
evidence:
I see the birds flit,
And I hear the bees hum.

questions.prompt: Where is Mister Lark?
facilitatorNotes: Up in the sky. The polite Mister and sir make Tommy sound as if he is speaking to a neighbour.
evidence: Up aloft in the sky,

questions.prompt: Does the poem tell us whether Tommy or the lark is happier?
facilitatorNotes: No; it ends with Tommy’s question. Both can seem happy, but the poem does not award a winner.
evidence: Is it you, sir, or I?

days.title: Autumn Fires
days.challenge: Compare colors across a change of season.
days.focus: The poem finds brightness after summer flowers have ended.
days.context: The poem describes old-fashioned autumn bonfires. Read and picture the colors; no fire activity is involved.

excerpt.locator: Autumn Fires; begins “IN the other gardens”; ends “Fires in the fall!”.

blocks.text:
IN the other gardens
And all up the vale,
From the autumn bonfires
See the smoke trail!

Pleasant summer over
And all the summer flowers,
The red fire blazes,
The grey smoke towers.

Sing a song of seasons!
Something bright in all!
Flowers in the summer
Fires in the fall!

questions.prompt: What rises from the autumn gardens?
facilitatorNotes: Smoke trails from the bonfires.
evidence: See the smoke trail!

questions.prompt: What colors appear together in the second stanza?
facilitatorNotes: Red fire and grey smoke contrast.
evidence:
The red fire blazes,
The grey smoke towers.

questions.prompt: How does the ending answer the thought that pleasant summer is over?
facilitatorNotes: It finds something bright in fall too; flowers and fires belong to different seasons.
evidence: Something bright in all!

days.title: Little Miss Patty and Master Paul
days.challenge: Explain a fanciful comparison between moving bodies and speaking tongues.
days.focus: A child measures snail movement against the speed of conversation.
days.context: Two children find snails on a garden wall, and Paul makes an unusual comparison. Let the child imitate slow movement with fingers while listening to his quick words.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “PAGE 51”; opening “LITTLE Miss Patty and Master Paul”; ending “In a race with our tongues you’d be beaten to-day.””.

blocks.text:
LITTLE Miss Patty and Master Paul
Have found two snails on the garden wall.
“These snails,” said Paul, “how slow they walk!—
A great deal slower than we can talk.
Make haste, Mr. Snail, travel quicker, I pray;
In a race with our tongues you’d be beaten to-day.”

questions.prompt: What do Patty and Paul discover on the garden wall?
facilitatorNotes: Two snails. The poem names both children but only Paul speaks.
evidence: Have found two snails on the garden wall.

questions.prompt: What does Paul ask Mr. Snail to do?
facilitatorNotes: Travel quicker. He treats the snail as if it could understand a polite request.
evidence: Make haste, Mr. Snail, travel quicker, I pray;

questions.prompt: What unusual racers does Paul compare with the snails?
facilitatorNotes: Their tongues, meaning how quickly they talk. The joke compares speaking speed with walking speed; it is not a real race result.
evidence: In a race with our tongues you’d be beaten to-day.

days.title: The Old Woman and Her Pig, part 1: nobody will help
days.challenge: Join in a growing chain of requests and keep every link in order.
days.focus: Cumulative repetition makes each new refusal longer and funnier.
days.context: This old English tale grows by adding one more link each time. A stile is a set of steps for climbing over a fence; a sixpence was a small coin; to quench a fire is to put it out. The adult can pause and let the child supply the repeated part.
days.contentNote: In this nonsense chain the old woman asks a dog to bite, a stick to beat, fire to burn, a butcher to kill and a rope to hang; each one refuses until the cat agrees, and the chain ends with the pig hopping over the stile.

excerpt.locator: The Old Woman and Her Pig, 1922 edition pp. 252–253, paragraphs 1–8; begins “An old woman was sweeping her house, and she found …” and ends “… I shan't get home till midnight." But the butcher wouldn't.”.

blocks.text: An old woman was sweeping her house, and she found a little crooked sixpence. "What," said she, "shall I do with this little sixpence? I will go to market, and buy a little pig."
So she bought a little pig; but as she was coming home, she came to a stile, and the piggy would not go over the stile.
She went a little further, and she met a dog. So she said to him, "Dog! dog! bite pig; piggy won't go over the stile; and I shan't get home till midnight." But the dog wouldn't.
She went a little further, and she met a stick. So she said, "Stick! stick! beat dog; dog won't bite pig; piggy won't get over the stile; and I shan't get home till midnight." But the stick wouldn't.

She went a little further, and she met a fire. So she said, "Fire! fire! burn stick; stick won't beat dog; dog won't bite pig; pig won't get over the stile; and I shan't get home till midnight." But the fire wouldn't.

She went a little further, and she met some water. So she said, "Water! water! quench fire; fire won't burn stick; stick won't beat dog; dog won't bite pig; pig won't get over the stile; and I shan't get home till midnight." But the water wouldn't.

She went a little further, and she met an ox. So she said, "Ox! ox! drink water; water won't quench fire; fire won't burn stick; stick won't beat dog; dog won't bite pig; pig won't get over the stile; and I shan't get home till midnight." But the ox wouldn't.

She went a little further, and she met a butcher. So she said, "Butcher! butcher! kill ox; ox won't drink water; water won't quench fire; fire won't burn stick; stick won't beat dog; dog won't bite pig; pig won't get over the stile; and I shan't get home till midnight." But the butcher wouldn't.

questions.prompt: What does the old woman buy with the sixpence, and what stops her on the way home?
facilitatorNotes: A little pig, which will not go over the stile. Establish the problem before following the chain.
evidence: and the piggy would not go over the stile.

questions.prompt: What happens to her request each time she meets someone new?
facilitatorNotes: It grows by one link: the newcomer is asked to act on the one before, and the old chain is repeated. Invite the child to say the newest link and the list behind it.
evidence: Stick! stick! beat dog; dog won't bite pig;

questions.prompt: How does every meeting end so far? Do you think anyone will ever say yes?
facilitatorNotes: Each one ends with a short refusal. Predictions may differ; ask for a reason, such as the pattern or the need for a different kind of helper.
evidence: But the butcher wouldn't.

days.title: The Old Woman and Her Pig, part 2: the chain begins to move
days.challenge: Trace a chain of causes backward from the last event to the first.
days.focus: One small bargain sets the whole chain moving in a single long sentence.
days.context: The old woman has asked a dog, a stick, a fire, some water, an ox and a butcher for help, and each refused. Yonder means over there; hay is dried grass that cows eat. Read the final sentence steadily, one link at a time.
days.contentNote: In this nonsense chain the old woman asks a dog to bite, a stick to beat, fire to burn, a butcher to kill and a rope to hang; each one refuses until the cat agrees, and the chain ends with the pig hopping over the stile.

excerpt.locator: The Old Woman and Her Pig, 1922 edition pp. 253–255, paragraphs 9–14 (end); begins “She went a little further, and she met a rope. …” and ends “… stile; and so the old woman got home before midnight.”.

blocks.text: She went a little further, and she met a rope. So she said, "Rope! rope! hang butcher; butcher won't kill ox; ox won't drink water; water won't quench fire; fire won't burn stick; stick won't beat dog; dog won't bite pig; pig won't get over the stile; and I shan't get home till midnight." But the rope wouldn't.

She went a little further, and she met a rat. So she said, "Rat! rat! gnaw rope; rope won't hang butcher; butcher won't kill ox; ox won't drink water; water won't quench fire; fire won't burn stick; stick won't beat dog; dog won't bite pig; pig won't get over the stile; and I shan't get home till midnight." But the rat wouldn't.

She went a little further, and she met a cat. So she said, "Cat! cat! kill rat; rat won't gnaw rope; rope won't hang butcher; butcher won't kill ox; ox won't drink water; water won't quench fire; fire won't burn stick; stick won't beat dog; dog won't bite pig; pig won't get over the stile; and I shan't get home till midnight." But the cat said to her, "If you will go to yonder cow, and fetch me a saucer of milk, I will kill the rat." So away went the old woman to the cow.
But the cow said to her, "If you will go to yonder hay-stack, and fetch me a handful of hay, I'll give you the milk." So away went the old woman to the hay-stack; and she brought the hay to the cow.
As soon as the cow had eaten the hay, she gave the old woman the milk; and away she went with it in a saucer to the cat.

As soon as the cat had lapped up the milk, the cat began to kill the rat; the rat began to gnaw the rope; the rope began to hang the butcher; the butcher began to kill the ox; the ox began to drink the water; the water began to quench the fire; the fire began to burn the stick; the stick began to beat the dog; the dog began to bite the pig; the little pig squealed and jumped over the stile; and so the old woman got home before midnight.

questions.prompt: Who is the first one to make a bargain instead of refusing, and what does it want?
facilitatorNotes: The cat, who wants a saucer of milk. A bargain means doing something in return, which is different from simply refusing.
evidence: fetch me a saucer of milk

questions.prompt: Why must the old woman go to the hay-stack before she can get the milk?
facilitatorNotes: The cow wants hay first. Getting the milk takes two errands, so the chain gets one more step.
evidence: fetch me a handful of hay, I'll give you the milk.

questions.prompt: In the last sentence everything happens in a row. Why does the pig finally jump over the stile?
facilitatorNotes: The dog begins to bite it, after the cat, rat, rope, butcher, ox, water, fire and stick have each started in turn. Children may enjoy that a saucer of milk started it all.
evidence: the little pig squealed and jumped over the stile;

days.title: What are heavy?
days.challenge: Connect one concrete example with one feeling or idea.
days.focus: Four paired answers use everyday descriptions in literal and figurative ways.
days.context: Read one line at a time, then the whole poem. The child need not define every abstract idea; discuss a concrete example first.

excerpt.locator: What are heavy?; begins “What are heavy? sea-sand and sorrow:”; ends “What are deep? the ocean and truth.”.

blocks.text:
What are heavy? sea-sand and sorrow:
What are brief? to-day and to-morrow:
What are frail? Spring blossoms and youth
What are deep? the ocean and truth.

questions.prompt: Which heavy thing could you actually carry in a bucket?
facilitatorNotes: Sea-sand is physically heavy; sorrow is a feeling that can seem burdensome.
evidence: sea-sand and sorrow:

questions.prompt: What might make a spring blossom seem frail?
facilitatorNotes: A blossom is delicate and can be damaged easily. The pairing with youth invites a broader sense of vulnerability.
evidence: Spring blossoms and youth

questions.prompt: Does “deep truth” mean we can put a ruler into truth as into water?
facilitatorNotes: No; it suggests something important or difficult to understand fully. Accept a child’s tentative explanation after the adult models ocean depth.
evidence: the ocean and truth.

days.title: The Storm
days.challenge: Track a change in weather and in the mood of the speaker.
days.focus: Strong sound words make sudden weather feel alive before calm returns.
days.context: ‘Anon’ means soon. Read the storm sounds expressively, and listen for the line where the weather starts to change.
days.contentNote: Includes thunder, a rising flood and fear, followed by sunshine. Keep the reading expressive without startling sound effects.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “THE STORM.”; opening “SEE lightning is flashing,”; ending “But soon every cloud will be gone.”.

blocks.text:
SEE lightning is flashing,
The forest is crashing,
The rain will come dashing,
A flood will be rising anon;
The heavens are scowling,
The thunder is growling,
The loud winds are howling,
The storm has come suddenly on!
But now the sky clears,
The bright sun appears,
Now nobody fears,
But soon every cloud will be gone.

questions.prompt: What flashes at the beginning, and what growls later?
facilitatorNotes: Lightning flashes and thunder growls. The sound word makes thunder resemble a voice or animal.
evidence: The thunder is growling,

questions.prompt: Which line first tells us the frightening weather is changing?
facilitatorNotes: But now the sky clears. Pause there to hear the turn from storm to calm.
evidence: But now the sky clears,

questions.prompt: How do the people seem to feel after the sun appears?
facilitatorNotes: They no longer fear, according to the poem. This describes the poem’s scene; it does not mean every real storm ends so quickly.
evidence: Now nobody fears,

days.title: Fairy Bread
days.challenge: Interpret an invitation to an impossible meal.
days.focus: Smell, shade, and storytelling turn an outdoor resting place into fairy hospitality.
days.context: Broom is a flowering shrub here, not a cleaning brush. The meal belongs to imagination.

excerpt.locator: Fairy Bread; begins “COME up here, O dusty feet!”; ends “Fairy stories hear and tell.”.

blocks.text:
COME up here, O dusty feet!
Here is fairy bread to eat.
Here in my retiring room,
Children, you may dine
On the golden smell of broom
And the shade of pine;
And when you have eaten well,
Fairy stories hear and tell.

questions.prompt: What clues suggest the invited children have been walking or playing?
facilitatorNotes: Their feet are dusty and they are invited to come rest or dine.
evidence: COME up here, O dusty feet!

questions.prompt: Can someone really eat the smell of a flower or the shade of a tree?
facilitatorNotes: No; the imaginary meal offers pleasant sensations as if they were food.
evidence: On the golden smell of broom

questions.prompt: What will the guests do after the fairy meal?
facilitatorNotes: They will both listen to and tell fairy stories, sharing the storyteller's role.
evidence: Fairy stories hear and tell.

days.title: Trees
days.challenge: Listen for specific differences rather than treating all trees as alike.
days.focus: An ordered list gives each tree a distinguishing shape, movement or use.
days.context: Eight kinds of trees appear in a short list. A glade is an open place in woodland, and timber is wood used for building. The adult can reread pairs of lines for comparison.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “TREES.”; opening “THE Oak is called the king of trees,”; ending “The Beech amid the Forest lives.”.

blocks.text:
THE Oak is called the king of trees,
The Aspen quivers in the breeze,
The Poplar grows up straight and tall,
The Peach-tree spreads along the wall,
The Sycamore gives pleasant shade,
The Willow droops in watery glade,
The Fir-tree useful timber gives,
The Beech amid the Forest lives.

questions.prompt: Which tree quivers in a breeze?
facilitatorNotes: The Aspen. Quivers means trembles; a small hand flutter can represent the movement.
evidence: The Aspen quivers in the breeze,

questions.prompt: How do the Poplar and Willow seem to hold themselves differently?
facilitatorNotes: The Poplar is straight and tall; the Willow droops. Demonstrate upright and hanging shapes without claiming all trees always look identical.
evidence: The Willow droops in watery glade,

questions.prompt: Which tree offers pleasant shade, and which offers useful timber?
facilitatorNotes: Sycamore gives shade and Fir-tree gives timber, or wood. These are the uses this poem chooses to name.
evidence: The Sycamore gives pleasant shade,

days.title: The Mole and His Home, part 1: a body made for digging
days.challenge: Connect each body part to the work it does.
days.focus: A careful description shows how the mole’s nose, paws and fur suit life underground.
days.context: A mole is a small animal that lives underground. Farmers sent for mole-catchers because mole-hills spoil fields. “Wunt” is a country name for a mole. He-moles and she-moles are males and females.
days.contentNote: The mole-catcher traps moles and brings in many dead ones.

excerpt.locator: Book I, The Mole and His Home, printed pages 46–47, paragraphs 1–5; begins “There were so many moles in the barn field last …” and ends “… for slugs and snails. There are more he-moles than she-moles.”.

blocks.text: There were so many moles in the barn field last summer. We used to see mole heaps thrown up all over the field. At last Paul's father sent for the mole-catcher. He put traps in the runs and brought in many dead moles.

A mole is a curious creature. We country children call him a "wunt." He has a long, plump body and a short, stumpy tail. His dark brown fur is like velvet, it is so soft and close. He has a long, pointed snout, very hard at the tip, and his mouth is full of strong, sharp teeth.

His feet are very curious. They have no fur on them, but are naked and pink. His front paws are like broad flat hands with very strong claws. They turn away from his body, and look too big for such a small, soft creature.

Paul says these paws are the mole's shovels. He lives under the ground and catches worms to eat. As he goes along he makes a hole with his hard nose, and then shovels away the earth with his strong hands. In this way he makes a tunnel, and when he wants to get rid of the loose earth he pokes it above ground with his snout. This is how the mole-hills are made.

But the moles do not always stay under the ground. We have seen them sometimes on a warm summer's evening poking about in the hedges, looking for slugs and snails. There are more he-moles than she-moles.

questions.prompt: Why did Paul’s father send for the mole-catcher?
facilitatorNotes: Mole heaps were thrown up all over the barn field.
evidence: We used to see mole heaps thrown up all over the field.

questions.prompt: Why does Paul call the mole’s front paws shovels?
facilitatorNotes: They are broad and flat with strong claws, and the mole shovels earth away with them.
evidence: these paws are the mole's shovels.

questions.prompt: How is a mole-hill made?
facilitatorNotes: The mole digs a tunnel with its hard nose and paws, then pushes the loose earth up with its snout.
evidence: he pokes it above ground with his snout.

days.title: The Mole and His Home, part 2: the hidden nest
days.challenge: Use a clue about safety to predict where a home will be.
days.focus: The mole-catcher’s knowledge leads the children to a hidden nest, which they leave safe.
days.context: The children have learned how moles dig. A mound is a small hill; runs are tunnels. The children open a nest only because a visitor asked the mole-catcher to show it.
days.contentNote: The narrator says a father mole may die of cold in frosty weather.

excerpt.locator: Book I, The Mole and His Home, printed pages 47–48, paragraphs 6–11 (end of lesson); begins “We wanted so much to find a mole's home. We …” and ends “… of cold. He only takes a wife in the spring.”.

blocks.text: We wanted so much to find a mole's home. We dug down below some of the mole-hills hoping to find one, but we only found a tunnel. The mole-catcher laughed at us for digging there. He asked us if we thought that the mole would put a heap of loose earth over his home, to tell his enemies where to find him.
At last, one day a gentleman came to Paul's father and asked him to open a mole's home for him. He wanted to see what it was like. This was just what we wanted, so we went too.
The mole-catcher took us some way across the field. At the corner near the wood we came to a large mound, under the trees, covered with grass.

Then he began to dig away the side of the mound. By-and-bye, about the middle, he stopped and cleared away the earth very carefully with his hands. And there, just below the ground, was a big round hole covered with a roof of very hard earth. He had taken away the side, and we could see in. The hole was lined with dry grass, and in it lay four tiny moles. We filled it in again very carefully and left the baby moles safe and quiet.

We saw four holes in the sides of the nest. These led to the runs through which the old moles went in and out to feed. We are afraid they got rather filled with earth from our digging, but the mole-catcher said that they would soon be put right by the old moles.

He says that the father mole lives in another home like this all alone in the winter, feeding on worms. Sometimes he comes up above the ground, and if it is very frosty weather he dies of cold. He only takes a wife in the spring.

questions.prompt: Why does the mole-catcher laugh at the children for digging under a mole-hill?
facilitatorNotes: A mole would not put a heap of loose earth over its home to show its enemies where it lives.
evidence: to tell his enemies where to find him.

questions.prompt: What did they find inside the big mound?
facilitatorNotes: A round hole lined with dry grass, holding four tiny moles.
evidence: in it lay four tiny moles.

questions.prompt: What did the children do after looking, and why might that matter?
facilitatorNotes: They filled the nest in carefully and left the baby moles safe; they worry about the runs, and the mole-catcher says the old moles will mend them.
evidence: left the baby moles safe and quiet.

days.title: Lift up your face, little daisy
days.challenge: Infer an unstated gift from the speaker's request.
days.focus: A child passes along affection while leaving a flower growing.
days.context: Jamie is ill and has sent a messenger to the daisy. Read the last line again before guessing the gift.

excerpt.locator: Lift up your face, little daisy; begins “LIFT up your face, little daisy, pray;”; ends “So hold up your cheek, little daisy, do.”.

questions.prompt: Why has Jamie sent someone else to the daisy?
facilitatorNotes: Jamie is sick, so another speaker delivers the message.
evidence: Jamie sent me, and Jamie is sick.

questions.prompt: Why will this visitor leave the flower unpicked?
facilitatorNotes: Jamie says the daisy is too sweet to pick.
evidence: He says you are far too sweet to pick,

questions.prompt: What might Jamie's gift be, if the daisy must hold up its cheek?
facilitatorNotes: A kiss is a strong inference, though the poem never names the gift; acknowledge another suggestion that fits the cheek detail.
evidence: So hold up your cheek, little daisy, do.

days.title: Fruit
days.challenge: Compare what fruit looks and feels like using precise descriptive words.
days.focus: Colour and texture make four fruits inviting to imagine.
days.context: Four fruits receive different colors, textures, and uses. ‘Amber’ means golden yellow or orange here; the descriptions belong to the varieties pictured by this historical speaker.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “FRUIT.”; opening “THE Nectarine on yonder wall”; ending “Are equally inviting.”.

blocks.text:
THE Nectarine on yonder wall
Grows red, when ripen’d fully;
The ruddy Peach, admired by all,
Is somewhat rough and woolly.
The Apricot, of amber hue,
In tarts the taste delighting;
And purple Plum, so fair to view,
Are equally inviting.

questions.prompt: What happens to the Nectarine’s colour when it ripens?
facilitatorNotes: It grows red. The line describes this nectarine; different fruit varieties may look different.
evidence: Grows red, when ripen’d fully;

questions.prompt: Which fruit is called rough and woolly?
facilitatorNotes: The Peach. Woolly evokes its fuzzy skin rather than saying it is made from sheep’s wool.
evidence: Is somewhat rough and woolly.

questions.prompt: What colours are given to the Apricot and Plum?
facilitatorNotes: Amber for Apricot and purple for Plum. Explain amber as golden yellow or orange, and invite a colour gesture or spoken comparison.
evidence: And purple Plum, so fair to view,

days.title: The Prune
days.challenge: Follow the contrast between a fresh fruit and its dried form.
days.focus: An ordinary snack opens a small inquiry into how foods change.
days.context: An adult pauses before giving Herbert a snack and invites him to learn about it. Listen closely to the difference between something once being a plum and something being like a pear.

excerpt.locator: Complete poem “THE PRUNE.”; opening “TO give you this savoury Prune”; ending “And find out what things really are.”.

blocks.text:
TO give you this savoury Prune
I’m sure was a very good turn;
My Herbert will eat it up soon—
But first he has something to learn.

This dry wrinkled thing that you see
Has once been a soft swelling plum;
It grew, like our plums, on a tree,
And from a great distance has come.

The figs that are sold in the shop
Were once like the firm shapely pear;
It always is better to stop,
And find out what things really are.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker want Herbert to do before eating?
facilitatorNotes: Learn something about the prune. The pause turns an everyday snack into an observation.
evidence: But first he has something to learn.

questions.prompt: What was the dry, wrinkled prune before it dried?
facilitatorNotes: A soft, swelling plum that grew on a tree. Compare the two textures without requiring tasting.
evidence: Has once been a soft swelling plum;

questions.prompt: Does the final verse say that figs were once pears?
facilitatorNotes: No; they were like the firm, shapely pear. Like makes a comparison of shape or firmness, not a claim that one kind of fruit changes into another.
evidence: Were once like the firm shapely pear;

days.title: To Any Reader
days.challenge: Understand the book as a window into a childhood that has passed.
days.focus: The closing poem invites closeness to an imagined child while explaining the limits of that meeting.
days.context: This poem speaks directly to anyone reading or hearing the book. The adult can compare looking through a window with listening to a poem.

excerpt.locator: To Any Reader; begins “AS from the house your mother sees”; ends “That lingers in the garden there.”.

blocks.text:
AS from the house your mother sees
You playing round the garden trees,
So you may see, if you will look
Through the windows of this book,
Another child, far, far away,
And in another garden, play.
But do not think you can at all,
By knocking on the window, call
That child to hear you. He intent
Is all on his play-business bent.
He does not hear; he will not look,
Nor yet be lured out of this book.
For, long ago, the truth to say,
He has grown up and gone away,
And it is but a child of air
That lingers in the garden there.
